APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE IN THE LIGHT OF THE INGREDIENTS OF SECTION 138 OF THE NI ACT AND THE DEFENCE RAISED BY THE ACCUSED 9. It is not disputed by the accused that the Cheque's in Question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 are drawn on the account maintained by her. Signature's on the cheque's in question has also not been disputed by the accused. Further the presentation, dishonor of the Cheque's in question and the cheque returning memo has also not been challenged by the accused. Therefore in view of the evidence on record it stands proved that the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 were signed by the accused and the same were drawn on account maintained by her. Further it also stands duly proved that the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 were dishonored vide cheque returning memo Ex. Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 5/11 CW1/3 dated 20.03.2013 both with the reason "Account Closed" 10. From the perusal of the entire evidence it has come to fore that two fold defence has been taken by the accused. Firstly, that she has not been served with the legal demand notice by the complainant. And secondly that the blank signed cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 has been issued by her to the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal as a security when she stood as a guarantor for Sandhu Vikas Sahu who took loan from the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal and not in discharge of her loan liability as alleged by the complainant. 11

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: security when she stood as a guarantor for Sandhu Vikas Sahu who took loan from the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal and not in discharge of her loan liability as alleged by the complainant. 11. Coming to the first line of defence taken by the accused that she has not been served with the legal demand notice from the complainant, it is pertinent to note that the complainant Smt. Pushpa who has examined herself as CW­1 has specifically stated in her evidence affidavit Ex. CW1/A that she got issued the legal notice of demand dated 03.04.2013 to the accused which is Ex. CW1/4 and it was sent to the accused by speed post and courier on 05.04.2013 and 08.04.2013 respectively, receipts of which are Ex. CW1/6 & Ex. CW1/5 respectively. The complainant has also tendered the speed post tracking report as Ex. CW1/7. 12. The accused has denied the receipt of legal demand notice both at the time of framing of Notice U/s 251 of the Code and also in his state­ ment U/s 313 of the Code. I have perused the legal notice of demand. It bears the correct address of the accused and the speed post receipt Ex. CW1/5 issued by the postal authorities in ordinary course is also on record. Further Section 114 Illustration (f ) of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 also raises a rebuttable presumption in favour of the complainant that common course of business has been followed in a particular case, that is to say, when a letter is sent by post by prepaying and properly addressing it, the same is presumed to have been received by the addressee. Further­ more the speed post tracking report Ex. CW1/7 is also on record by the Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 6/11 complainant which shows the status as 'delivered' and the same has not been disputed by the accused in evidence

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: also on record by the Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 6/11 complainant which shows the status as 'delivered' and the same has not been disputed by the accused in evidence. Except denial no evidence has been lead by the complainant to corroborate her stand. Therefore, mere denial on the part of the accused at the time of framing of Notice U/s 251of the Code and also in her statement U/s 313 of the Code would not be sufficient to dislodge the burden of presumption casted upon her by Section 114 Illustration (f ) of Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Moreover, sum­ mons was served upon the accused at the address mentioned in the com­ pliant and the accused has put his appearance in compliance thereof. 13. In C.C. Alavi Hazi Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr. (2007) 6 Supreme Court case 555, it was held that the course open to the drawer where he claims not to have received the notice sent by post but has received copy of the complaint with the summons is that he can within a 15 days of the receipt of summons make payment of the cheque amount and he then cannot contend that there was no proper service of notice. 14. Therefore, considering the evidence on record I find that the accused has not brought any credible evidence to rebut the presumptions provided in Section 114, Illustration (f ) of the Evidence Act, 1872 and further looking at the mandate given by the H'onble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Hazi Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr (Supra), I hold that the legal notice of demand Ex. CW1/4 was duly served upon the accused. 15. Now coming to the second line of defence which has been taken by the accused that she has issued the blank signed cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: Ex. CW1/4 was duly served upon the accused. 15. Now coming to the second line of defence which has been taken by the accused that she has issued the blank signed cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 to the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal as a security when she stood as a guarantor for Sandhu Vikas Sahu who took loan from the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal and not in discharge of her loan liability as alleged by the complainant. 16. Before I advert to the second line of the defence taken by the accused it is imperative for me to go through the provisions of Sections Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 7/11 118(a) and 139 of the Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. --Until the contrary is proved, the following pre­ sumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable instru­ ment was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been ac­ cepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the na­ ture referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." 17. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janard­ han Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the ac­ cused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of 'preponder­ ance of probabilities'. 18

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: 4 SCC 54, has held that the ac­ cused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of 'preponder­ ance of probabilities'. 18. In Rangappa Versus Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the com­ plainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not even adduce evidence of his/her own. 19. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judgments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promis­ sory note is admitted, the presumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttable in nature. The accused can prove the non­ existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 8/11 discharges the initial onus of proof by showing that the existence of con­ sideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a mat­ ter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a mat­ ter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by ref­ erence to the circumstances upon which he relies. In case, where the ac­ cused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­exis­ tence of the consideration, the complainant would invariably be held en­ titled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Sec­ tion 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 20. Now coming back to the case in hand, in the instant case the complainant has examined herself as CW­1 and stated that the accused is known to her and the accused has approached her for grant of the loan, and accordingly a loan of Rs 1,20,000/­ was granted to the accused by the complainant and in order to discharge the loan liability the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 has been issued by the accused. The complainant in support of her claim has also examined one Mahender Singh as CW­2. CW­2 Mahender Singh in his evidence supported the stand of the complainant and stated that the entire loan transaction between the complainant and the accused has taken place in his presence. CW­2 also stated that he has also given Rs. 15,000/­ to the complainant at her request as she needed the same for advancing the loan to the accused. The accused has examined herself as DW­1 and denied the allegation of the complainant and stated that the blank signed cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: same for advancing the loan to the accused. The accused has examined herself as DW­1 and denied the allegation of the complainant and stated that the blank signed cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 has been issued by her to the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal as a security when she stood as a guarantor for Sandhu Vikas Sahu who took loan from the husband of the complainant Parveen Pal and not in discharge of her outstanding loan liability as alleged by the complainant. Perusal of the entire evidence reveals that except denials and suggestion the accused has not lead any cogent evidence to corroborate her stand and dent the stand of the Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 9/11 complainant. Further it is also surprising to see that the accused has not even examined the said Sandhu Vikas Sahu in her defence for whom she has purportedly issued the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 to the husband of the complainant. It is trite to say that mere denial on the part of the accused and putting suggestions to the complainant's witness and giving explanations without leading any defence to corroborate her stand would not absolve her from any liability. It was for the accused to prove the circumstances under which the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 were issued by her by leading cogent evidence so as to discharge and rebut the presumption raised against her by the Statute U/s 139 and 118 (a) of the NI Act and mere simplicitor denying the allegations would not be at her advantage. The accused has not brought any material on record and also no cogent explanations or any probable defence which would rebut the shadow of presumption existing in favour of the Complainant

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: advantage. The accused has not brought any material on record and also no cogent explanations or any probable defence which would rebut the shadow of presumption existing in favour of the Complainant. Therefore, this court do not find any force in the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the accused that she has succeeded in rebutting the presumption under Section 139 of the Act. 21. From the materials brought on record and evidence lead by the complainant it is sufficient to hold that the accused has taken loan from the complainant and has issued the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 in discharge of her liability. 22. Now coming to the issue that except signatures other particulars in the cheque's in question Ex. CW1/1 & Ex. CW1/2 has not been filled by the accused, for this defence also except arguments, denials and sugges­ tions accused has not brought any evidence on record to support her stand i.e. except signatures she has not filled the other particulars in the cheque's in question. Furthermore even believing the stand of accused to be correct, still there is also no evidence on record to show that she has not even authorized the complainant to fill the said particulars. More so it is trite to say that by putting the name and date there is no material Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa Versus Smt. Bandana Jha Page 10/11 alteration on the cheque U/s 87 of the NI Act as there is no rule of banking business that the name of the payee as well as the amount should be written by the drawer himself, as no law provides that in case of cheque the entire body has to be written by the drawer only

title: Case No. : 4339/14 Smt Pushpa vs Smt. Bandana Jha Page 1/11 on 3 May, 2014
content: business that the name of the payee as well as the amount should be written by the drawer himself, as no law provides that in case of cheque the entire body has to be written by the drawer only. Therefore, once the signature on the cheque in question is admitted as has hap­ pened in the case in hand the plea that particulars in the cheque in ques­ tion has not been filled by the drawer is of no consequence unless some cogent evidence has been lead by the accused that he/she has not ex­ pressly or impliedly authorized the payee to fill the particulars therein. (See Ravi Chopra Vs. State and Another, 2008(2) JCC (NI) 169, Delhi, Jaipal Singh Rana Vs. Swaraj Pal 149 (2008) DLT 682,) Therefore, this defence of the accused also holds no ground. 23. Considering the evidence on record, It stands duly proved that the accused has miserably failed to rebut the presumptions U/s 118 (a) and section 139 of the NI Act. Furthermore, accused has also failed to prove that she has made payment to the complainant within 15 days from the receipt of the legal demand notice. 24. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I hereby hold that the complainant has proved and substantiated its allegation against the accused and all the ingredients of Section 138 of NI Act also stands proved against the accused. Accordingly, Smt. Bandana Jha W/o Sh. Mihir Kumar Jha is hereby convicted of the offence u/s 138 NI Act. This judgment contains 11 pages. The brief facts of the present complaint filed U/s. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "NI Act") are that the complainant Ms. Meenu's husband had friendship with the accused. The accused is stated to have been in the business of construction of flats and also CC No. 16/11 Meenu Vs Shaheen Akhtar Page 1 of 12 running a jewellary shop in the name of M/s Madeena Jewellarers. 2. It is stated that in the month of January, 2006 the accused approached the complainant with proposal for investment in property business run by him which would earn huge profits and represented that if the complainant invests Rs. 10 lacs for a period of 21 months, then she would be able to earn Rs. 8 lacs over and above Rs. 10 lacs. Upon such inducement, the complainant is stated to have given Rs. 9,20,000/­ to the accused upon assurance of the accused that she will get Rs. 8 lacs over and above the principal amount. 3

title: Meenu vs Shaheen Akhtar Page 1 Of 12 on 10 February, 2014

As far as the contention of the accused that the complaint is not maintainable in respect of cheque no. 801133, Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act states that the complaint can be filed either by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque. 13. In Chandra Babu Vs Ramani II (2004) BC 152 (DB), the Kerala High Court has after drawing reference to Sections 7, 9, 53, 75, 78 and other case laws on the entitlement of a legal representative to initiate legal action against the drawer held that the legal representative of the payee can file a complaint under Section 138 NI Act and observed: "Apart from the above, in this case, complainant holds the cheque after the death of the payee as a legal heir and she is entitled to possess the same in her own name and in view of Section 53, being a legal heir, she is a holder in due course and he can get a full discharge. The party was CC No. 16/11 Meenu Vs Shaheen Akhtar Page 5 of 12 free to pay the amount to her and to get back the cheque. In view of Section 53 of the Act, legal heir of the payee or holder in due course can maintain a complaint under Section 138 of the Act". (emphasis added) 14. In Smt. Bhagava Vs Shri Kadaisiddeshwara Trading ILR 2004 KAR 367, it was observed that: "12. In the case on hand, the payee had died and the wife of the payee, as the legal heir, had presented the cheque in question and on the cheque being dishonoured, legal notice had also been issued and thereafter, the proceedings had been initiated under Section 138 of the NI Act." To that extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra) may not be correct. content: Bhat (supra) may not be correct. However, this does not in any way cast doubt on the correctness of the decision in that case since it was based on the specific facts and circumstances therein. As noted in the citations, this is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. However, there can be no doubt that there is an initial presumption which favours the complainant. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of CC No. 16/11 Meenu Vs Shaheen Akhtar Page 7 of 12 the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions. In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden

content: cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of 'preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. A distinction has to be drawn between a cheque issued as security and a cheque issued towards discharge of a liability to pay notwithstanding that the money is by way of security for due performance of the contract. A cheque given as security is not to be encased in presenti. It becomes enforceable if an obligation in future is not enforced. It is not tendered in discharge of a liability which has accrued. 32. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act reads as: "Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account:Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in while or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No

content: for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 4/10 nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation:For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 8. Now I am dealing with each of the ingredients of section 138 of the NI Act in light of the defence raised by the accused. 9. In the instant case, it is not disputed by the accused that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/A is drawn on the account maintained by her. Further the signature on the cheque in question Ex. CW1/A is also not disputed by the accused. The presentation and dishonor of the cheque in question is also not disputed by the accused. Further the accused has also not disputed the receipt of the legal demand notice Ex CW1/C. In fact the accused has herself admitted during her statement recorded under section 313 of the Code that she has received the legal demand notice Ex CW1/C

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: of the legal demand notice Ex CW1/C. In fact the accused has herself admitted during her statement recorded under section 313 of the Code that she has received the legal demand notice Ex CW1/C. Therefore, In view of the evidence on record it stands proved that the cheque in question Ex CW1/A was signed by the accused and the same was drawn on account maintained by her. It also stands proved that the cheque in question was presented within the period of its vailidity and the same was dishonored vide cheque returning Memo Ex. CW1/B with remarks "Account Closed". And further it also stands proved that the legal demand notice Ex CW1/C has been served upon the accused. 10. Perusal of the entire evidence reveals that the only defence taken by the accused in the present complaint case is that she has not taken any loan from the complainant and that she has taken loan from one Rajesh Kumar with Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 5/10 whom she has already settled the matter and the blank signed Cheque in question Ex CW1/A was given by her to Rajesh Kumar as security and the same has been misused by the complainant. 11. It is trite to say that the crux of penal liability under Section 138 of the Act is that the Cheque in question must be issued for the discharge of any legal debt or liability. Existing of legal debt or liability is sine qua non for constituting the offence. Before proceeding further it is imperative for me to take notice of the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act which read as under: "118

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: is sine qua non for constituting the offence. Before proceeding further it is imperative for me to take notice of the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments.--Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 12. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probabale defence on the strength of preponderance of probabilites. 13. In RANGAPPA Versus SRI MOHAN AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of 'preponderance of probabilities'. The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence. 14. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judgments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: From the reading of the above said provisions and the judgments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 6/10 is admitted, the presumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such presumptions are rebuttable. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused discharges the initial onus of proof by showing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­ existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he/she relies. In case, where the accused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the complainant would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 15. Now coming to case in hand it is the case of the complainant that he has granted loan to the accused on the same date in the year 2008 when the accused had come to his house along with her brother in law (Jija)

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: to case in hand it is the case of the complainant that he has granted loan to the accused on the same date in the year 2008 when the accused had come to his house along with her brother in law (Jija). The complainant examined himself as CW­1 and during his cross examination it was revealed that for making payment to the accused the complainant has borrowed money from his friend Mukesh Kumar (DW­4) and the accused has also handed over the cheque in question Ex CW1/A to the complainant for payment to the complainant. 16. To rebut the shadow of presumption casted upon the accused by Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act, the accused has examined herself as DW­1 and reiterated that she has not taken any loan from the complainant Madan Lal and further stated that she has taken a loan from one Rajesh Kumar which has already been repaid by her during settlement in court proceedings which were pending at Rohini Courts. Interestingly, DW­1 during her cross examination was confronted with the documents Ex. DW­1/P, on which the signatures has been admitted by the accused however accused also stated Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 7/10 that the contents of the same has not been written by her and further stated that she has given blank signed papers to Rajesh Kumar who has misused the same. Looking at the content of the document Ex. DW1/P it is revealed that the same is an acknowledgment given by the accused stating that she owes an amount of Rs. 5,00,000/­ to the complainant and she would be repaying the same by 15th of April, 2009. Further during cross examination of DW­1 (accused) it is also revealed that a document Ex

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: an amount of Rs. 5,00,000/­ to the complainant and she would be repaying the same by 15th of April, 2009. Further during cross examination of DW­1 (accused) it is also revealed that a document Ex. CW1/G dated 23.10.2009 was also written by the accused which also reiterates the admission of the accused that she has taken loan from the complainant and she needs one month time for making the payment. During further cross examination of DW­1 (accused) it was revealed that the said document Ex. CW1/G is also in the hand writing of the accused as the same was admitted by the accused. Even believing the accused that the acknowledgment letter Ex. DW1/P is not written by her and the same bears only her signatures, even then there is no explanation from the accused as to why the letter Ex. CW1/G dated 23.10.2009 admittedly bearing her handwriting and signature acknowledging her liability towards the complainant has been written by the accused, as there is no occasion for her to write the letters CW1/G. The admissions of the accused through her letter CW1/G itself established that she has taken loan from the complainant. The aforesaid letter Ex CW1/G written by the accused also dents the evidence given by DW­3 (brother in law of the accused) who stated that he had never accompanied the accused to the complainant's house for taking any loan for the accused. Therefore testimony of DW­3 cannot be relied upon in light of surrounding contrary facts and evidence on record which supports the claim of the complainant that accused has taken loan from the complainant and further DW­3 is also an interested witness being the relative of the accused herein. 17. The accused has also produced Rajesh Kumar as DW­2 and he denied that he has taken any document from the accused

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: DW­3 is also an interested witness being the relative of the accused herein. 17. The accused has also produced Rajesh Kumar as DW­2 and he denied that he has taken any document from the accused. However, it is admitted by the witness that he has settled a case with the accused herein in Rohini Courts. It is the defence of the accused that she has taken loan from Rajesh Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 8/10 Kumar (DW­2) and she has given the signed cheque in question Ex. CW1/A to him. Evidence reveals that the matter pending between Rajesh Kumar and the accused was settled between the accused herein and Rajesh Kumar in the year 2011 whereas the present proceedings relates to the year 2008. Further on perusal of the certified copies of the judicial proceeding placed on by the accused herself i.e DW1/A (Colly) showing settlement between accused and the DW­2 it is surprising to see that the same does not find any mention of the present proceedings. It is highly inconceivable that a honest debtor returning all the money to its creditor would not make a reference of all the pending proceedings between him and the creditor. Further the acknowledgement CW1/G written by the accused shows that she has also taken loan from the complainant and the present proceedings is qua a different transaction which took place between him and the complainant. Altogether the testimony of DW­2 has not at all supported the stand of the accused. 18. Further the accused also produced one Mahesh Kumar as DW­4

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: which took place between him and the complainant. Altogether the testimony of DW­2 has not at all supported the stand of the accused. 18. Further the accused also produced one Mahesh Kumar as DW­4. However, the said Mahesh Kumar stated that he and the complainant used to have financial dealing/transactions with each other and the complainant Madan Lal has taken loan from him in the year, 2008 which supports the claim of the complainant only that he given loan to the accused after borrowing from his friend Mahesh Kumar DW­4. 19. The entire evidence favours and supports the stand of the complainant. Accordingly, I hold that the accused has taken loan from the complainant and has issued the cheque in question to the complainant in discharge of her liability. Further it is also trite to say that once the signature on the cheque in question is admitted by the accused, as has happened in this case, the defence of the accused that the particulars in the cheque in question has not been filled by the accused also do not holds any ground. 20. It is settled that mere denial and putting suggestions to the witnesses would not absolve the accused from any liability. It was for the accused to Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal Versus Kavita Pawa Page No. 9/10 prove by leading cogent evidence how and in what manner the cheque in question has come in possession of the complainant. The accused has miserably failed to lead any evidence in this regard and inturn the presumptions U/s 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act raised against her by the statute stands unrebutted. Further from the evidence on record it also stands proved that the accused has failed to pay the cheque amount within 15 days from the receipt of legal demand notice

title: Case No. : 2849/12 Madan Lal vs Kavita Pawa Page No. 1/10 on 15 March, 2014
content: by the statute stands unrebutted. Further from the evidence on record it also stands proved that the accused has failed to pay the cheque amount within 15 days from the receipt of legal demand notice. Accordingly, I hold that complainant has proved all the ingredients of the offence U/s 138 of NI Act against the accused. Accordingly, accused Kavita Pawa D/o Sh. Baldev Raj Pawa, is hereby convicted of the offence U/s 138 of NI Act. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost. Versus 1. M/s Sachit Creations (P) Ltd, 2. Sh. Sachit Chawla, Director of M/s Sachit Creations (P) Ltd, WZ­165/A, First Floor, Opp. Pusa Institute, Village Dasghara, Delhi ......... Accused. COMPLAINT U/s 138 OF THE NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT Offence complained of : U/s 138 N.I. Act Date of commission of offence : 06.01.2013 Plea of Accused : Not guilty Complaint filed on : 05.02.2013 Final Arguments heard & Concluded on : 19.03.2014 Date of decision of the case : 28.03.2014 Final order : Conviction CC No. 308/13 page no. 1 /15 BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE 1. By way of the present judgment, this court shall decide the complaint case U/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1881 (as amended up to date) filed by the complainant M/s Tripti Enterprises, through its sole proprietor, Sh. Ajay Sood, against the accused M/s Sachit Creations (P) Ltd and its director Sh. Sachit Chawla. 2. The prosecution story in brief necessary for the disposal of the present case is that, the complainant is a Sole Proprietorship firm engaged in the business of manufacturing and supplying of hosiery knitted fabrics and the accused had approached the complainant for purchase of 2 x 1 RB Lycra, Micro Approx 450 Kg on credit basis and in pursuant to the order of the accused, the complainant supplied the said goods to the accused on credit basis. Hence, the accused had purchased goods worth Rs

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: Approx 450 Kg on credit basis and in pursuant to the order of the accused, the complainant supplied the said goods to the accused on credit basis. Hence, the accused had purchased goods worth Rs. 10,28,682/­ from the complainant during the period from 24.03.2012 till 12.09.2012 (though in complaint, affidavit and legal notice it was mentioned by the complainant that he had supplied goods worth Rs.8,49,986/­ but in cross examination complainant clarified that he had supplied goods worth Rs. 10,28,682/­). The copies of relevant bills and invoices whereby goods were sent are on record as Ex. CW1/1(colly) & Ex. CW1/2(colly). The accused had issued a certificate in favour of the complainant certifying that the goods were exclusively for export to Dubai (UAE). To discharge the liability towards the CC No. 308/13 page no. 2 /15 complainant, the accused issued four cheques of Rs.1,00,000/­ each i.e. bearing no.069129, 069130, 069131 & 069132 all are drawn on Axis Bank Ltd, Karol Bagh branch, Delhi out of which the present case has been filed on the basis of cheque bearing no. 069131 dated 26.09.2012 of Rs.1,00,000/­ & bearing no. 069132 dated 26.09.2012 of Rs.1,00,000/­ both are drawn on Axis Bank, Karol Bagh, Delhi branch in favour of the complainant but on presentation the said cheques were returned back dishonored with the remark "INSUFFICIENT FUND" vide dishonour memos dated 27.11.2012. Thereafter a legal notice was sent to the accused on 18.12.2012 by way of regd AD and UPC. It is further alleged that despite service of legal notice accused has not paid the cheques amount to the complainant till the filling of the case. 3

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: accused on 18.12.2012 by way of regd AD and UPC. It is further alleged that despite service of legal notice accused has not paid the cheques amount to the complainant till the filling of the case. 3. After the complaint was filed, summons were issued against the accused vide order dated 07.02.2013 for the offence U/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1881. On appearance of the accused notice U/s 251 Cr.P.C. dated 01.05.2013 was framed upon the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 4. In order to prove the case, the complainant examined himself as CW­1 and reiterated the contents of the complaint on oath before this court and filed an affidavit in evidence. He also collectively exhibited certificate issued by the accused in favour of the complainant and original bills as Ex. CW1/1(colly), copies CC No. 308/13 page no. 3 /15 of statement of account as Ex. CW1/2 (Colly), original cheque bearing no. 069131 as Ex. CW1/3, original cheque bearing No. 069132 as Ex. CW1/4, the cheque returning memos as Ex. CW1/5 & Ex. CW1/6, the legal notice of demand dated 18.12.2012 as Ex. CW1/7(colly), The original receipts of registered post and courier are Ex. CW1/7(colly), net tracking report as Ex. CW1/8. Thereafter, the complainant evidence was closed at request. 5. After that on 15.10.2013 the statement of accused was recorded U/s 313 Cr.P.C in which all the incriminating evidence along with exhibited documents were put to the accused. In his statement accused stated that he had not purchased the goods worth Rs.10,28,682/­ from the complainant. It is accepted by him that the document which is on page no.1 of Ex. CW1/1 was issued by him and the same is bearing his signatures, however, the same is in respect of an order which complainant failed to supply on time

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: that the document which is on page no.1 of Ex. CW1/1 was issued by him and the same is bearing his signatures, however, the same is in respect of an order which complainant failed to supply on time. It is submitted by the accused that the complainant delayed the delivery by two and half to three months. It is further submitted by him that the four cheques were given by him to the complainant for security as well as payment to be deposited for encashment from time to time. It is further submitted by him that out of these four cheques two cheques were duly honored. He accepted delivery of legal notice. It is further submitted by him that he did not made the payment to the complainant as he was not liable to pay in respect of the CC No. 308/13 page no. 4 /15 two cheques in question, however, he was liable to pay only a sum of Rs.1,00,000/­ to the complainant. It is further submitted by him that the goods supplied by the complainant were of inferior quality and were supplied with delay, due to the same he suffered losses around Rs.12,00,000/­. It is further submitted by him that he had paid a sum of Rs.1,00,000/­ to the complainant by way of RTGS. Thereafter the case was fixed for Defence evidence. However, on 06.12.2013 vide separate statement of the Ld. Defence Counsel the defence evidence was closed and the matter was fixed for final arguments. 6. I have heard Ld. counsels and perused the entire record of the case file and the evidence on record. Both the counsel have referred to a number of cases, I have discussed them at the relevant place. 7. Before proceeding further let us go through the relevant provisions of law

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: the evidence on record. Both the counsel have referred to a number of cases, I have discussed them at the relevant place. 7. Before proceeding further let us go through the relevant provisions of law. The main ingredient of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are as follows:­ (a) The accused issued a cheque on an account maintained by him with a bank. (b) The said cheque has been issued in discharge of any legal debt or other liability. (c) The cheque has been presented to the bank within the period of six months from the date of the cheque or within the period of its validity. (d) When the aforesaid cheque was presented for encashment, CC No. 308/13 page no. 5 /15 the same was returned unpaid/ dishonoured. (e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque. (f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand. If the aforesaid ingredients are satisfied then the drawer of the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. 8. Now let us deal with the each ingredient of the section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act to see whether the case against the accused has been proved or not. 9. In the present matter issuance of cheques in favour of the complainant by the accused is not disputed. It is also accepted by the accused at the time of framing of notice that all the particulars on the cheques in question except date are in his own handwriting. Presentation of the cheques within period of their validity and their dishonor due to the reason 'funds insufficient' vide memo dated 27.11.2000 is also not disputed

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: date are in his own handwriting. Presentation of the cheques within period of their validity and their dishonor due to the reason 'funds insufficient' vide memo dated 27.11.2000 is also not disputed. Service of legal notice and non payment of cheques amount within 15 days there from is also not disputed. The only disputed question is whether the cheques were given towards discharge of any liability or not. WHETHER THE CHEQUES IN QUESTION HAVE BEEN ISSUED IN DISCHARGE OF ANY LEGAL DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY: CC No. 308/13 page no. 6 /15 10. It is accepted by the accused that the cheques in question were issued by him in fully filled up condition in favour of the complainant. It is submitted by the complainant that the cheques in question were issued by the accused to pay back his liability towards goods supplied to him. In this situation the presumption of law Under Section 118 (a) & Section 139 NI Act would arise in favour of the complainant. 11. At this stage let us go through the relevant provisions of law. There is a presumption in favour of the complainant u/s 118 (a) Negotiable Instruments Act that until the contrary is proved, it will be presumed that every negotiable instrument was drawn for consideration and every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration. 12. Further Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides that it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved that the holder of the cheque received the cheque of the nature referred in the Section 138 for the discharge in whole or in part of his debt or liability. 13

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: be presumed until the contrary is proved that the holder of the cheque received the cheque of the nature referred in the Section 138 for the discharge in whole or in part of his debt or liability. 13. Now it will have to be examined whether the accused has rebutted the presumption as contemplated by Section 118 (b) and Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 14. It has been observed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in V.S. Yadav Vs. Reena 172(2010) DLT 561 that the offence u/s 138 NI Act is a technical offence and the complainant is only CC No. 308/13 page no. 7 /15 supposed to prove that the cheques issued by the respondent were dishonored, his statement that cheques were issued against liability or debt is sufficient proof of the debt or liability and the onus shifts to the respondent / accused to show the circumstances under which the cheques came to be issued and this could be proved by the respondent only by way of evidence and not by leading no evidence. It was further observed that in order to rebut the presumption u/s 139 of the NI Act, the accused, by cogent evidence, has to prove the circumstance under which the cheques were issued. It was for the accused to prove if no loan was taken why he did not write a letter to the complainant for return of the cheques. Unless the accused had proved that he acted like a normal businessman / prudent person entering into a contract he could not have rebutted the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. If no loan was given but cheques were retained he immediately would have protested and asked the cheques to be return and still cheques were not returned he would have served a notice as complainant. Further such cogent evidence can be the cross examination of the complainant or his witnesses (as held in Birender Singh V

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: cheques were not returned he would have served a notice as complainant. Further such cogent evidence can be the cross examination of the complainant or his witnesses (as held in Birender Singh V. state (NCT of Delhi) 2008(1)JCC (NI) 15). 15. Similarly in the present case it was for the accused to prove why he did not write a letter to the complainant for return of the cheques in question. Unless the accused had proved that he acted like a normal businessman / prudent person entering CC No. 308/13 page no. 8 /15 into a transaction he could not have rebutted the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. It was for the accused to have protested and asked the complainant to return the cheques and if still cheques were not returned he would have served a notice as complainant. 16. In the present case there is no cogent evidence whatsoever adduced by the accused to support his plea that the cheques in question were not issued towards any liability. It is held by the Apex Court in Krishan Janardan Bhat v. Dattatrey G. Hegde 2008 that it is for the Court to do a balancing act between the statutory presumption arising in favour of the complainant on one side and the material produced by the accused to rebut such presumption on the other side with the view to ascertain the truth. The following points shows that the defence of the accused is false: a) The present accused had not written any letter to the complainant for returning his cheques. He had also not written any letter to his banker to stop payment of the cheque in question, despite he was aware that his cheques were with the complainant who can misuse the same. Further the accused has not made any complaint to any authority regarding alleged misuse of his cheques by the complainant.(Reliance being placed on Jose Vs. P.C

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: complainant who can misuse the same. Further the accused has not made any complaint to any authority regarding alleged misuse of his cheques by the complainant.(Reliance being placed on Jose Vs. P.C. Joy 2008 (4) RCR (Crl) 251( Kerala HC). b) In the present matter accused has not led any defence evidence. However, in his statement U/s 313 Cr. PC it was submitted by him that the cheques in question along with two CC No. 308/13 page no. 9 /15 other cheques were given by him to the complainant as security as well as for payment. It is submitted by him that out of the four cheques two cheques were duly honored. It is not submitted by him that those two cheques were mistakingly encashed. He has not specified any difference in respect of status of those four cheques. Thus it appears that the present two cheques in question were on similar footing with the two cheques which were encashed. Thus apparently these two cheques were also meant to be encashed. c) It is accepted by the accused that he received the legal notice sent by the complainant, however, it is submitted by him that he could not reply the same. Non reply of the legal notice shows that accused had nothing to say against the legal notice. It shows that he had no objection regarding presentation of the cheques for encashment (Reliance being placed on Rangappa Vs Mohan 2010­TLPRE­0­300 and Iftikar Alam v. Naved Hasan 2012 (1) LRC 172 Delhi). d) The fact that accused has not got the payment of cheques in question stopped, further non replying the legal notice, clearly suggest that all the defences taken by the accused are afterthought. Why the accused kept silent and did not got the payment of the cheques stopped or why not he had written a letter to the complainant stopping them from misusing his cheques

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: accused are afterthought. Why the accused kept silent and did not got the payment of the cheques stopped or why not he had written a letter to the complainant stopping them from misusing his cheques. e) The main defence of the accused in the present case CC No. 308/13 page no. 10 /15 is that, the complainant had supplied goods worth Rs.8,49,986/­ to him and he had already made payment of Rs.7,50,000/­ and now he is liable to pay only a sum of Rs.1,00,000/­ and not Rs. 2,00,000/­. It is pointed out by the Ld. Defence Counsel that complainant had written in his legal notice, complaint and affidavit that he had supplied goods worth Rs.8,49,986/­. On the other hand it is clarified by the complainant in his cross examination that he had mistakingly written in his legal notice, complaint and affidavit that he supplied good worth Rs. 8,49,986/­ while infact he had supplied goods worth Rs. 10,28,682/­. To support his contention complainant has relied on the document already filed on record as Ex. CW1/2 which are the summery of the accounts apparently sent by the complainant to the accused (which are not objected by the defence side as no question in respect of these documents was put in the cross examination of CW­1). These two statements clearly shows that till 30.07.2012 complainant has supplied goods worth Rs. 8,49,986/­ to the accused and had received payment of Rs. 5,53,000/­ from him, leaving the balance as Rs.2,96,986/­. The second statement which is dated 01.10.2012 which is also a non disputed document shows that after 30.07.2012 goods worth Rs. 1,12,906/­ (bill no. 4220 date 18.08.2012) & goods worth Rs. 65,790/­ (bill no. 4230 dated 12.09.2012) were supplied to the accused, hence, his total liability became Rs.2,96,986/­ + Rs

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: worth Rs. 1,12,906/­ (bill no. 4220 date 18.08.2012) & goods worth Rs. 65,790/­ (bill no. 4230 dated 12.09.2012) were supplied to the accused, hence, his total liability became Rs.2,96,986/­ + Rs. 1,12,906/­ + Rs.65,790/­ total amounting to Rs.4,75,682/­. The complainant had taken into consideration payment received by CC No. 308/13 page no. 11 /15 way of two cheques on 25.08.2012 total amounting to Rs. 2,00,000/­. Thus as on 01.10.2012 accused was liable to pay a sum of Rs.2,75,682/­ to the complainant. These calculations prove that the amount Rs.8,49,986/­ was mistakingly written by the complainant while actual sales were infact Rs.10,28,682/­. Further these calculations are also supported by the accompanying bills and delivery challans which are collectively exhibited as Ex. CW1/1. The defence choses not to dispute any such bills. Thus the bills have been duly proved. Hence, it can be said that complainant has proved liability of the accused by positive unchallenged evidence as well, while on the other hand the accused has not brought any document whatsoever on record to prove his defence that he did not receive the goods. f). The Ld. Defence counsel relying on the Judgment passed by Hon'ble Delhi High Court in case titled, M/s Alliance Infrastructure Project (P) Ltd & Anr v. Sanjeev Kapoor Cited as Criminal M.C. No.2225 of 2009 has argued that the case of the complainant is liable to be dismissed as he presented cheques of Rs.2,00,000/­ while he was entitled only for an amount of Rs.1,00,000/­. It has already been proved as un­ objected that accused was liable to pay a sum of Rs.2,75,682/­ to the complainant as on 01.10.2012. Hence, the above mentioned case is of no help to the accused, as facts in the present case are different. 17

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: that accused was liable to pay a sum of Rs.2,75,682/­ to the complainant as on 01.10.2012. Hence, the above mentioned case is of no help to the accused, as facts in the present case are different. 17. Thus the bald plea of the accused having not been CC No. 308/13 page no. 12 /15 substantiated by any cogent, convincing and clear evidence would not be sufficient to rebut the presumption of law. The presumption U/s 118 & 139 of NI Act are mandatory presumptions in favor of the complainant and the same can not be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable. It must further be shown that the explanation is a true one. The task of the accused is not as simple as for rebutting the statutory presumption he must placed such material which can inspire confidence of the Court to believe the case of the accused then that of the complainant who is in possession of the dishonored cheques issued by none else but the accused himself (reliance placed on Attar Singh Wadhwa v. NCT of Delhi, Delhi High Court 23.12.2009). A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. In the present matter it has been established that the defence taken by th accused is a false one. Since the accused has failed to rebut the presumption this Court can not ask the complainant to prove the liability of the accused by positive evidence as the presumption is living and existing. 18. It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa Vs Mohan 2010­TLPRE­0­300 (A Three Judges Bench Judgement): CC No. 308/13 page no

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: evidence as the presumption is living and existing. 18. It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa Vs Mohan 2010­TLPRE­0­300 (A Three Judges Bench Judgement): CC No. 308/13 page no. 13 /15 We are in agreement with the respondent­ claimant that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra) may not be correct. 19. Thus from the above stated discussion it is clear that the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions U/s 118 (b) and 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act. Further when the legal presumption is in favour of the complainant U/s 118 & 139 NI Act he is not required to prove his case independently otherwise there would be no use of the presumption in his favour. The presumptions will live, exists and survive and shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability. No doubt a presumption is not in itself evidence, but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. However, in the present case with the help of unchallenged documents Ex. CW1/1 (bills and chllans) and Ex. CW1/2 (statement of account) the complainant has been able to positively prove liability of the accused. 20. Considering the entire evidence on record, it stands duly proved that the cheques in question which are CW1/3 & Ex. CW1/4 were issued and drawn in discharge of legal liability of CC No. 308/13 page no. 14 /15 the accused and for consideration. 21

title: By Way Of The Present Judgment vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 28 March, 2014
content: duly proved that the cheques in question which are CW1/3 & Ex. CW1/4 were issued and drawn in discharge of legal liability of CC No. 308/13 page no. 14 /15 the accused and for consideration. 21. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I am of the considered opinion that the complainant has proved his case against the accused beyond shadow of reasonable doubts. All the ingredients of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act have been duly proved on record. Accordingly, accused M/s Sachit Creations (P) Ltd and it's director Sh. Sachit Chawla, WZ­165/A, First Floor, Opp. Pusa Institute, Village Dasghara stands convicted of the offence U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. Let the copy of this judgment be supplied to the accused free of cost. content: 138, 139 and Section 118(a) of Negotiable Instruments Act at the very ­: 7 :­ outset, which reads as follows :­ Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act reads as follows: 138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account - Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for [a term which may be extended to two years], or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless­ ­: 8 :­ (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, [within thirty days] of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation - For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability.] Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act reads as follows: Presumption in favour of holder - It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that6 ­: 9 :­ the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Section 118 of Negotiable Instruments Act reads as follows: Presumption as to negotiable instruments - Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:­ (a) of consideration - that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; 10. Regarding the scope of presumptions u/s.118(a) and u/s.139 of the NI Act, there is no doubt about the settled legal position that once the signatures on the cheque are admitted by the drawer of the cheque, there arises a presumption in favour of the payee/holder in due course in terms of Section 139 and 118(a) of Negotiable Instruments Act that the cheque has been issued for consideration and in discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability. It is also well settled that (a) the presumption does not go to the extent of presuming the existence of debt and (b) the ­: 10 :­ aforesaid presumption is rebuttable in nature (see Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs. Pattatraya G.Hegde (SC)2008(1) RCR Criminal 695

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: go to the extent of presuming the existence of debt and (b) the ­: 10 :­ aforesaid presumption is rebuttable in nature (see Krishna Janardhan Bhatt vs. Pattatraya G.Hegde (SC)2008(1) RCR Criminal 695. Further, it is also well settled that for the rebuttal of the presumptions it is not necessary that the accused must step into the witness box but the presumptions can be rebutted either by cross examination of complainant's witness (see M.S.Narayana Manon vs. State of Kerala & Another AIR 2006 SC 3366 and Krishna Jnardhan Bhat vs. Dattatraya Hegde SC 2008(1) RCR Criminal 695 or even by raising presumptions of fact or law from the material available on record (see Kundan Lal Kala Ram vs. Custodian Evacuee Property, reported as AIR 1961 SC 1316). In Mallavarapu Kasivisweswara Rao Vs. Thadikonda Ramulu Firm and Others AIR 2008 SC 2898 it was held as under: "12. Under Section 118 (a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the court is obliged to presume, until the contrary is proved, that the promissory note was made for consideration. It is also a settled position that the initial burden in the regard lies on the defendant to prove the non­existence of consideration by bringing on record such facts and circumstances which would lead the Court to believe the non­existence of the consideration either by direct evidence or by preponderance of probabilities showing ­: 11 :­ that the existence of consideration was improbable, doubtful or illegal. ... ... ... The bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff. To disprove the presumption, defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exist or its non­existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, shall act upon the plea that it did not exist. ... ... ..." 11. Standard of proof of rebuttal of presumptions by any person accused of an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is preponderance of probabilities and It is not at all necessary for the accused to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubts. Though, bare denial or bald suggestions given by the accused would not be sufficient to rebut the aforesaid presumption (see Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee AIR 2010 SC 1898). Thus, whether the presumption has or has not ­: 12 :­ been rebutted depends on the facts of each case to be analyzed in the light of aforesaid legal principles. 12. Question which is to determined here is whether the accused handed over the cheque in question to the complainant was given in discharge of any legal debt or liability. Counsel for the complainant has contended that accused has handed over the cheque in question to the complainant against his liability of paying the ticket amount purchased through complainant from M/s Avon Trip.com. It is the case of the complainant that the accused in discharge of his liability issued cheque bearing no. 198780 dtd. 1­3­2013 drawn on HDFC, Dwarka, New Delhi for a sum of Rs

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: M/s Avon Trip.com. It is the case of the complainant that the accused in discharge of his liability issued cheque bearing no. 198780 dtd. 1­3­2013 drawn on HDFC, Dwarka, New Delhi for a sum of Rs. 60,000/­with the assurance that the said cheque would be encashed upon presentation. Accused being the counsel represented himself on the other hand, contended that he had given the cheque which is Ex.CW1/1, as security cheque on the request of the complainant and not for the discharging of any pending liability as alleged by the complainant. 13. Written submissions filed by the complainant and the accused perused carefully. Firstly, it is submitted by the complainant in his written arguments that accused has settled the matter with the complainant in the mediation cell but fails to honour that settlement. It is also submitted by the complainant that accused has himself admitted in his reply to the legal notice of the ­: 13 :­ complainant that cheque was issued to the complainant in his name. Thus, there is no question of any cheque given as security. It is further submitted by the complainant that the cheque was put up for encashment only at the request of the accused so again there is no question of accused not knowing the fact of dishonour of the cheque. With respect to the question of difference in the amount of the tickets raised by the accused, complainant submitted that accused had issued the cheque in question of the sum of Rs.60,000/­. The difference of the amount as per the accused is of Rs.5050/­ and total amount shown in para 4 of the complaint is of Rs.65,300/­ so the same has been explained. It is also submitted by the complainant in his written arguments that accused had admitted that he had purchased /booked the air ticket on telephone from the complainant

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: the same has been explained. It is also submitted by the complainant in his written arguments that accused had admitted that he had purchased /booked the air ticket on telephone from the complainant. It is also submitted by the complainant that since check­in of the passenger starts two hours before the scheduled departure of the flight and after the check­in status no ticket is sold by the airlines. Thus, the submissions offered by the accused that since the flight offered by the complainant was after two hours, he had purchased the ticket from the airport counter, is totally false. Infact, no ticketing agent has their office at the airport counter. While, accused submits in his written submissions that the bill pertaining to the cheque amount not produced by the complainant. The print outs of the tickets have never been ­: 14 :­ certified by the complainant in accordance with law. Thus, in the absence of the legally enforcible debt or liability there can not be any presumption mandated u/s 139 of NI Act. It is further submitted by the accused that complainant does not have anything to do with the payment liability of the accused towards the M/S Avon Trip.com. The tickets were in the name of M/S Avon Trip.com who paid the amount to the Airlines clearly makes out a case forth rebuttal of that presumption. There is neither any list established between the complainant and M/S Avon Trip.com nor is there any authorisation or approval from M/S Avon Trip.com to receive the amount from the accused towards his liability which is basically towards the M/S Avon Trip.com not towards the complainant. It is also submitted by the accused that complainant has himself stated that he is commission agent of M/S Avon Trip.com

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: which is basically towards the M/S Avon Trip.com not towards the complainant. It is also submitted by the accused that complainant has himself stated that he is commission agent of M/S Avon Trip.com. Not even a single document/witness has been put forward by the complainant to establish the same fact. It is also submitted by the complainant that the ticket amount if calculated, does not totals to the amount mentioned in the cheque in question. 14. It is submitted by the complainant in his complaint as well as in his evidence that accused had purchased tickets from the complainant and issued the cheque in question to bear that liability. Complainant himself submitted in his complaint that tickets were purchased by the accused from M/s Avon Trip.com ­: 15 :­ through him being the commission agent. Though, even after availing ample effective opportunities complainant miserably fails to put on record any relevant authority in that regard i.e. any letter or any other document from M/s Avon Trip.com which will show his ability/power to issue the tickets on behalf of M/s Avon Trip.com and to ask for clearing the liability from the customers of M/s Avon Trip.com. Accused has vehemently raised the issue of the issuance of the air tickets as well as the total price of all the air tickets issued in the name of the accused, in the cross examination of the complainant as well as at the time of his recording of statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C and in his defence evidence. Even having effective opportunities to produce the relevant document viz. bill or even the air ticket itself, complainant miserably fails to produce the same

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: 313 Cr.P.C and in his defence evidence. Even having effective opportunities to produce the relevant document viz. bill or even the air ticket itself, complainant miserably fails to produce the same. Submissions of the complainant in his written arguments that accused has settled the matter in the mediation cell has no relevance in the eyes of law as mediation proceedings are entirely distinct from the present case. Submissions of the complainant that after check­in starts no ticket is sold by the airline, has no relevance in the eyes of laws unless proved by the relevant piece of the evidence. 15. Thus in the light of above mentioned discussion complainant miserably fails to divulge the existence of legally enforceable debt or liability of the accused. Accused has from inception onwards ­: 16 :­ contested the factum of existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. In the absence of compelling justification reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail (Rangappa vs. Mohan 2010 Cri.L.J. 2871) In Builders vs Arihant Fertilizers & Chemicals and Anr., (2008) 2 SCC 321, Negotiable Instruments Act envisages that: "...application of the penal provisions which needs to be construed strictly. Therefore, even if two view in the matter are possible, the Court should lean in favour of the view which is beneficial to the accused

title: Atul Kumar Singh vs . B.N. Singhvi on 29 January, 2014
content: of the penal provisions which needs to be construed strictly. Therefore, even if two view in the matter are possible, the Court should lean in favour of the view which is beneficial to the accused. This is more so, when such a view will also advance the legislative intent, behind enactment of this criminal liability." Further, in view of the ratio decidendi in the judgment passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Krishna Janardhan Bhat vs Dattatraya G. Hedge, (2008) 4 SCC 54, the prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond reasonable doubt whereas the standard of proof on the part of ­: 17 :­ the accused is "preponderance of probabilities". The burden was on the accused to disprove the presumption u/s.139 NI Act, a burden which in the light of abovementioned discussion has been successfully discharged by him. It is apparent that the accused has furnished cogent reasons which resulted in shifting the burden of proof on the complainant, which the latter failed to discharge. 16. In the view of the foregoing observation and in view of the evidence, documents put forth and arguments of both the parties, the accused is hereby acquitted for the offence punishable u/s. 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. By way of the present judgment, this court shall decide the complaint case U/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1881 (as amended up to date) filed by the complainant SBL (P) Ltd through its AR Sh. D.C. Varshney, against the accused M/s Chaudhary Homeo Pharmacy and its proprietor Sunil Kumar. 2. The prosecution story in brief necessary for the disposal of the present case is that, complainant is a private limited company incorporated under the Indian Laws and carries on the business inter alia, of preparation, production, manufacture, supply and sale of Herbal / Homeopathic Medicines/ goods and the present case has been filed by the company through its AR

title: Cc No.6223/10 Sbl (P) Ltd vs . Chaudhary Homeo Pharmacy Page ... on 18 December, 2013
content: carries on the business inter alia, of preparation, production, manufacture, supply and sale of Herbal / Homeopathic Medicines/ goods and the present case has been filed by the company through its AR. The accused has placed the orders for the purchase of herbal / homeopathic medicines / goods from the complainant and in terms of their business transaction as on 02.03.2010 the accused firm was liable to pay Rs.82,057.34 to the complainant against the purchases. The accused firm was also liable to pay interest on the due amount at the rate of 15% per annum from 02.03.2010 to onwards till the date of realization of the amount with up to date interest. To discharge the liability of Rs. 82,057.34 towards the complainant company the accused issued a post dated cheque bearing no.004661 dated 02.03.2010 for the sum of Rs. 82,057.34 drawn on Canara Bank, South Extention branch in favour of the complainant but on presentation the said cheque was returned back dishonored with the remark "INSUFFICIENT CC No.6223/10 SBL (P) Ltd Vs. Both the counsel have referred to a number of cases, I have discussed them at the relevant place. 7. Before proceeding further let us go through the relevant provisions of law. The main ingredient of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are as follows:­ (a) The accused issued a cheque on an account maintained by him with a bank. CC No.6223/10 SBL (P) Ltd Vs. Chaudhary Homeo Pharmacy Page no. 6 of Pages 14 (b) The said cheque has been issued in discharge of any legal debt or other liability. (c) The cheque has been presented to the bank within the period of six months from the date of the cheque or within the period of its validity. (d) When the aforesaid cheque was presented for encashment, the same was returned unpaid/ dishonoured. (e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque. (f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand
