content: Being cumulative, it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under section 138 of the Act. 12. In order to appreciate whether aforesaid ingredients have been completed to constitute offence U/s. 138 NI Act, I find that there are certain rebuttable presumptions in favour of holder of a cheque. They are mentioned in section 118 and section 139 NI Act. 13. Hon'ble Apex Court in various cases had the occasion to harmoniously construe aforesaid special rules of evidence mentioned in NI Act. Some of the said case laws, which I found relevant, are mentioned in my subsequent paragraphs. 14. In the case of Bharat Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company Vs. Amin Chand Payrelal (Ref: 1999 II AD(S.C.) 221=AIR 1999 SC 1008) it was held that Although the Court is under an obligation to raise the presumption contemplated under sections, 118, 138 and 139 NI Act in every case, where the factual basis for raising the presumption has been established by the complainant, the accused is required to raise a probable defence Page no. 6 Allied Automation Engineering Vs. P. Shankar CC No. 188/1/12 or rebut such a presumption by leading evidence or bringing such facts on record in the cross examination of the complainant that could make the latter's case improbable. For doing so, it is no necessary for the accused to disprove the existence of consideration by way of direct evidence. The standard of proof has been held to be preponderance of probabilities and the inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials that have been placed on record, but also by reference to the circumstances upon which the accused relies

title: Allied Automation Engineering vs . P. Shankar on 22 August, 2014
content: and the inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials that have been placed on record, but also by reference to the circumstances upon which the accused relies. If the accused is proved to have discharged the initial onus of proof placed on him by showing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or illegal, then the onus will shift back to the complainant who will then be under an obligation to prove its as matter of fact and failure to do so will dis­entitle him to any relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. 15. In case of Hiten P. Dalal Vs. Bratindranath Banerjee 2001 V AD (S.C.) 206= (2001) 6 SCC. 16 it was held that It is a settled legal position that under the scheme of Negotiable Instruments Act, a statutory presumption has been created in favour of the holder of the negotiable instrument in due course. Section 139 stipulates that the Court shall presume liability of the drawer of the cheque for the amount for which the cheque is drawn and section 118 envisages that unless the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that the negotiable instrument including a cheque has been drawn for Page no. 7 Allied Automation Engineering Vs. P. Shankar CC No. 188/1/12 consideration. The aforesaid presumption therefore can be rebutted by the accused. The said rebuttal need not to be in the form of defence evidence. If the case of complainant fails, at it end on the basis of probabilities raised by the accused during course of cross examination, then the aforesaid presumptions, stands rebutted. 16. Section 118 NI Act talks about certain rebuttable presumptions which Court has to presume, in cases like the case in hand, viz

title: Allied Automation Engineering vs . P. Shankar on 22 August, 2014
content: cross examination, then the aforesaid presumptions, stands rebutted. 16. Section 118 NI Act talks about certain rebuttable presumptions which Court has to presume, in cases like the case in hand, viz. that every cheque was made or drawn for consideration, that every cheque bearing a date was made or drawn on such date, that every transfer of cheque was made before its maturity, that the endorsement appearing on a cheque was made in order in which they appear thereon, that a cheque is duly stamped and that holder of such cheque is a holder in due course. There is a proviso annexed with the said section, which says that if the said cheque is obtained by means of offence or fraud or for unlawful consideration then the burden of proving that holder is a holder in due course lies upon the person, asserting it. Section 139 NI Act directs that unless contrary is prove, it shall be presumed that holder of a cheque received the cheque in the manner mentioned in section 138 NI Act for the discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. Both the aforesaid presumptions, mentioned above tilt the case of dishonor of cheque, in favour of the holder/complainant. It is for the accused to rebut those presumptions, either through defense evidence or through shortcomings in the case of complainant, based on probabilities. 1 17. In the present case complainant through affidavit of its AR Ex.CW1/1 in para 5 mentioned that accused had E­ Mailed Tin number(which is a number for the purpose of taxation, given in business transactions) to complainant company, which was issued by accused, being proprietor of Convotech Projects instead of Convotech Projects Limited, suggested that accused in his capacity as proprietor of Convotech Projects had conceded the delivery of goods in question, which were ordered by Convotech Projects Limited. content: material available in hand and to appreciate the evidence adduced before the lower court, in a better position, I hereby take-up the instant Point No's.1 & 2 together admixingly for discussion. 22. It is the specific contention of the complainant by way of his complaint that, in the instant case in hand, the complainant and the accused being known to each other for more than two years, the accused being approached the complainant in the second week of August 2008 for the hand-loan of Rs.60,000/- to meet her financial contingencies, the complainant lent Rs.60,000/-, for which the accused agreed to repay the same within six months there-from and later-on, the accused issued a cheque bearing No.908476, dated 29.06.2009, for Rs.60,000/-, drawn on State Bank of Mysore, HSR Layout Branch, Bengaluru. The accused being fully aware that, there is no sufficient amount in her account to honor the cheque bearing No.908476 towards the legally enforceable debt, has committed the offence punishable U/Sec.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 23

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: sufficient amount in her account to honor the cheque bearing No.908476 towards the legally enforceable debt, has committed the offence punishable U/Sec.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 23. To substantiate his contentions, the complainant has got adduced the evidence of himself alone as P.W.1 and placed his reliance on the documents marked at Exs.P.1 to P.8, in which Ex.P.1 is the original cheque; Ex.P.2 is the bank challen; Ex.P.3 is the bank endorsement; Ex.P.4 is the copy of the legal notice issued against the accused on 11.11.2009; Ex.P.5 is the RPAD receipt; Ex.P.6 is the UCP receipt; Ex.P.7 is the RPAD postal acknowledgement and Ex.P.8 is the complaint. 24. Denying the entire case of the complainant, it is the specific defence of the accused that, she does not know reading and writing the English language except putting her signature in the Kannada language, and the complainant was working under one Shekar Reddy who is running the finance business, is well-acquainted with her husband, and her husband had raised the hand-loan from the said Shekar Reddy, towards which the accused had issued a blank-cheque in discharge of the said loan borrowed from Shekar Reddy by her husband. But, the said Shekar Reddy has misused the said blank-cheque which was issued by the instant accused as towards the security, and thereby the instant complainant has got created the said cheque in-collusion with the Shekar Reddy by writing the said contents of the said cheque as per his whims and fancies. There is no any transaction between herself and the complainant and at no point of time, either she has borrowed the loan of Rs.60,000/- from the complainant or she has issued any cheque in favour of the complainant. Hence, prayed for dismissing the instant appeal. 25

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: no point of time, either she has borrowed the loan of Rs.60,000/- from the complainant or she has issued any cheque in favour of the complainant. Hence, prayed for dismissing the instant appeal. 25. At the very outset, on meticulous consideration of the rival contentions of both the sides, along-with their respective oral and documentary evidence meticulously, it is clear that, there is no dispute in so-far-as the said cheque which is marked as per Ex.P.1 belongs to the instant accused, along-with her signature, thereon. But, the only point in dispute is that, it was issued as a blank-cheque not to the instant complainant but to one Shekar Reddy, towards the security in connection with the hand-loan transaction made by her husband with the said Shekar Reddy. 26. In view of that matter, it is incumbent-upon this court to look-into as to whether the complainant has established the prima-facie case that, the accused had raised the hand-loan of Rs.60,000/- from him and in discharge of the same, the accused had issued the said cheque as per Ex.P.1. 27. It is pertinent to note that, though the complainant himself has got examined as P.W.1, he has clearly stated in his cross-examination by the learned counsel for the accused that, he has not obtained any contemporary document as an endorsement for having advanced the alleged loan of Rs.60,000/- to the accused and also he had no any hurdle to obtain such contemporary documentary endorsement. It is also further stated by P.W.1 that, he has no any documentary evidence to show that, he was having Rs.60,000/- at the time of the alleged transaction

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: such contemporary documentary endorsement. It is also further stated by P.W.1 that, he has no any documentary evidence to show that, he was having Rs.60,000/- at the time of the alleged transaction. By virtue of these particular fatal versions of the P.W.1, it certainly goes to the very root of his case and also the legal aspect because, it is a well-settled principle of precedent law, reported in 2010(2) Kar.L.J. 284 in a case between B. Girish vs. S. Ramaiah, which reads thus: "NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT, 1881, Section 138-Dishonour of cheque - Trial Court acquitted accused/respondent for offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act - Complainant has presented this appeal on grant of special leave - Presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act would not extend as to existence of debt or other liability as observed by Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatreya G. Hegde, 2008(6) Kar. L.J. 538 (SC) - Presumption under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act is rebuttable - Defence of accused that cheque was not issued for discharge of any debt or liability - Admittedly accused had no financial capacity to pay Rs.50,000/- nor he had any savings - No contemporary documents have come into existence - Absence of any such documentary evidence would create great amount of doubt about genuineness of transaction - Section 269-SS of the Income Tax Act, 1961 insists that all transactions involving Rs.20,000/- and above should be through 'account payee cheque' - Defence of accused is highly probable and that accused has rebutted presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act - Trial Court justified in acquitting accused - Appeal dismissed

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: - Defence of accused is highly probable and that accused has rebutted presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act - Trial Court justified in acquitting accused - Appeal dismissed. K.N.Keshavanarayana, J., Held: No doubt, under Section 139 of the N.I.Act, the presumption is required to be drawn that the holder of the cheque has received the same for discharge of any debt or other liability. As held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat v Dattatraya G. Hegde, 2008(6) Kar. L.J. 538 (SC), the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I.Act would not extend as to the existence of debt or other liability. Of course, as per clause(a) of Section 118 of the N.I.Act, it has to be presumed that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration and as per clause (b) it shall be presumed that every negotiable instrument bearing a date was made or drawn on such date. Both these presumptions are rebuttable presumptions. As held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the aforesaid decision, the question as to whether these presumptions have been rebutted or not have to be considered by looking into the entire material on record and it is not necessary for the accused to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt nor be is required to step into the witness-box to prove his defence. In the case on hand, it is the specific defence of the accused that there was no monetary transaction between him and the complainant and that he has not received any loan from the complainant at any point of time and the cheque was not issued for discharge of any debt or liability

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: transaction between him and the complainant and that he has not received any loan from the complainant at any point of time and the cheque was not issued for discharge of any debt or liability. Admittedly, the accused had no financial capacity to pay Rs.50,000/- nor he had any savings. In the absence of any evidence placed by the complainant, it is highly difficult to believe that he had borrowed money from a Credit Co-operative Society and others for the purpose of lending the loan to the accused. In addition to this, except the cheque in question there is no other documentary evidence to show that the complainant had lent Rs.50,000/- to the accused and the accused acknowledged the receipt of the same. No contemporary documents have come into existence. When a substantial amount of Rs.50,000/- was lent, it is reasonable to expect that the creditor would insist on the debtor to execute some document evidencing such transaction. Absence of any such documentary evidence would create great amount of doubt about the genuineness of the transaction. Section 269(ss) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 insists that all transactions involving Rs.20,000/- and above, should be through 'account payee cheques'. All these circumstances, as rightly pointed out by the learned Magistrate are sufficient to hold that the defence of the accused is highly probable and that the accused has rebutted the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I.Act. (Para 7) 28

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: out by the learned Magistrate are sufficient to hold that the defence of the accused is highly probable and that the accused has rebutted the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I.Act. (Para 7) 28. On meticulous perusal of this particular principle of law, it clearly emerges a principle that, whenever there is a substantial amount lent, it is reasonable to expect that the creditor would insist on the debtor to execute some document evidencing such transaction and in the absence of any such documentary evidence, it would create great amount of doubt about the genuineness of the transaction. 29. Similarly, in the instant case in hand, the complainant having taken the contention that, he had advanced the loan of Rs.60,000/- in favour of the accused, as he himself has clearly stated in the cross- examination, he has not obtained any contemporary document with respect to the hand-loan transaction alleged to have been made in the year 2008-09, in connection with the Ex.P.1 alleged disputed cheque. Therefore, in the absence of such substantial contemporary documentary evidence from the complainant's side, it is only vista left as a last resort to the instant court to suspect regard the very genuineness of the alleged transaction since it creates the great amount of doubt. 30

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: the complainant's side, it is only vista left as a last resort to the instant court to suspect regard the very genuineness of the alleged transaction since it creates the great amount of doubt. 30. Further, the P.W.1 has denied the suggestions made by the learned counsel for the accused to the effect that, he (complainant) was working as Writer in the finance of one Shekar Reddy and he has further stated that, he does not know who is Shekar Reddy and also disclosed his ignorance and no knowledge of the suggested factum to him that, the said Shekar Reddy had secured a blank-cheque towards the security in connection with the hand-loan raised by the husband of the accused from Shekar Reddy, and also he has denied that, he is accompanying the said Shekar Reddy to come to the ACMM Court, in which the said Shekar Reddy has lodged the complaint against the husband of the instant accused in connection with the other loan transaction. It is also denied the suggestion specifically by the P.W.1 that, the accused has not raised any loan from him, at any point of time and also he (complainant) was not capable of advancing the loan and he has not given any Rs.60,000/- to the accused on 25.08.2008. Therefore, ultimately, the prima-facie absolute heavy burden lies on the complainant to establish that, he has advanced the loan of Rs.60,000/- in favour of the accused on 25.08.2008 and he was capable of advancing the same. Meaning-thereby, the source of income of the complainant is also required to be delved-into, to ascertain and determine as to whether he was capable of advancing the said loan of Rs.60,000/- to the accused. 31. It is significant to note that, in the cross- examination, the P.W.1 has stated that, he is doing the tailor work in his house

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: capable of advancing the said loan of Rs.60,000/- to the accused. 31. It is significant to note that, in the cross- examination, the P.W.1 has stated that, he is doing the tailor work in his house. But, as per the defence of the accused, the complainant is working as a Writer in the finance business of one Shekar Reddy who has been got examined by the accused, as DW.1. Thereby, the said DW.1 has clearly stated that, he has no any familiarity with the instant complainant and also denied that, the instant complainant is working in his finance business institution, wherefore, the learned counsel for the accused has treated the said DW.1 as hostile witness by invoking the provisions of Section 154 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with the permission of the said ACMM lower court and cross-examined him and thereby extracted and elicited the admission through the mouth of DW.1 to the effect that, he has filed the CC No.36285/2010 against the husband of the instant accused and the notice in the said case was issued to the husband of the instant accused in connection with the said transaction with him through his learned counsel Sri Sathish, but he has denied the suggestion that, the said instant Ex.P.1/cheque was obtained by the DW.1, towards the security in dischargence of the said loan amount which was used by the husband of the accused, from him. 32

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: the suggestion that, the said instant Ex.P.1/cheque was obtained by the DW.1, towards the security in dischargence of the said loan amount which was used by the husband of the accused, from him. 32. On overall consideration of these particular versions of the DW.1 coupled-with the very versions of the P.W.1, it is clear that, though the P.W.1 has denied that, he is the employee under the said DW.1, the learned counsel for the instant complainant who is none other than Sri Sathish himself is the advocate for the said DW.1 in connection with the CC No.36285/2010 pertaining to the alleged loan transaction between the instant DW.1 and the husband of the instant accused. Meaning-thereby, it is clear that the advocate by name Sri Sathish is a common advocate to both the instant complainant as well as the DW.1, in their respective cases. 33. It is the specific allegation of the accused that, the said instant Ex.P.1/cheque has been misused by the complainant in-collusion with the instant DW.1. There is some force prevailing in the said contention taken by the accused in respect of likelihood-ness of misusing the said cheque stated to have been issued by the instant accused towards the security in connection with the loan raised by her husband from the instant DW.1. This particular aspect cannot be ignored or overlooked at-an-ease unless the substantial chunk of material is placed on record and established by the complainant in favour of his case, over-riding the said allegation and defence endeavored to put-forth by the accused. 34. It is also significant to note that, as stated by the P.W.1 in his cross-examination, he has no any documentary evidence to establish that, he was capable of paying and advancing the loan to the accused

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: is also significant to note that, as stated by the P.W.1 in his cross-examination, he has no any documentary evidence to establish that, he was capable of paying and advancing the loan to the accused. The said alleged Rs.60,000/- is not a meager amount as per the said principle of law, as discussed herein before supra; Whereas, it is a substantial sum of amount, in respect of which, in the ordinary course, it is expected from the complainant to make-out and establish regarding his source of income to advance Rs.60,000/- as the hand-loan to the complainant. But, unfortunately, the complainant/P.W.1 has failed in establishing the same, prima-faciely. 35. It is further stated by the P.W.1 himself in the cross-examination that, the said Ex.P.1/cheque has been returned by the accused herself and thereafter given to him. But, again at the later-stage of his cross- examination, when he was suggested by the learned counsel for the accused that, the accused is unknown with the English writing, the P.W.1 has retracted his earlier version and stated in the fashion of improvement, to the effect that, the accused herself has got returned the said Ex.P.1/cheque and given to him. 36. On meticulous consideration of these two different versions of the P.W.1, it clearly goes to indicate that, the complainant himself is not firm with his own stand in respect of writings of the said cheque as per Ex.P.1

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: of these two different versions of the P.W.1, it clearly goes to indicate that, the complainant himself is not firm with his own stand in respect of writings of the said cheque as per Ex.P.1. Apart from the same, by virtue of the response of the P.W.1 in his cross-examination in the fluctuating fashion in a dubious manner, it creates the substantial amount of doubt leading to arrive at a conclusion that, the said alleged transaction, along-with the alleged Ex.P.1/cheque are absolutely shrouded with the fatal suspicious circumstances which are essentially required to be cleared-of and establish his case by the complainant. But, no such substantial material is forthcoming from the complainant's side to over-ride and clear-of the said suspicious circumstances shrouded around his own case and the alleged Ex.P.1/cheque. 37. It is significant to note that, in so-far-as the writing of the said Ex.P.1/cheque is concerned, the D.W.2 who is none other than the accused person, has clearly stated that, she does not know the English language. In view of that matter, on meticulous consideration of the said contents of the Ex.P.1/cheque, it is clear on the face of the record itself that, the admitted signature of the DW.2/accused, is in Kannada language; Whereas, the other contents are in English language. Therefore, the contention taken by the complainant that, the said Ex.P.1/cheque was issued either by the DW.2 or later-on, his changed version that, the accused has got written the said Ex.P.1/cheque and handed-over to him, certainly stands under the suspicious circumstances creating the fatal doubts in the mind of this court. 38

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: version that, the accused has got written the said Ex.P.1/cheque and handed-over to him, certainly stands under the suspicious circumstances creating the fatal doubts in the mind of this court. 38. Apart from the same, the accused/DW.2 having specifically taken the defence that, she had issued the blank-cheque in favour of the DW.1/Shekar Reddy who has clearly stated that, he is well-known to his counsel since last ten years, and there is no any nexus between the instant accused as well as the complainant in respect of the alleged loan transaction which is in dispute. 39. Therefore, under these peculiar circumstances, it is clear that, the entire case of the complainant itself being prevailing under the major suspicious circumstances prima-faciely, the question of adhering the presumptions U/Secs.118 & 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, to the very case of the complainant, along-with the Ex.P.1, does-not arise at-all. When that is so, the question of rebutting the contrary as against the case of the complainant, by the instant accused, also does-not arise at-all. But, however, the accused/DW.2 having made-out specifically regarding her own defence on the face of record prima-faciely, certainly it prevails over the case of the complainant, dominantly creating the absolute suspicion regarding the genuineness of the complainant's case. 40. It is also significant to note that, the lower court has discussed at much-length in it's judgment and appreciated the evidence in the right perspective by relying on the cardinal principles laid-down by the various Hon'ble High Courts and the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, citation reported in 2010(1) Kar.L.J. 197 in a case between Shrimathi Vs. Renuka; citation reported in 2003 Crl. L.J. 411 in a case between C. Antony Vs

title: B.M. Raju vs Smt. Ashwathamma on 21 October, 2015
content: Courts and the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, citation reported in 2010(1) Kar.L.J. 197 in a case between Shrimathi Vs. Renuka; citation reported in 2003 Crl. L.J. 411 in a case between C. Antony Vs. K.G. Raghavan Nair; citation reported in 2008 AIR SCW 738 in a case between Krishna Janardhan Bhat Vs. Dattatraya G. Hegde; citation reported in ILR 2008 Kar. 4629 in a case between Shiva Murthy Vs. Amruthraj, in the right perspective, wherefore, it is clear that, there is no substantiality in the case of the complainant to convict the accused. 41. Therefore, under all these circumstances, to put-into simple terms, the complainant having utterly failed to establish the guilt against the accused U/Sec.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, in respect of which the lower court has discussed at much- length in it's judgment at Para No's.9 to 21 in the right perspective on the sound principles of law without there being any kind of infirmities and illegalities, in respect of which the instant court also being in agreement of the same, the lower court's acquittal judgment does not deserve for warranting the interference by the instant court. 42. With these observations, I am inclined to answer the Point No.1 in the 'Affirmative' and Point No.2 in the 'Negative'. 43

However, he has cleared the payment through RTGS to the complainant. Despite this and his repeated requests the impugned cheque was not returned to him by the complainant. He further stated that impugned cheque bears his signature and he has also filled the other details in the impugned cheque. However, he admitted the dishonour of the impugned cheque and also stated that he had received the legal demand notice. However, accused did not preferred to lead defence evidence and matter was listed for final arguments. Defence pleaded by the accused 7. From the cross­ examination of the complainant and the statement of the accused recorded U/s 313 Cr. P.C, it appears that the accused in his defence pleaded that the impugned cheque was issued by him in discharge of his legal liability, however, payment was made through RTGS to the complainant. He has also received legal demand notice. CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 3 of pages 10 Judgment and Reasons 8. Final arguments of both the parties were heard at length and later on clarifications were sought. 9. It has been observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa v Sri Mohan1, that ordinarily in cheque bouncing cases, what the courts have to consider is whether the ingredients of the offence enumerated in Section 138 of the Act have been met and if so, whether the accused was able to rebut the statutory presumption contemplated by Section 139 of the Act. It was further observed that the test to be applied in cases U/s 138 NI Act is one of preponderance of probabilities, which has been held in various other case law as well

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: by Section 139 of the Act. It was further observed that the test to be applied in cases U/s 138 NI Act is one of preponderance of probabilities, which has been held in various other case law as well. For the purpose of reaching a decision in the present matter, it is thus important to first decide whether the complainant has been able to fulfill the ingredients as enumerated under section 138 NI Act and if yes, then decide if the accused has been able to rebut the statutory presumption contemplated by Section 139 of NI Act. 10. Further in M/s Kumar Exports v. M/s Sharma Carpets2 it has been observed as follows:­ The accused in a trial U/s 138 NI Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the non existence of consideration or debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration or debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumption the accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. 11. The essential ingredients which need be proved for constituting the offence under Section 138 NI Act were discussed in the case Jugesh Sehgal v. Shamsher Singh Gogi3. In view of the judgment and also the provisions U/s 138 NI Act, an offence U/s 138 NI Act is committed when a person draws a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, and that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid due to "insufficient funds" or "exceeds arrangements" or any other such reasons

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, and that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid due to "insufficient funds" or "exceeds arrangements" or any other such reasons. Further, as per proviso to Section 138 NI Act, the drawer shall be liable only if; 1 2010 Cri. L.J. 2871 2 AIR 2011 SC 1518 3 2009 (9) SCALE 455 CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 4 of pages 10 A) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of validity, whichever is earlier; B) the holder of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the cheque amount by giving a legal notice to the drawer within 30 days of receipt of information by him from the bank regarding dishonor; C) the drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment to the drawee within 15 days from receipt of legal notice. 12. On perusal of the file it is seen that the cheques bearing no.437808 dated 19.04.2011 drawn on Canara Bank Wazirpur Delhi, was given to the complainant allegedly towards the repayment of loan amount. However, when the complainant presented the impugned cheque to her bankers the same cheque was returned unpaid/dishonoured with remarks' Funds insufficient' on 22.07.2011. Thereafter, a legal notice dated 06.08.2011 was sent to the accused within stipulated time, however, accused failed to discharge his liabilities despite the service of the legal demand notice within stipulated time i.e 15 days from the service of legal notice. Thus the complainant has filed sufficient evidence to raise the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. 13. The issue is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption U/s 139 NI Act

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: of legal notice. Thus the complainant has filed sufficient evidence to raise the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. 13. The issue is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption U/s 139 NI Act. In order to answer this question, it is important to see the cross examination of the complainant and defence of the accused. 14. The documents filed by the complainant and the accused have been carefully perused. After going through all the records placed in the case file by both the parties, evidence adduced by both the parties and after hearing the submissions of both the parties, it came to the fore that the accused is relying on the defence that he has paid the entire payment towards the cheque amount through RTGS on 23.04.2011 and he has no liability towards the complainant. 15. As far as the plea of defence of the accused is concerned i.e that he has paid the entire payment towards the cheque amount through RTGS on 23.04.2011 and he has no liability towards the complainant, it is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the accused that the impugned cheque in question was issued to discharge legal liability on 19.04.2011 for a sum of Rs.1,35,000/­. However, accused made the payment of Rs.1,35,000/­ towards the cheque amount through RTGS on 23.04.2011. It is further submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the accused that despite the fact that accused has cleared the payment towards the cheque amount, the complainant has not returned the impugned cheque in question, despite repeated request from the accused and CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 5 of pages 10 presented the same for the encashment before the bank just to create a false ground for lodging a false complaint u/s 138 N.I. Act to extort illegal money from the accused. Per contra, it is submitted by the Ld

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: same for the encashment before the bank just to create a false ground for lodging a false complaint u/s 138 N.I. Act to extort illegal money from the accused. Per contra, it is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that accused has made a payment of Rs.1,35,000/­ on 23.04.2011. However, the payment of Rs.1,35,000/­ on 23.04.2011 was made by the accused to discharge some other liability than the impugned cheque in question. After hearing the submissions of both the parties and after going through the evidence adduced by both the parties and after going through documents produced by both the parties, it is observed by the Court that the impugned cheque in question was issued to discharge the liability of Rs.1,35,000/­ dated on 19.04.2011. It is also observed by the Court that it is submitted by the accused in his defence throughout the trial that he had made payment towards the impugned cheque in question through RTGS on 23.04.2011. It is also pertinent to mention here that it is admitted by the complainant in his cross­examination as CW1 that he had received a payment of Rs.1,35,000/­ through RTGS in his account on 23.04.2011, though the complainant has denied that the payment was towards the impugned cheque in question. The relevant para is quoted as under for the sake of clarity. "It is wrong to suggest that I have received the payment in respect of cheque in question. It is correct that I have received a payment of Rs.1,35,000/­ through RTGS in my account on 23.04.2011". It is also observed by the Court that the document annexed with the complaint i.e. the confirmation of the account are the computer generated documents and the same are not accompanied with the certificate/affidavit under Section 65­B of Indian Evidence Act

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: with the complaint i.e. the confirmation of the account are the computer generated documents and the same are not accompanied with the certificate/affidavit under Section 65­B of Indian Evidence Act. So keeping in mind the provisions under Section 65­B of Indian Evidence Act and also keeping in mind the observation made by Hon'ble Apex Court in "State Vs. Md. Afzal and Others, 2003 IV AD (CR) 205" as well as observations made by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in "Devesh Kumar Vs. State (Cr. Appeal No. 793/2004) decided on 10.02.2010", the documents cannot be read into evidence as the same are not accompanied with the affidavit/certificate under Section 65­B of the Indian Evidence Act. It is again pertinent to mention here that the accused has maintained same defence throughout the trial i.e. that he had made payment through RTGS on 23.4.2011; It is admitted fact that impugned cheque in question is dated 19.4.2011 for the sum of Rs. 1,35,000/­ and admittedly a payment of Rs. 1,35,000/­ was made by the accused on 23.4.2011 through RTGS. The admitted fact that the same amount as mentioned in the impugned cheque had been made by the accused after the issuance of the cheque support the version of the accused that he had made payment to discharge his liability of Rs. 1,35,000/­ as mentioned in the impugned cheque in question. After CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 6 of pages 10 going through the above mentioned observations and discussions, the Court of the view that accused has raised a probable defence. 16. It is now trite that the accused may rebut the presumptions from the circumstances of the case and need not lead positive evidence for rebuttal

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: view that accused has raised a probable defence. 16. It is now trite that the accused may rebut the presumptions from the circumstances of the case and need not lead positive evidence for rebuttal. At this stage, the court deem it fit to quote certain material observations as made by Hon.Supreme Court in Krishan Janardhan Bhat vs. Dattatraya G. Hegde4. "...20. Indisputably,a mandatory presumption is required to be raised in terms of Section 118 (b) and Section 139 of the Act. Section 13 (1) of the Act defines "negotiable instrument" to mean " a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer." Section 138 of the Act has three ingredients, viz: (i) that there is a legally enforceable debt; (ii)that the cheque was drawn from the account of bank for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability which presupposes a legally enforceable debt; and (iii)that the cheque so issued had been returned due to insufficiency of funds. 21. The proviso appended to the said section provides for compliance of legal requirements before a complaint petition can be acted upon by a Court of law. Section 139 of the Act merely raised a presumption in regard to the second aspect of the matter. Existence of legally recoverable debt is not a matter of presumption Under Section 139 of the Act. It merely raises a presumption in favour of a holder of the cheque that the same has been issued for discharge of any debt or other liability. 24. In Bharat Barrel & Drum Manufacturing Company vs. Amin Chand Pyarelal 1999 AIR SCW 636, para 12

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: a holder of the cheque that the same has been issued for discharge of any debt or other liability. 24. In Bharat Barrel & Drum Manufacturing Company vs. Amin Chand Pyarelal 1999 AIR SCW 636, para 12. interpreting Section 118 (a) of the Act, this Court opined: "Upon consideration of various judgments as noted herein above, the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted, the presumption under Section 118 (a) would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttal. The defendant can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the defendant is proved to have discharged the initial onus of proof showing that the existence of 4. AIR 2008, Supreme Court 1325 CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 7 of pages 10 consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the plaintiff who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would dis­entitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the defendant of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In such an even, the plaintiff is entitled under law to rely upon all the evidence led in the case including that of the plaintiff as well. In case, where the defendant fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably to be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118 (a) in his favour

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably to be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118 (a) in his favour. The Court may not insist upon the defendant to disprove the existence of consideration by leading direct evidence as the existence of negative evidence is neither possible not contemplated and even if led, is to be seen with a doubt..." (emphasis supplied) 25. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of an accused is "preponderance of probabilities". Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on records by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies.(emphasis supplied) A statutory presumption has an evidentiary value. The question as to whether the presumption whether stood rebutted or not, must, therefore, be determined keeping in view the other evidences on record. For the said purpose, stepping into the witness box by the appellant is not imperative. In a case of this nature, where the chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration." 17. In Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets5 discussing at length the question of the rebuttal of the presumption, it was observed: 5. (2009) 2 SCC 513 CC No

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: are required to be taken into consideration." 17. In Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets5 discussing at length the question of the rebuttal of the presumption, it was observed: 5. (2009) 2 SCC 513 CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 8 of pages 10 "....Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on to the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of The Act. The accused has also an option to prove the non existence of consideration and debt or liability either by letting in evidence or in some clear and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial...." 18. In Birender Singh Vs. State (NCT of Delhi) and Anr.6 it was held: "5. There is no doubt that the burden rests on the accused to rebut the presumption as raised under Sections 139 and 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. However, this presumption can be rebutted by the accused not merely by examining his own witnesses but even by cross­examination of the complainant and his witnesses and bringing out on record, through cross­ examination, that the complainant was altar and there was no privity of contract between the complainant and the accused and cheques were misused." 19

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: and bringing out on record, through cross­ examination, that the complainant was altar and there was no privity of contract between the complainant and the accused and cheques were misused." 19. As quoted above, the standard of proof so as to establish a defence on the part of an accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. After carefully scrutinizing and analyzing the evidence together with the circumstances discussed above,there is no doubt in the mind of Court that the accused has come up with a highly probable defence. The Court is of the opinion that there is sufficient material on record to displace the presumptions raised under The Act. Infact the circumstances and material on record contradict the averments made in the complaint and rather indicate towards the fact that the complainant has infact instituted a false and fabricated complaint. 20. In totality of the circumstances and the discussions above, the Court is of the considered view that the accused has proved his defence on the 6 .I (2008) BC 452, CC No. 271/12 Rakesh Gupta v Devender Jain 9 of pages 10 basis of preponderance of probabilities and successfully rebutted the presumptions raised under The Act. Conclusion 21. As quoted above, the standard of proof so as to establish a defence on the part of an accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies

title: Sh. Rakesh Gupta vs . Devender Jain on 17 January, 2014
content: probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. After carefully scrutinizing and analyzing the evidence together with the circumstances discussed above,there is no doubt in my mind that the accused has come up with a highly probable defence. I am of the opinion that there is sufficient material on record to displace the presumptions raised under The Act. Infact the circumstances and material on record contradict the averments made in the complaint and rather indicate towards the fact that the complainant has infact instituted a false and fabricated complaint. 22. In totality of the circumstances and the discussions above, I am of the considered view that the accused has proved his defence on the basis of preponderance of probabilities and successfully rebutted the presumptions raised under The Act. content: I have also carefully perused the entire case file. Before proceeding further it is imperative for me to go through the relevant provisions of law. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides that: "Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account:Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in while or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation:For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE IN THE LIGHT OF DEFENCE RAISED BY THE ACCUSED AND THE INGREDIENTS OF SECTION 138 OF THE NI ACT. 8. The issuance of the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 to the complainant by the accused has not been disputed. It is also not disputed by the accused that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/3 is drawn on the CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 5/13 account maintained by her. Further signature on the cheque in question CW1/3 has also not been disputed by the accused. The presentation, dishonor of the cheque in question and the cheque returning memo has also not been challenged by the accused. Therefore, In light of the evidence on record it stands duly proved that the cheque in question Ex CW1/3 is issued by the accused from her own account and the same is also signed by the accused. Further it also stands duly proved that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 was dishonored vide cheque returning memo Ex. CW1/4 with the reason "Funds Insufficient". 9. From the perusal of the entire evidence it has come to the fore that two fold defence has been taken by the accused. Firstly, that she has not been served with the legal demand notice by the complainant and Secondly that the Cheque in question Ex

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: come to the fore that two fold defence has been taken by the accused. Firstly, that she has not been served with the legal demand notice by the complainant and Secondly that the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 has been issued by her to the complainant in a blank manner only after putting her signatures thereon towards guarantee in respect of the Jewellery taken by her husband and not in discharge of her outstanding liability against bills Ex. CW1/2 dated 23.04.2005 and 24.04.2005 as alleged by the complainant. 10. Coming to the first line of defence taken by the accused that she has not been served with the legal demand notice from the complainant, it is pertinent to note that Sh. Sanjay, who has appeared as complainant's witness CW­1 has specifically stated in his affidavit Ex. CW1/A that the complainant has got issued the legal notice of demand dated 01.02.2006 to the accused which is Ex. CW1/5 and it was sent to the accused on 01.02.2006 itself vide registered Post, receipt of which is Ex. CW1/6. The Complainant has also placed on record the returned AD card Ex. CW1/7. CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 6/13 11. The accused at the time of framing of the notice under section 251 of the Code has admitted the receipt of the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/5. However, surprisingly in her statement under section 313 of the code the accused has denied the receipt of the legal demand Ex. CW1/5. Interestingly, the accused during her cross examination as DW­1 has admitted that in the year 2006 she was residing at H.No. 633, Sector 12, R.K Puram Delhi i.e. the same very address mentioned on the legal demand notice. Further in her evidence as DW­1 the accused also stated that her relative has received the legal demand notice

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: 12, R.K Puram Delhi i.e. the same very address mentioned on the legal demand notice. Further in her evidence as DW­1 the accused also stated that her relative has received the legal demand notice. Further the accused during her cross examination again stated that the returned AD card Ex. CW1/7 bears the signature of her relative. The admission of the accused that the legal demand notice has been received by her relative and the returned AD Card also bears signatures of her relative itself evidences that the legal demand notice was sent on the correct address of the accused. It is trite to say that personal delivery of notice upon the drawer is not a precondition for launching a prosecution u/s 138 of the NI Act. In cases under section 138 NI Act merely sending of notice at correct address is sufficient compliance and not that the notice must be received by the drawer of the cheque personally, otherwise, trickster cheque drawer would avoid receiving the legal demand notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the NI Act. Therefore it is patently clear that the legal demand notice has been served upon the accused. Moreover, In "C.C. Alavi Hazi Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr." Reported in (2007) 6 Supreme Court case 555, it has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that the course open to the drawer where he claims not to have received the notice sent by post but has received copy of the complaint with the summons is that he can within a 15 days of the receipt of summons make payment of the cheque amount and he then cannot contend that there was no proper service of notice, which CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 7/13 admittedly the accused in the instant case has not done

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: contend that there was no proper service of notice, which CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 7/13 admittedly the accused in the instant case has not done. As such non receipt of notice as a defence on part of the accused has no force. 12. Now coming to the second line of defence which has been taken by the accused that the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 has been issued by her to the complainant in a blank manner only after putting her signatures thereon towards guarantee in respect of the Jewellery taken by her husband and not in discharge of her outstanding liability towards the bills Ex.CW1/2 as alleged by the complainant. Taking up the first limb of the defence i.e except signatures no other particular in the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 has been filled by the accused. It is not disputed by the accused that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/3 is drawn on the account maintained by him. Further signature on the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 has also not been disputed by the accused. However, it is also submitted by the accused that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 was given by her to the complainant towards guarantee in respect of the Jewellery taken by her husband and except signatures no other particulars in the Cheque in Question has been filled by her. During the course of arguments Ld. Counsel for the accused also reiterated the same contentions. Surprisingly except denials and suggestions accused has not brought any evidence on record to support her stand that except signatures she has not filled the other particulars in the cheque in question

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: except denials and suggestions accused has not brought any evidence on record to support her stand that except signatures she has not filled the other particulars in the cheque in question. Furthermore even believing the stand of accused to be correct still there is also no evidence on record to show that she has not even authorized the complainant to fill the said particulars. More so it is trite to say that by putting the name and date there is no material alteration on the cheque U/s 87 of the NI Act as there is no rule of banking business that the name of the payee as well as the amount should be written by the CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 8/13 drawer himself, as no law provides that in case of cheque the entire body has to be written by the drawer only. Therefore, once the signature on the cheque in question is admitted as has happened in the case in hand, the plea that particulars in the cheque in question has not been filled by the drawer is of no consequence unless some cogent evidence has been lead by the accused that he has not expressly or impliedly authorized the payee to fill the particulars therein. ( Ravi Chopra Vs. State and Another, 2008(2) JCC (NI) 169, Delhi, Jaipal Singh Rana Vs. Swaraj Pal 149 (2008) DLT 682,) Therefore, this defence of the accused also holds no ground 13. Before I advert to the second limb of the defence taken by the accused i.e. the cheque in question Ex

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: Swaraj Pal 149 (2008) DLT 682,) Therefore, this defence of the accused also holds no ground 13. Before I advert to the second limb of the defence taken by the accused i.e. the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 has been issued by her towards guarantee in respect of the Jewellery taken by her husband and not in discharge of her outstanding liability outstanding liability towards the bills Ex.CW1/2 dated 23.04.2005 and 24.04.2005, it is imperative for me to go through the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments.--Until the con­ trary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the dis­ charge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 14. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Ja­ nardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of "preponder­ ance of probabilities". CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 9/13 15

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of "preponder­ ance of probabilities". CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 9/13 15. In RANGAPPA Versus SRI MOHAN AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecu­ tion can fail. 16. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judg­ ments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted, the presumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a considera­ tion. Such a presumption is rebuttable in nature. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused discharges the initial onus of proof by showing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be ei­ ther direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be ei­ ther direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In case, where the accused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­ex­ istence of the consideration, the complainant would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 17. Now coming to the case in hand, to corroborate her stand the accused has examined herself as DW­1. The accused has admitted that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/3 bears her signatures. It is also CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 10/13 admitted by the accused that she and her husband used to have transaction with the complainant. Further the accused has admitted that she had purchased gold Necklace set worth Rs 23,419 from the complainant vide bill dated 24/4/2005 and also admitted that she had purchased Gold Kare, gold Tops (earrings) and ladies diamond ring worth Rs. 30,761 from the complainant vide bill dated 23/4/2005. But the accused has contended that she has made the payment against said purchase i.e bills in question Ex. CW1/2 Collectively dated 23/4/2005 & 24/4/2005. Therefore so far as transaction between the accused and the complainant vide the bills in question Ex. CW1/2 is concerned the same is not disputed. Now coming to the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3, during the cross examination of CW­1 a bill Ex CW­1/X1 (also written as Mark A in examination­in­chief of DW­1) issued by the complainant in the name of the husband of the accused dated 12/02/2005 amounting to Rs 70,080/­ is placed on record by the accused

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: written as Mark A in examination­in­chief of DW­1) issued by the complainant in the name of the husband of the accused dated 12/02/2005 amounting to Rs 70,080/­ is placed on record by the accused . The accused allegedly contends that the cheque in question has been issued by her as a guarantee for jewellary purchased by her husband from the complainant vide bill Ex CW­1/X1. Interestingly, this stand of the accused itself establishes that the complainant knows the accused as well as her husband and further it is also stands established that the complainant used to sell jewellery to the husband of the accused on credit basis. Further the accused as DW­1 in order to prove that she has made payment to the complainant against the bill Ex. CW1/2 collectively dated 23.04.2005 and 24.04.2005 has also placed on record the bills Ex DW­1/X1 and Ex DW­1/X2. On perusal of the bill Ex DW­1/X1 it is revealed that the same is for sum of Rs. 30,761 and is dated 23/4/2005 and is the original of one bill Ex. CW1/2 dated 23.04.2005 tendered by the complainant. The bills Ex DW­1/X2 is for sum of Rs. 9,950 and is also dated 23/4/2005 but the same is not connected with the present complaint case. From the CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 11/13 mere production of the original bill Ex. DW1/X1 it is not proved that payment has been made by the accused against the said bill. Further the said bills placed on record by the accused also does not proves that the accused has issued the cheque in question for guarantee against the purchase made by her husband vide bill Ex CW­1/X1. Furthermore the accused has even failed to examine her husband in defence for whom she has purportedly issued the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3

title: Cc No. 4459A/14 M/S Popular ... vs Smt. Rubina Thakur Page 1/13 on 19 April, 2014
content: the purchase made by her husband vide bill Ex CW­1/X1. Furthermore the accused has even failed to examine her husband in defence for whom she has purportedly issued the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3. Apart from the aforesaid denials and vague defence no corroborative evidence has been lead by the accused to support her stand. 18. It is trite to say that mere denial on the part of the accused would not absolve her from any liability. It was for the accused to prove the circumstances under which the cheque in question was issued by her by leading cogent evidence so as to discharge and rebut the presumption raised against him by the Statute U/s 139 and 118 (a) of the NI Act and mere simplicitor denying the allegations would not be at her advantage. 19. The accused has not brought any material on record and also no cogent explanations or any probable defence which would rebut the shadow of presumption existing in favour of the Complainant. This court do not find any force in the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the accused that he has succeeded in rebutting the presumption under Section 139 of the Act. 20. From the materials brought on record and evidence lead by the parties It stands duly proved that the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions U/s 118 (a) and section 139 of the NI Act. Therefore, I here­ by hold that the Complainant has proved and substantiated the allega­ tions that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/3 was issued by the accused in CC No. 4459A/14 M/s POPULAR JEWELLERY MART (HUF) Vs SMT. RUBINA THAKUR Page 12/13 discharge of her legal liability and for consideration. Furthermore, ac­ cused has also failed to prove that she has made payment to the com­ plainant within 15 days from the receipt of the legal demand notice. 21

title: Khan Bahadur C.B. Taraporwala And ... vs Kazim Ali Pasha And Ors. on 27 August, 1965
content: ORDER Krishna Rao, J. 1. This is a batch of 21 applications made under Order I Rule 10, Order XXII Rule 10 and Section 151, C. P. C. by the same two petitioners for adding them as parties in C. S. No. 14 of 1958 on the ground that they have purchased the right, title and interest in the suit properties from the particular defendant mentioned in each application. The defendants concerned as the vendors arc defendants Nos. 35, 50, 91, 21, 100, 10, 92, 13, 24, 12, 25, 9, 40, 132, 131, 26, 14, 29, 3, 2 and 4 respectively C. S. No. 14 of 1958 is a suit brought by Dildar-Un-Nissu Begum for partition of the maleruka properties left by Nawab Kurshid Jah who died in 1302 The defendants arc her co-heirs and their legal representatives and alienees pendente lite except defendant No 43, the Jagir Administrator and defendants Nos 53 and 55, the States of Andhra Pradesh and of Mysore respectively. Defendant No 38, who was one of the co-heirs, was transposed as plaintiff No. 2 on 4-10-1958. Most of the parties entered into a compromise on 16-8-1961 and the suit was contested only by defendants 2 to 4, 10, 39, 47, 94 and 98. A receiver for the suit properties was appointed by this Court on 24-8-1962 and a preliminary decree for partition was made on 28-6-1963. Under the preliminary decree, each of the sharers was given a specified share in the suit properties and a commissioner was appointed to effect the partition. The suit is pending for the passing of the final decree

In all the applications the aforesaid vendees figure as the petitioners. As it is conceded that the 1st petitioner made all the purchases for and on behalf of H. E. H. the Nizam, who is the ex-Ruler of the State of Hyderabad, Sri K.A. Noori Azad argues that the real 1st petitioner is H. E. H., the Nizam and that the consent of the Central Government is necessary under Section 87-B read with Section 86 (1), C. p. C. 5. The answer to the point turns on Section 230 of the Contract Act which reads : "In the absence of any contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal, nor is he personally bound by them. Such a contract shall be presumed to exist in the following cases : * * * * * (3) Where the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued." If there is a contract to that effect an agent may personally enforce the contract entered into by him on behalf of his principal. Here, there is no mention of H. E. H. The Nizam at all throughout the sale-deeds except in the description of the 1st vendee. Khan Bahadur Sri C. B. Taraporwala. On the other hand, there is a specific provision in Clause 16 (g) that the vendees will implead themselves in C. S. No. 14/58 and this is exactly the object of the applications All the vendors except defendant No 24 have unequivocally stated in their counters that they have no objection to the petitioners being impleaded

title: Khan Bahadur C.B. Taraporwala And ... vs Kazim Ali Pasha And Ors. on 27 August, 1965
content: and this is exactly the object of the applications All the vendors except defendant No 24 have unequivocally stated in their counters that they have no objection to the petitioners being impleaded. Only defendant No. 24, who is the vendor concerned in Application No. 162 of 1964, has confined himself in his counter to admitting the sale and has stated nothing about the petitioners being impleaded The form in which these sale-deeds have been drawn up shows that the petitioners were personally treated as the vendees to whom the legal title passed. In Clause 16 (g) there is a contract to the effect that the two petitioners as such may enforce the sales. The intention of the parties will be ascertained not only from the form of the contract but also from the surrounding circumstances. If the intention here was to transfer the legal title to H. E. H. the Nizam, the vendors would have had to seek the consent of the Central Government in order to sue him for any relief such as for the balance of the consideration. They would have naturally preferred to transfer the legal title to the 1st petitioner. Sri C.B. Taraporwala, rather than to H. E. H., the Nizam. In my opinion, there was clearly a contract entitling the 1st petitioner to enforce the sales. 6. In H. O. Brandt & Co. v. H.N. Morris and Co.; (1917) 2 K B 784, a suit for damages for non-delivery was brought by H. O. Brandt & Co. The bought note addressed to the defendants was headed as "From Messrs. H. O. Brandt & Co. were the contracting parties and were entitled to sue upon the contract. The mention of Messrs Sayles Bleacheries was held to be intended for making known the destination of the goods. 7. In Agacio v. Forbes, (1861) 14 Moore, P.C. 160, the agreement to pay money was inform with the plaintiff, Agacio, although it was for the benefit of his firm to whom the debt was due and the firm also might have been entitled In sue upon it. The Judicial Committee reversed the decision of the Supreme Court of Hong Kong and held that Agacio was competent to sue upon the agreement in his own name. 8. The fact that Sri C.B. Taraporwala was the Attorney and Financial Adviser to H. E. H. the Nizam and described himself as such in the sale deed would not militate against the parlies having intended the legal title to be transferred to him As he states that he made the purchases for and on behalf of H. E. H., the Nizam, the latter would be the beneficial owner although the legal title vests in the former. It is settled in GUR Narayan v Sheolal Singh, AIR 1918 PC 140 that a benamindar can sue in his own name without making the beneficial owner a party. This authority was followed in Narendra Nath v. Midnapore Zamindary Co. Calcutta AIR 1940 Cal 115 and Raj Narain v Ahmadi Jan, AIR 1941 All 81 Hence there can be no objection to the 1st petitioner seeking to be impleaded in his own name although he made the purchases on behalf of H. E. H. the Nizam. 9. Sri A. Bhujanga Rao, the learned Counsel for defendant No

title: Khan Bahadur C.B. Taraporwala And ... vs Kazim Ali Pasha And Ors. on 27 August, 1965
content: no objection to the 1st petitioner seeking to be impleaded in his own name although he made the purchases on behalf of H. E. H. the Nizam. 9. Sri A. Bhujanga Rao, the learned Counsel for defendant No. 16, has raised a point that the power of attorney dated 17-11-1962 in favour of the 1st petitioner does not specifically authorise him to obtain sale-deeds and sue in his own name. A perusal of the power of attorney shows that it empowers the 1st petitioner to transact almost all financial affairs on behalf of H. E. H. the Nizam. Clause 14 authorises the 1st petitioner. " To purchase or take on lease or otherwise any lands, houses, tenements or chattels as he ray said Attorney may think desirable for my purpose and to do and execute all acts, deeds, and things for effecting and completing such purchases. " Clause 5 authorises the 1st petitioner " to commence any action or proceeding in any Court of Justice .... for the recovery of any . . . property." No doubt, as pointed out by Sri A. Bhimjanga Rao, a power of attorney is construed strictly -- Mulla's Contract Act, Eighth Edition (1957), at page 628. The rules for the construction of powers of attorney are stated In Bowstead's Law of Agency, Eleventh Edition (1951). at page 49 thus : (1) The operative part of the deed is controlled by the recitals where there is ambiguity. (2) Where authority is given to do particular acts, followed by general words, the general words are restricted to what is necessary for the proper performance of the particular acts. (3) General words do not confer general powers, but are limited to the purpose for which the authority is given, and are construed as enlarging the special powers only when necessary for that purpose

title: Khan Bahadur C.B. Taraporwala And ... vs Kazim Ali Pasha And Ors. on 27 August, 1965
content: (3) General words do not confer general powers, but are limited to the purpose for which the authority is given, and are construed as enlarging the special powers only when necessary for that purpose. (4) The deed must be construed so as to include all incidental powers necessary for its effective execution. There is nothing in the power of attorney here, which may be construed as preventing the 1st petitioner from obtaining sale-deeds and commencing proceedings in his own name, though on behalf of H E H the Nizam. On the other hand, this power may be inferred as an incidental power necessary for the executiou of the large variety of transactions authorised by the instrument. It follows that no inference can be drawn from the power of attorney that the 1st petitioner would not have intended to obtain the legal title in himself. 10. Although Ibis is sufficient to negative the first contention aforesaid of Sri K.A. Noori Azad, I shall also deal with the contention of the assumption that H. E. H. the Nizam is in reality, though not in form, the 1st petitioner, because elaborate arguments were advanced on that footing. The position taken by Sri V. K. Vaidya is : (1) Sub-section (1) of Section 86. C. P. C., does not apply because this is not a case where H. E. H. the Nizam is being sued (2) Even if Sub-section (1) of Section 86 C. P. C., applies, the privilege accorded thereunder is waived by H. E. H. the Nizam and any further statement to that effect will, if necessarv be filed. 11. It appears to me that the latter point may be briefly disposed of, although a large number of decisions were cited by both sides. Articles III and IV of H. E. H

content: will, if necessarv be filed. 11. It appears to me that the latter point may be briefly disposed of, although a large number of decisions were cited by both sides. Articles III and IV of H. E. H. the Nizam's Agreement of Accession dated 25.1.1950, a copy of which in the printed while paper (Appendix VII at page 884) was produced by Sri V.K. Vaidya in response to Application No. 382 of 1964 read thus : ARTICLE III. " His Exalted Highness the Nizam of Hyderabad and the members of his family shall be entitled to all the personal privileges, dignities and titles enjoyed by them whether within or outside the territories of the State Immediately before the fifteenth day of August 1947." ARTICLE IV. The Government of India guarantees the sucession according to law and custom to the Gaddi of the State and to the personal rights, privileges, dignities and titles of His Exalted Highness the Nizam of Hyderabad. The relevant personal privilege as it existed before 16-8-1947 depends on Section 86, C. P. C. prior to its amendment by Act II of 1951. The earlier conflict of views on the question whether the privilege could be waived was set at rest by the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Gaekwar Baroda State Ry. v. Hafiz Habib-Ul-Haq. AIR 1938 PC 165. Sir Lancelot Sanderson held that the provisions of Section 80, C. P. C., are statutory and imperative, and having regard to the public purposes which they served, they cannot be waived. 12. The subsequent amendment by Act II of 1951 has introduced Clause (d) in Section 86 (2), which proceeds on the footing that the privilege can be expressly or impliedly waived. But the intention of Articles III and IV of the Agreement of Accession was to preserve the personal privileges as they existed before 158 1947

title: Khan Bahadur C.B. Taraporwala And ... vs Kazim Ali Pasha And Ors. on 27 August, 1965
content: that the privilege can be expressly or impliedly waived. But the intention of Articles III and IV of the Agreement of Accession was to preserve the personal privileges as they existed before 158 1947. It was settled by AIR 1938 PC 165 that the privilege could not be waived No doubt, Section 87-B, C. P.
