It was further submitted that he had received the legal notice. It was further submitted that he had stopped the payment of the cheque as Amit Gupta had threatened him that he would fill an exaggerated amount of Rs. 2.5 lacs each in the cheque and would falsely implicate him in court cases. It was further submitted that Amit Gupta has expired and he does not wish to lead any defence evidence. 11. Thereafter the matter was fixed for final arguments. 12. I have heard the arguments as advanced by the Ld. counsels for the complainant and the accused and have gone through the material placed on record alongwith the evidence adduced by both the parties before the court. 13. Before adverting to the case in hand it is necessary to discuss the law of the land as applicable to the present case in hand. The main ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are as follows:- (a) The accused issued a cheque on an account CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 4 of Pages13 maintained by him with a bank. (b) The said cheque has been issued in discharge of any legal debt or other liability. (c) The cheque has been presented to the bank within the period of six months from the date of the issuance of the cheque or within the period of its validity. (d) When the aforesaid cheque was presented for encashment, the same was returned unpaid/ dishonoured. (e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: was returned unpaid/ dishonoured. (e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque. (f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand. 14. If the aforesaid ingredients are satisfied then the drawer of the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. 15. In the present case in hand the complainant has proved before the court the existence of a cheque Ex. CW-1/1 which was dishonored vide memo Ex. CW-1/2 and the sending of legal notice Ex. CW-1/3. 16. In the present matter at the stage of framing of notice U/s 251 Cr.P.C. though it was submitted by the accused that he has not received the legal notice, however, at the stage of recording statement of accused, it was submitted by accused that he has received legal notice in the present matter. 17. In the present case in hand at the stage of framing of notice the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque, however, has denied that he has given the cheque in question to the complainant and has made a specific averment that he had given the cheque in question to one Amit Gupta in relation to gambling as he has lost to Amit Gupta and he does not know the complainant CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 5 of Pages13 and Amit Gupta might have handed over the cheque in question to the complainant and have got filled the same. It was submitted by the accused that the same was done without his consent. 18

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: of Pages13 and Amit Gupta might have handed over the cheque in question to the complainant and have got filled the same. It was submitted by the accused that the same was done without his consent. 18. In the present matter it is an admitted case of both parties that said Amit Gupta has expired and therefore, he could not appear before the court to testify regarding the present matter. 19. The complainant was cross examined by the counsel for accused at length, wherein it was deposed by the complainant that he is not an income tax payee and has met with accused through one Amit Gupta who was in the same business as that of the complainant. It was further deposed by the complainant that his monthly income is approximately Rs. 10,000/- to Rs. 30,000/- per month depending upon sales. It was further deposed by the complainant that in December 2012 Amit Gupta alongwith accused came to his house and on asking of Amit Gupta he immediately gave Rs. 2.5 lacs to the accused and no written agreement was made between him and the accused. It was further deposed by the complainant that blank cheque was given by the accused to him on that day and the loan was taken for one month. It was further deposed by the complainant that after one month when he requested the accused to repay the loan amount the accused paid him an interest of Rs. 25,00/- in presence of Amit Gupta and assured him that he will pay the prinicpal amount after one month. It was further deposed by the complainant that after the expiry of that month when he again requested the accused to repay the loan amount he asked him to present cheque in bank and therefore he deposited the cheque in February 2013. 20

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: that after the expiry of that month when he again requested the accused to repay the loan amount he asked him to present cheque in bank and therefore he deposited the cheque in February 2013. 20. Section 118 NI Act raises a number of presumptions of consideration, date, time of acceptance, time of transfer and status of holder in due course unless the contrary is proved. The section lays down special rule of evidence applicable to negotiable instruments and presumptions are one of law and the court shall presume that the negotiable instrument which is the cheque in the present case, was made for consideration, was made on the date which it bears and that it was handed over to the complainant by CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 6 of Pages13 the accused in due course. 21. Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act raises presumption that the holder of the cheque which is the complainant in the present case received the cheque for the discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. 22. However, these presumption U/s 118 and Section 139 NI Act are rebuttable in nature. These presumptions have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted to accused to prove otherwise. A presumption is not itself evidence, but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. 23. In the present case in hand the accused has admitted before the court that the cheque in question bears his signatures though he has disputed the handing over of the cheque to the complainant for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: the court that the cheque in question bears his signatures though he has disputed the handing over of the cheque to the complainant for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability. Thus in the present case the execution of the cheque is admitted by the accused before the court. As per the Negotiable Instruments Act, there is no legal requirement that the body of the cheque would also be filled by the person who is signing the same and once the signatures are admitted by the drawer, the presumptions come into force. However, these presumptions are rebuttable in nature, but the onus to rebut the same is upon the accused. 24. Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Krishna Janardhan Bhatt Vs Dattatraya G. Hegde (2008) 2 Supreme Court Cases (Cri.) 166 has cautioned that the court must be on guard to see that merely on the application of presumption as contemplated U/s 139 of the NI Act, the same may not lead to injustice or mistaken conviction. 25. It was held by Hon'ble Apex Court in the said case that for proving the defence the accused is not required to step into the witness box and need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the material already brought on record as he a constitutional right to maintain silence. Standard of proof on the part of the accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 7 of Pages13 different. The prosecution must prove the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: the prosecution in a criminal case is CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 7 of Pages13 different. The prosecution must prove the guilt of accused beyond all reasonable doubts. However, the standard of proof, so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is preponderance of probabilities whose inference can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties, but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. It was held that where chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration. 26. It has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Catena of judgments that the standard of proof in discharge of the burden in terms of section 139 of the Act being preponderance of probabilities the inference therefore, can be drawn not only from the material brought on record but also from the reference to the circumstances upon which the accused relies upon. Furthermore it is not essential for the accused to get himself examined as witness and he can discharge the burden of proof which has been shifted upon him due to the presumptions even by cross examination of the complainant's witnesses. 27. In the case of Kumar Exports VS Sharma Carpets 2009 II AD (SC) 117 it was held by the Hon'ble Apex Court that to rebut the statutory presumptions the accused may either adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: presumptions the accused may either adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist on every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence, because the existence of negative evidence at all times is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time mere denial of passing of consideration and existence of debt also would not serve the purpose of accused, something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. It was further held that once the rebutal evidence is adduced and accepted by the court the evidential burden shifts back upon the complainant and thereafter, the presumptions U/s 118 and 139 of CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 8 of Pages13 the Act will not again come to the complainant's rescue. 28. Thus it has been held by Hon'ble Apex Court that Section 139 of the Act is an example of reverse onus clause which has been included for improving the credibility of Negotiable Instruments. However, as the offence U/s 138 is a regulatory offence only, therefore, test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof. 29

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: only, therefore, test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof. 29. In view of the above said decisions it can be safely said that the onus upon the accused is only to show a probable defence which is not high as that of beyond reasonable doubt and only the accused has to prove his defence to the extent of preponderance of probabilities in order to shift back the onus upon the complainant to prove his case before the court. 30. In the present case in hand the accused has been able to rebut the presumptions as raised U/s 118 and 139 of NI Act on the following grounds. 31. Firstly, in the present matter it is admitted by the complainant that he is not an Income Tax Payee, neither he has mentioned regarding the loan transaction to any government authority. It was held in the case of Krishna Janardhan Bhatt Vs Dattatraya Hegde Supra as under:- "26. The courts below failed to notice that ordinarily in terms of Section 269-SS of the Income Tax Act, any advance taken by way of any loan of more that Rs. 20,000/- was to be made by way of an account payee cheque only." 32. Secondly, in the present matter it is deposed by the complainant in his cross examination that he immediately gave Rs. 2.5 lacs to the accused on asking of Amit Gupta, despite the fact his monthly income varies from Rs. 10000/- to Rs. 30,000/- and no written agreement was made between the parties with respect to the same. 33. Thirdly, it is deposed by the complainant that at the time of CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: no written agreement was made between the parties with respect to the same. 33. Thirdly, it is deposed by the complainant that at the time of CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 9 of Pages13 taking the loan the accused gave to him blank signed cheque and after two months when he requested the accused to refund the loan amount, the accused asked him to present the cheque in bank. 34. Fourthly, perusal of the body of the cheque reveals that the cheque was signed in one ink and handwriting and was filled with different ink and handwriting. 35. Considering all these four grounds in totality, the accused has succeeded to prove a probable defence in his favour as in the present case the loan transaction is shown to be a friendly loan of Rs. 2.5 lacs which has not been shown in the Income Tax Returns by the complainant as per his own admission, thereby casting a suspicion upon the version of the complainant as a transaction which is bad in one law cannot be said to be good in another. 36. Further more in the present matter the cheque is written in different handwriting and is signed in different handwriting. Section 20 of Negotiable Instruments Act makes such cheque a valid cheque however, the facts and circumstances of each case decide the legality and validity of such cheque as to whether the same was given as security or towards a liability or otherwise. In the present matter, it is admitted by the complainant that the cheque was handed over to him blank by the accused. No written instruction is placed on record by the complainant to show that the accused has authorised him later on to present the cheque in question after filling the same before the bank. 37

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: No written instruction is placed on record by the complainant to show that the accused has authorised him later on to present the cheque in question after filling the same before the bank. 37. Further, it is the case of the complainant that the accused has given him interest on the loan. However, no statement of account in order to show the payment of interest by the accused to the complainant is proved before the court. 38. In the case of M/s Collage Culture VS Apparel Export Promotion Council, 2007 (4) JCC (NI) 388, it was held by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that a post dated cheque may be issued under two circumstances, one, it may be issued for a debt in presenti but payable in future, second it may be issued for a debt which may become payable in future upon occurrence of a contingent event. The second types of cheque would be by way of CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 10 of Pages13 security. 39. In the case of Vipul Kumar Gupta Vs Vipin Gupta 2012 (4) JCC (NI) 248 it was held by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi as under :- I find myself in agreement with reasoning given by Ld. ACMM that before a person is convicted for having committed an offence under section 138 of the Act, it must be proved beyond reasonable doubt that the cheque in question, which has been made as a basis of prosecuting the respondent/accused, must have been issued by him in the discharge of his liability or a legally recoverable debt. In the facts and circumstances of this case, there is every reason to doubt the version given by the appellant that the cheque was issued in the discharge of a liability or a legally recoverable debt. The reasons for this, are a number of facts which have been enumerated by the Learned ACMM also

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: the appellant that the cheque was issued in the discharge of a liability or a legally recoverable debt. The reasons for this, are a number of facts which have been enumerated by the Learned ACMM also. Some of them are that non-mentioning by the appellant in his Income Tax Return or the Books of Accounts, the factum of the loan having been given by him because by no measure, an amount of Rs. 9,00,000/- can be said to be a small amount which a person would not reflect in his Books of Accounts or Income Tax Return, in case the same has been lent to a person. The appellant, neither in the complaint nor in his evidence, has mentioned the date, time or the year when the loan was sought or given. The appellant has presented a cheque, which obviously is written with two different inks, as the CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 11 of Pages13 signatures is appearing in one ink, while as the remaining portion, which has been filled up in the cheque, is in a different ink. All these factors prove the defence of the respondent to be plausible to the effect that he had issued these cheques by way of security to the appellant for getting a loan from Prime Minister Rojgar Yojna. The respondent/accused has only to create a doubt in the version of the appellant, while as the appellant has to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt in which in my opinion he has failed miserably." 40. Thus in the said judgment also the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi uphelded the judgment of the trial court on the reasoning that the loan transaction was not shown in either Books of Accounts or Income Tax Returns and the cheque was written in two different inks, signatures in one ink and body in the another

title: Cc No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar vs Ashish Batra Page No. 1 Of Pages13 on 4 February, 2014
content: the reasoning that the loan transaction was not shown in either Books of Accounts or Income Tax Returns and the cheque was written in two different inks, signatures in one ink and body in the another. In the present case in hand as well the complainant has failed to show before the court that the loan transaction was shown in the Income Tax Returns, the transaction was not by way of an account payee cheque, the body of the cheque was written with different ink and the cheque was signed with different ink, the complainant has failed to show before the court his capacity to give a loan of Rs. 2.5 lacs to the accused and has further failed to show that any interest was paid by the accused to the complainant by way of any statement of account. 41. Thus in the present case, the accused has been able to rebut the presumptions as laid U/s 118 and 139 of NI Act and the onus has shifted upon the complainant to prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of all reasonable doubts. However, in the present case the complainant after the onus has shifted upon him has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of all reasonable doubts. 42. In view of the above said discussions and findings the CC No. 858/01/2012 Prashant Kumar Vs Ashish Batra page no. 12 of Pages13 accused is acquitted for the offence U/s 138 NI Act. 43. For the purpose of section 437 A Cr.P.C, the previous personal bond and surety bonds of the accused stands extended for the period of next six months. 44. title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF Ms. MANU GOEL KHARB METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE, DWARKA COURTS, NEW DELHI In Re: Case No. : 223/12 (Old CC no. 2663/1 dated 03.10.07) U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1. CC No. : 223/12 2. Date of Institution : 03.10.2007 3. Name of the complainant, : The Madhav Co­operative parentage and residence Urban Thrift & Credit Society Ltd., E­17, East Uttam Nagar, Near Pali Factory, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi­59 (Through Sh. Satish Kumar Garg S/o Sh. Ghanshyam Dass Gupta, President/AR) 4. Name of accused : Sh. Alamgeer his parentage S/o Sh. Rafiq Ahmad and residence R/o B­254, JJ Colony, Hastsal, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi­59 Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 1 of 20 5. Date when Judgment was reserved : 12.02.2014 6. Date when Judgment was pronounced : 22.02.2014 7. Offence complained of : U/s. 138 NI Act 8. Plea of accused : Not guilty 9. Final Judgment : Convicted ­ :: JUDGMENT :: ­ BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE 1. By way of the present judgment, I shall decide the complaint case U/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1881 (as amended up to date) filed by the complainant The Madhav Co­operative Urban Thrift and Credit Society Ltd through its President/AR Sh. Satish Kumar Garg against the accused Sh. Alamgeer S/o Sh. Rafiq Ahmad. 2. The facts in brief necessary for the disposal of the present case Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 2 of 20 are that as per the allegations in the complaint, on 11.08.04, the accused took a loan of Rs.25,000/­ from the complainant society vide loan account no. 2564 at interest of 18% per annum with the promise that the same shall be returned with interest and the accused executed loan agreement in this regard

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: the complainant society vide loan account no. 2564 at interest of 18% per annum with the promise that the same shall be returned with interest and the accused executed loan agreement in this regard. The accused was irregular in making the payment of installments and therefore, settled his account upto 18.07.2007 for a sum of Rs.29,200/­. The accused for discharge of the said liability issued cheque bearing no. 284229 drawn on ICICI Bank, B­1, Milap Nagar, Najafgarh Road, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi in favour of the complainant. On presentation of the above said cheque the same was returned unpaid with the reasons "INSUFFICIENT FUNDS" vide cheque return memo dated 21.07.2007. Thereafter, the complainant served the legal notice of demand dated 13.08.2007 to the accused which was sent by Speed post with AD thereby calling upon the accused to make the payment in lieu of dishonored cheque. It is alleged that accused has failed to pay any sum in response to the legal notice of demand. In consequence thereof the complainant has filed the instant complaint for prosecution of the accused U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 3 of 20 3. After the complaint was filed, the President/Authorized Representative of the complainant society led his pre­summoning evidence by way of an affidavit and after hearing the AR for the complainant and considering the entire material and documents on record, summons were issued against the accused vide order dated 03.10.2007 for the offence U/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 1881. On appearance of the accused, a separate notice U/s 251 Cr.P.C. dated 09.02.2012 was given to the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial and the matter was fixed for complainant evidence. 4

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: of the accused, a separate notice U/s 251 Cr.P.C. dated 09.02.2012 was given to the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial and the matter was fixed for complainant evidence. 4. In order to prove the case, Sh. Satish Kumar Garg, President/AR of the complainant got himself examined as CW­1 and reiterated the contents of the complaint on oath before this court and tendered his affidavit in evidence which is Ex. CW­1/X. He got exhibited the original cheque bearing no. 284248 dated 19.07.2007 of Rs.29,200/­ drawon on ICICI Bank, B­1, Milap Nagar, Najafgarh Road, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi as Ex. CW1/A, Original cheque return memo dated 21.07.2007 as Ex. CW1/B, Copy of notice dated Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 4 of 20 13.08.2007 as Ex. CW1/C, Postal receipt and acknowledgment Card is Ex. CW1/D and Ex. CW1/E. Sh. Satish Kumar Garg was cross­ examined by the ld. Counsel for the accused. Thereafter, the complainant evidence was closed by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant. Thereafter, counsel for the complainant moved an application under section 311 CrPC for calling a bank witness to prove the dishonor of cheque. This application was allowed and Sh. Bikesh Sharma, Customer Service Officer, ICICI Bank Ltd was examined as CW2. He brought statement of account of the accused and exhibited the same as Ex. CW2/X and also identified the original cheque Ex. CW1/A and return memo already Ex. CW1/B. CW2 Bikesh Sharma was cross­examined by the ld. Counsel for the accused. Thereafter, the complainant evidence was closed by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant and the case was fixed for statement of the accused. 5. In his statement recorded U/s 313 Cr.P.C r/w Sec. 281 CrPC, all the incriminating evidence along with exhibited documents Case No

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: complainant and the case was fixed for statement of the accused. 5. In his statement recorded U/s 313 Cr.P.C r/w Sec. 281 CrPC, all the incriminating evidence along with exhibited documents Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 5 of 20 were put to the accused Alamgeer in which he stated that he had issued the cheque in question as a blank signed cheque for security purpose and admitted the receipt of legal notice of demand. He further stated that he complainant has mis­used the blank signed cheque given by him to the complainant prior to the disbursement of loan. Thereafter, the case was fixed for defence evidence. 6. Ld. counsel for the accused moved an application U/s 315 Cr.PC for allowing the accused to appear in his defence. The aforesaid application was allowed and accused himself deposed as DW1. Accused deposed that he was sanctioned a loan of Rs. 25000/­ by the complainant and the latter also took one blank signed cheque from him at the time of disbursement of loan. He admitted the receipt of legal demand notice. Accused did not tender any document in support of his defence. Accused was cross­examined by the ld. Counsel for the complainant wherein he admitted that he did not give any reply to the legal notice of demand. In his defence, accused also examined his wife Shama Begum as DW2 who exhibited the payment receipts as Ex. DW2/A(15 pages Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 6 of 20 colly). DW2 deposed that she was present at the time of loan and on complainant's demand, her husband Alamgeer gave them one blank signed cheque for loan. She also deposed that on some occasions no receipt was issued by the complainant. DW2 was cross­examined by the ld. Counsel for the complainant

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: Alamgeer gave them one blank signed cheque for loan. She also deposed that on some occasions no receipt was issued by the complainant. DW2 was cross­examined by the ld. Counsel for the complainant. No other defence witness was produced on behalf of the accused. Thereafter, defence evidence was closed at request of Ld. counsel for the accused and the case was fixed for final arguments. 7. Final arguments were addressed on behalf of both the parties. I have heard Ld. counsels for both the parties and perused the entire record of the case file and the evidence on record. In order to bring home the conviction of the accused, the complainant has to show not only unbroken chain of events leading to commission of actual offence on record but also the ingredients of the offence complained of. 8. Before proceeding further let us go through the relevant provisions of law. The main ingredient of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are as follows:­ Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 7 of 20 (a) The accused issued a cheque on an account maintained by him with a bank. (b) The said cheque has been issued in discharge of any legal debt or other liability. (c) The cheque has been presented to the bank within the period of six months from the date of the cheque or within the period of its validity. (d) When the aforesaid cheque was presented for encashment, the same was returned unpaid/ dishonoured. (e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque. (f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque. (f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand. If the aforesaid ingredients are satisfied then the drawer of the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. 9. Now let us deal with the each ingredient of the section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act to see whether the case against the Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 8 of 20 accused has been proved or not. 10. WHETHER THE CHEQUE WAS ISSUED OR NOT The accused has himself admitted to have signed the cheque in question while answering to the question at the time of framing of notice U/s 251 Cr. PC. Further while answering to the question U/s 313 Cr.PC the accused has admitted to have given the cheque in question to the complainant but he stated that the same was given in blank only after putting his signatures there for purpose of security at the time of taking the loan from complainant. Therefore, so far as signing and delivery of the cheque in question by the accused is concerned the same is not disputed. Moreover, in Jaipal Singh Rana Vs. Swaraj Pal 149 (2008) DLT 682 it was held by Delhi High Court that "by putting the amount and the name there is no material alteration on the cheque U/s 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. In fact there is no alteration but only adding the amount and the date. It was further observed in the aforesaid judgment that there is no rule of banking business that the name of the payee as well as the Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 9 of 20 amount should be written by the drawer himself

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: judgment that there is no rule of banking business that the name of the payee as well as the Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 9 of 20 amount should be written by the drawer himself. No law provides that in case of cheques the entire body has to be written by the drawer only." In view of the evidence on record it stands proved that the cheque in question was issued by the accused. 11. WHETHER THE CHEQUE WAS PRESENTED WITHIN THE PERIOD OF VALIDITY Perusal of the record reveals that the cheque in question which is Ex. CW­1/A is dated 19.07.2007 which got dishonored vide cheque returning memo which is Ex. CW­1/B dated 21.07.2007 which is not disputed by the accused clearly shows that the cheque has been presented within period of its validity i.e. within six months from the date of issuance of the cheque. 12. DISHONOUR OF CHEQUE IN QUESTION In the instant case, Satish Kumar Garg who has appeared as complainant's witness has got exhibited the cheque returning memo which is Ex. CW1/B to prove the fact of dishonour of the cheque in Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 10 of 20 question. Complainant also examined bank witness Sh. Bikesh Sharma, to prove the dishonor of the cheque who correctly identified the cheque Ex. CW1/A and return memo Ex. CW1/B and stated that the same was issued by their bank mentioning 'insufficiency of funds' as the reason of dishonor. He produced the statement of account of the accused as Ex. CW2/X and stated that as the balance of the accused was not sufficient, so the entry of dishonor is not reflected in the statement of account. The dishonor of the cheque in question has not been disputed by the accused nor the cheque returning memo has been challenged by the accused

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: of dishonor is not reflected in the statement of account. The dishonor of the cheque in question has not been disputed by the accused nor the cheque returning memo has been challenged by the accused. Therefore considering the entire evidence on record it stands duly proved that the cheque in question was dishonored vide cheque returning memo dated 21.07.2007 which is Ex. CW1/B with the reason "Insufficient Funds". 13. SERVICE OF LEGAL NOTICE OF DEMAND UPON THE ACCUSED In the instant case, Satish Kumar Garg who has appeared as complainant's witness has specifically stated in his examination in Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 11 of 20 chief that the complainant got issued the legal notice of demand dated 13.08.2007 which is Ex. CW1/C and it was sent to the accused vide Spped Post with Regd. AD which are Ex. CW­1/D and Ex. CW1/E respectively. The accused has also admitted the receipt of legal notice of demand during framing of notice under section 251 CrPC and while answering to the question during his statement U/s 313 r/.w 281 Cr.PC as well as his examination in chief. In light of the evidence on record and the admission made by the accused, it stands proved that legal notice of demand was properly served upon the accused. 14. WHETHER THE CHEQUE IN QUESTION WAS ISSUED IN DISCHARGE OF ANY LEGAL DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY In the case in hand, Satish Kumar Garg who has appeared as complainant's witness has specifically stated in his examination in chief by way of affidavit that the accused was irregular in making payments and settled his account with the complainant for a sum of Rs. 29,200/­ and issued the cheque in question in discharge of that Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 12 of 20 liability

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: and settled his account with the complainant for a sum of Rs. 29,200/­ and issued the cheque in question in discharge of that Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 12 of 20 liability. The accused has however deposed in his examination in chief that he had issued cheque in question to the complainant before the disbursement of loan as blank signed cheque, by way of security only and the same has been misused by the complainant. Before deciding this issue let us go through the relevant provisions of law. Section 46 of the Negotiable Instruments Act speaks of the delivery, it reads as follows:­ "The making, acceptance or endorsement of a promisory notice, bill of exchange or cheque is completed by delivery, actual or constructive." Section 118 (b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides that until the contrary is proved, the following presumption shall be made. (b) As to date ­ that every Negotiable Instrument bearing a a date was made or drawn on such date. Moreover, there is a presumption in favour of the complainant Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 13 of 20 u/s 118 (a) Negotiable Instruments Act that until the contrary is proved, it will be presumed that every negotiable instrument was drawn for consideration and every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration. Further Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides that it shall be presumed until the contrary is proved that the holder of the cheque received the cheque of the nature referred in the Section 138 for the discharge in whole or in part of his debt or liability

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: be presumed until the contrary is proved that the holder of the cheque received the cheque of the nature referred in the Section 138 for the discharge in whole or in part of his debt or liability. Now the Court shall examine whether the accused is successful in rebutting the presumption as contemplated by Section 118 (b) and Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act. To rebut the presumption of section 139 of NI Act and section 118 (b) of NI Act, the sole ground of defence taken by the Ld counsel for accused is that the cheque in question was given to the complainant as blank signed cheque by way of security prior to the sanctioning of loan and that the cheque in question was issued by the Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 14 of 20 accused in blank with only his signatures. To support this contention, the accused has failed to bring anything on record. DW2 Shama Begum, who is the wife of the accused has also stated in her examination of chief that the accused gave the cheque of ICICI Bank to the complainant for loan. A Security cheque if issued for any debt payable in presenti but such payment has been deferred to a future debt can be subject matter of proceedings under section 138 NI Act. In the present case, even it is presumed that the cheque has been issued for security purpose, it was meant for discharge of debt but the payment of which has been deferred to a future date. In this regard, the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi has observed in its judgment titled as Krish International P. Ltd & Ors Vs. State & Ors. MANU/DE/0302/2013 as :­ "9. There is no dispute that the proposition of law as laid down in M/s Collage Culture that a cheque issued not for an existing due but issued by way of security would not attract the provisions of Section 138 of the Act

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: that the proposition of law as laid down in M/s Collage Culture that a cheque issued not for an existing due but issued by way of security would not attract the provisions of Section 138 of the Act. In M/s Collage Culture the learned Single Judge of this Court (Pradeep Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 15 of 20 Nandrajog, J.) drew distinction between a cheque issued for a debt in present but payable in future and second for a debt which may become payable in future upon the occurance of a contingent event. Paras 20 to 24 of the report in M/s Collage Culture are extracted hereunder :­ 20. A post dated cheque may be issued under 2 circumstances. Under circumstance one, it may be issued for a debt in presenti but payable in future. Under Second circumstance it may be issued for a debt which may become payable in future upon the occurrence of a contingent event. 21. The difference in the two kinds of post­dated cheques would be that the cheque issued under first circumstance would be for a debt due, only payable being postponed. The latter cheque would be by way of a security. 22. The word 'due' means 'outstanding at the relevant date'. The debt has to be in existence Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 16 of 20 as a crystallized demand akin to a liquidated damages and not a demand which may or may not come into existence; coming into existence being contingent upon the happening of an event." Hence, it is sufficiently proved on record that the cheque in question was not issued by way of security but for payment of the amount received by the accused from the complainant

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: of an event." Hence, it is sufficiently proved on record that the cheque in question was not issued by way of security but for payment of the amount received by the accused from the complainant. Further, even if we assume that the cheque in question was issued by the accused in blank with only his signatures, even then the law has been clearly laid down in this regard by Hon'ble Delhi High Court in M/s Jammu & Kashmir Bank vs. Abhishek Mittal, 2012 CD DCR 189, that :­ "When a blank cheque is signed and handed over, it means that the person signing it has given the implied authority to the holder of the cheque, to fill up the blanks which he has left. A person issuing a blank cheque is supposed to understand the consequences of Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 17 of 20 doing so. He cannot escape his liability only on the ground that blank cheque has been issued by him." "Once issuance of the cheque been admitted or stands proved, a presumption arises in favour of the holder of the cheque that he had received the cheque of the nature referred to under Section 138 of the Act for the discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or any other liability. This presumption arises in favour of the holder under Section 139 of the Act which envisages that it shall be presumed unless the contrary is proved that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to under Section 138 of the Act for discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or any other liability. Of course, this presumption is a rebuttable presumption and same can be rebutted only by the person who had drawn the cheque." Thus, the accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 118 (b) of Negotiable Instruments Act

title: Case No. 223/12 Madhav ... vs Alamgeer 1 Of 20 on 22 February, 2014
content: rebuttable presumption and same can be rebutted only by the person who had drawn the cheque." Thus, the accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 118 (b) of Negotiable Instruments Act. Therefore, presumption under section 118 (b) holds good and according to which cheque was issued by the accused in discharge of his legal Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 18 of 20 liability. Therefore, Court is of the considered opinion that the complainant has sufficiently been able to prove its case that the cheque in question was issued by the accused in discharge of his legal debt or liability. 15. THE DRAWER OF THE CHEQUE HAS FAILED TO MAKE THE PAYMENT WITHIN 15 DAYS OF THE RECEIPT OF SAID NOTICE In the instant case Sh. Satish Kumar Garg who has appeared as complainant's witness has deposed in his examination in chief by way of affidavit that despite service of legal notice of demand accused has failed to pay the cheque amount. Considering the evidence on record it stands proved that the accused has failed to make the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal notice of demand. 16.In view of the aforesaid discussion, I am of the considered Case No. 223/12 Madhav Co­operative Vs Alamgeer 19 of 20 opinion that the complainant has sufficiently proved its case against the accused. All the ingredients of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act have been duly proved on record. Accordingly, accused Alamgeer S/o Sh. Rafiq Ahmed is hereby convicted of the offence u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. Let copy of this judgment be given free of cost to the convict. content: IN THE COURT OF SHRI PUNEET PAHWA METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE ­ 01 (N.I. ACT) PATIALA HOUSE COURTS : NEW DELHI Sh. Ramesh S/o Sh. Kishan Lal, R/o 2028­1/E, Pillanji, Kotla Mubarakpur, New Delhi ....................... Complainant Vs. Sh. Mahender Singh @ Mahender Sardar (Senior Clerk, Steno) Block No.3, Punjab Cell, CGO Complex, Lodhi Road, New Delhi. . ................................Accused Case Number. : 267/1 Date of Institution of Present Case. : 31.05.2004 Offence Complained Of. : U/s 138 NI Act Case No. 267/1 Plea of the Accused. : Not Guilty Arguments Heard On. : 07.03.2014. Final Order. : Convicted. Date of Judgment. : 26.03.2014 - :: JUDGMENT :: ­ 1. Vide this judgment, I shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant u/s 138 Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "N.I Act"). 2. Brief facts of the case as alleged by the complainant are that the accused took a personal loan of Rs.6,500/­ from the complainant and the accused issue a cheque bearing no.901583 dated 15.03.2004 drawn on Corporation Bank, CGO Complex, Lodhi Road, New Delhi for a sum of Rs.6,500/­ in discharge of the liability towards the complainant. When the complainant presented the said cheque through his banker, the same was returned back unpaid with the remarks "Payment stopped by drawer". The complaint sent a legal demand notice through his counsel Case No. 267/1 on 19.03.2004 by Regd. Post and UPC. The accused failed to make payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of service of the Notice, therefore, the complainant has filed the present complaint u/s 138 of N.I. Act. 3. The present complaint was filed on 31.05.2004. The accused was summoned on 08.07.2004. The accused entered his first appearance on 03.03.2005

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: has filed the present complaint u/s 138 of N.I. Act. 3. The present complaint was filed on 31.05.2004. The accused was summoned on 08.07.2004. The accused entered his first appearance on 03.03.2005. The offence being bailable, the accused was admitted to bail on 05.08.2005. 4. Notice u/s 251 Cr. P.C was served upon the accused on 14.10.2005 to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The complainant evidence was closed on 09.05.2007. 5. Statement of the accused u/s 313 Cr. P.C was recorded on 03.07.2007 and the case was fixed for DE. DE was recorded and the case was fixed for final arguments. Thereafter the accused moved two applications, one u/s 311 Cr. P.C and another u/s 315 Cr. P.C. Both the applications were dismissed and the case was again fixed for final arguments. However, Ld. Revisionist Court had allowed the accused to lead DE and consequently the accused himself and SI Subhash Chander Case No. 267/1 from CBI deposed as defence witnesses. After the examination of these two witnesses, DE was closed and the case was again fixed for final arguments for 06.08.2013. Final arguments were heard as on 07.03.2014 and the case was fixed for orders for today. 6. To prove his case, the complainant himself deposed as CW 1 and supported the facts averred by him in the complaint. In his cross­ examination also he had more or less corroborated the averments made by him in his complaint. In his cross­examination the complainant had submitted that he knew the accused as he used to come with his father Sh. Kishan Lal. He further submitted that he did not know Tejpal Singh nor he was aware that his father knew Tejpal Singh. He had further submitted that he gave the amount to the accused on 15.03.2004 at his residence in the evening when he had come with his father

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: nor he was aware that his father knew Tejpal Singh. He had further submitted that he gave the amount to the accused on 15.03.2004 at his residence in the evening when he had come with his father. He further submitted that it was a friendly loan without any interest and at that time the accused handed over a cheque to him. He had denied the suggestion that the amount was given by one Tejpal in December 2002 on an interest of Rs.500/­ per month. He was also not aware that his father manhandled and threatened the accused on 04.03.2004 at CBI office with regard to the amount taken by the accused from Tejpal. He had also denied the Case No. 267/1 suggestion that the cheque in question was taken forcefully and payment of the same was stopped by the accused. He had further denied that the cheque in question was without any legal debt or liability or the same was issued by the accused involuntarily. The complainant has relied upon cheque in question which is Ex. CW 1/A, the cheque return memo Ex. CW 1/B, pay in slip of complainant bank Ex. CW 1/B1, the legal demand notice Ex. CW 1/C, postal receipts and UPC Ex. CW 1/D & Ex. CW 1/E respectively and the complaint Ex. CW 1/F. 7. The accused in his statement u/s 313 Cr. P.C had admitted that he had issued the cheque in question on 04.03.2004. He had also admitted that the notice was served upon him. The basic defence of the accused is that he had taken money from one Tejpal Singh and not from the complainant. He had further submitted in his statement that Kishan Lal was the father of the complainant and he had given him Rs.5000/­ in cash on 04.12.2002 and on 04.03.2004 he had come to his office and manhandled him and got the cheque filled

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: that Kishan Lal was the father of the complainant and he had given him Rs.5000/­ in cash on 04.12.2002 and on 04.03.2004 he had come to his office and manhandled him and got the cheque filled. He had further submitted that as all the persons in the office had gone to attend wedding of daughter of one of the colleagues, not much staff was in the office and finding no other alternative he had to issue the cheque in question to Kishan Lal. Case No. 267/1 The accused has further submitted that in fact Kishan Lal had taken Rs. 5000/­ from him in the year 2003 and he owed nothing from the complainant and the cheque was issued under coercion regarding which he had already lodged a complaint in the office and also with the police and had given instructions to his banker to stop payment. He had further stated that the only dispute was that the complainant was demanding interest @5% per month whereas Tejpal had told him to give two extra installments only. 8. To defend his case the accused had examined two witnesses, himself as DW 1 and Sh. Subhash Chander, SI from CBI, SC­II, CGO Complex, Lodhi Road, New Delhi as DW 2. In his cross­examination, DW 1 i.e. accused himself, had outrightly submitted that he did not know the complainant and he never met with the complainant prior to the institution of the instant complaint. On oath he had submitted that the father of the complainant visited the office of CBI on 04.03.2004 during lunch hours and started quarreling with him. He had further submitted that he had taken a sum of Rs.5,000/­ from Sh. Tejpal on recommendation of Sh. Kishan Lal, father of the complainant and had handed over a cheque of Rs.5,000/­ to Sh. Tejpal. He had further Case No

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: that he had taken a sum of Rs.5,000/­ from Sh. Tejpal on recommendation of Sh. Kishan Lal, father of the complainant and had handed over a cheque of Rs.5,000/­ to Sh. Tejpal. He had further Case No. 267/1 submitted that the said loan was taken from Tejpal and the same was to be repaid in 10 equated monthly installments of Rs.500/­ each and the accused had to pay two additional installments as interest on the said loan. The said cheque was never presented by Tejpal. He had further submitted that the father of the complainant thrashed him by holding from the collar in the office premises and asked him to make the repayment. This as per the accused took place in the presence of 3­4 other staff members. The accused then reported the matter to the SP, CBI. Copy of which was also sent to the Ilaka PS i.e. Lodhi Road. The accused after a few days instructed his bank to stop payment of the said cheque. In the cross examination the accused stuck to the story put forth in his chief examination and there were no major contradictions. 9. Defence exhibited in evidence the enquiry report conducted on the complaint of the accused at his office as Ex. DW1/A. 10. I have heard the arguments advanced by ld. Counsel for complainant and the defence, and have also perused the case file. 11. The five ingredients required for proving an offence under Case No. 267/1 Section 138 of the NI Act are as follows-- i. Drawing of the cheque, ii. Presentation of the cheque with the bank, iii. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank, iv. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque demanding payment of the cheque amount, and v. Failure of the drawer to make payment within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. 12

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: bank, iv. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque demanding payment of the cheque amount, and v. Failure of the drawer to make payment within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. 12. The defence of the accused is two fold--first that the cheque was taken under coercion by the father of the complainant in the name of the complainant and that there is actually no debt or consideration on which this was done. Secondly that the funds in the account weren't insufficient but that the accused on purpose instructed his bank to stop the payment as the cheque was issued under force and coercion. 13. In regards the essential ingredients mentioned above and the first defence put forth by the accused, the accused admits to have drawn a Case No. 267/1 cheque however he disputes the date as per his statement under Section 313, CrPC. Advancement of loan through the father of the complaint, Shri Kishan Lal has not been called in question. 14. At this juncture it is also pertinent to note that Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, raises the presumption that that every negotiable instrument is made or drawn for consideration. By virtue of this clause, the Court is obliged to presume that the promissory note was made for consideration or until the contrary is proved. In Mallavarapu Kasivisweswara Rao v. Thadikonda Ramulu Firm and Others, AIR 2008 SC 2898, it was held as under-- "...The bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff. To disprove the presumption, defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the Case No. 267/1 consideration did not exist or its non­existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, shall act upon the plea that it did not exist..." 15. This is further strengthened by the presumption under Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act that it "shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for discharge in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." Under this Section, there is a legal presumption that the cheque was issued for discharging a liability and that presumption can be rebutted only by the person who drew the cheque. This presumption can be rebutted by the accused by adducing evidence. So the burden of proof is on the accused. 16. In Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee, AIR 2010 SC 1898, it was held as under-- "The words 'unless the contrary is proved' which Case No. 267/1 occur in this provision (Section 139) make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted......" 17

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted......" 17. Moreover the accused has not called in question the execution of the cheque. It is on record and has been proved sufficiently by the complainant that the said cheque was presented and was returned unpaid by the drawee bank as per the return memo on record which is Ex. CW1/B with the reason endorsed as the transaction having been stopped by the drawer. Further the stage of giving notice in writing to drawer/ accused (Ex. CW1/C) and demanding payment of the cheque amount is not under dispute. This factum is further not denied by the accused and is so admitted in his statement u/s 313, CrPC. Case No. 267/1 18. In view of the presumptions raised against the accused u/s 118 and 139 of N.I. Act and the other evidence made out, the duty was upon the accused to show that the offence u/s 138 of N.I. Act was not made out against him. So far as the ingredients of Section 138 of N.I. Act are concerned, the issuance of cheque by the accused and return of the same dishonoured has been sufficiently proved. 19. In regards the second contention, Hon'ble Supreme Court in MMTC Ltd. v. M/s Medchal Chemicals & Pharma P. Ltd., AIR 2002 SC 182, has held that though on the ground of "stop payment", provisions of Section 138 are attracted but the accused if he proves that there were sufficient funds in his account and stops payment instructions were given not due to insufficiency or paucity of funds but due to some other reason including absence of debt or liability, then no offence shall be made out against the accused. 20

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: instructions were given not due to insufficiency or paucity of funds but due to some other reason including absence of debt or liability, then no offence shall be made out against the accused. 20. In the instant matter, the accused alleges that Shri Kishan Lal came to his office on 04.03.2004. Shri Kishan Lal manhandled and humiliated him there. It was thus under fear and coercion that he was Case No. 267/1 made to sign and give the cheque in question to Shri Kishan Lal. The accused states that an enquiry by his office was conducted in this regard. The enquiry officer has placed the enquiry report on record marked as Ex. DW1/A. This report however doesn't lend much support to the version of the accused. It states that though Kishan Lal was seen with the accused on 04.03.2004 however no altercation was witnessed by the people present. Instead the report corroborates to some extent the case of the complainant that the accused had indeed borrowed a sum of Rs. 5,000 from the complainant who was believed to be the son of Tejpal and he owed the complainant Rs. 6,500. 21. Moreover neither has the accused brought on record either his account statement or anything else to substantiate that sufficient amount was present in his account. Nor has the accused examined Tejpal Singh to further clarify his stance. There is thus no basis on which to believe that the funds weren't insufficient and this ground is thus not proved. 22. On the date of the final order the accused filed written arguments wherein the accused has raised further grounds which are Case No. 267/1 discussed below. 23. First three contentions--that there was no liability; allegations in the complaint are vague and bland and that the cheque has been admitted to be without liability

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: No. 267/1 discussed below. 23. First three contentions--that there was no liability; allegations in the complaint are vague and bland and that the cheque has been admitted to be without liability. These contention have no basis as the onus was on the accused to dispute it and he has failed to do so in his defence. It is actually the contentions of the accused which seems to be vague and made without proof. 24. Secondly, the defence has stated that the documents such as the cheque, return memo, legal notice have not been exhibited properly, is not made out as these documents have been proved as per the procedure. They have been duly exhibited and proved by the complainant and the accused has failed to disprove these documents. 25. Thirdly, in regards to the issue raised that the return memo bears no date and that as per the date of the legal notice mentioned in the complaint, the affidavit is premature and complaint is time barred, hence the complaint is liable to be dismissed. It is pertinent to note that though the return memo doesn't carry a date, however the paying slip Ex. Case No. 267/1 CW1/B1 indicates the date of 05.04.2004 which implies that the cheque would have been presented by the complainant to the bank on 05.04.2004. Thus the return memo has to be one of a date subsequent to that date. The legal notice is dated 19.04.2004. Therefore the complaint is neither premature nor time barred. 26. Fourthly, a contention is raised that filing of two affidavits is barred by law, this contention of the accused holds no water as there is no such bar in law. 27. Fifthly, Contention has been put forth that no witness was examined as regards the date of returning memo

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: by law, this contention of the accused holds no water as there is no such bar in law. 27. Fifthly, Contention has been put forth that no witness was examined as regards the date of returning memo. This contention was never raised before and if the same was to be fabricated the onus was on the defence to bring evidence to prove it. 28. Sixthly, a further argument raised is that the Complaint regarding this cheque (dated 15.03.2004) was already lodged on 04.03.2004. As per the record the only thing which could be said to be have done on 04.03.2004 is that the complainant's father and the accused Case No. 267/1 has met each other that day and that the accused had given a cheque to the complainant's father. The accused has failed to prove that the cheque given bore a date or not or whether the cheque in question is false and fabricated. In the absence of which the cheque as it is, is taken to be proved. 29. The last three contentions as to there being no specific nature of the loan finding mention in the complaint; why the loan is alleged to be without interest if it is actually a loan and that complainant and accused were never known to each other holds no legal ground and has no impact on the decision of the case. 30. The grounds raised by the learned counsel for the accused are not being supported by any evidence or material they are just barred averments and it appears that the accused is just trying to defeat the case of the complainant on frivolous grounds and most of the arguments raised have already been dealt with herein above. As there are presumptions against the accused it was the accused who had to show that the cheque was issued without any debt or liability. Case No. 267/1 FINAL ORDER. 31

title: Vide This Judgment vs . on 26 March, 2014
content: been dealt with herein above. As there are presumptions against the accused it was the accused who had to show that the cheque was issued without any debt or liability. Case No. 267/1 FINAL ORDER. 31. In the end it can be said that the complainant has proved beyond all reasonable doubts the guilt of the accused whereas the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions raised against him under Section 118 & 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act and Section 27 of General Clauses Act. Accordingly, the accused is convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. Counsel for Complainant has argued that the complainant and the convict were familiar to each other and had cordial relations and the convict taking benefit of such cordial relations, has breached the trust of the complainant. He further argued that the present complaint was filed in the year 2004 and without having any defence the convict has tried to drag the matter and therefore a strict view be taken against the convict so that right example is set and right message should go to the society. On the other hand, Ld

content: the convict has tried to drag the matter and therefore a strict view be taken against the convict so that right example is set and right message should go to the society. On the other hand, Ld. Counsel for the convict has submitted that the convict has neither tried to delay the matter and he was always ready to compound the present complainant with the complainant but the complainant was adamant to harass the convict. He has further submitted that the convict is a govt employee and in case he is sentenced to imprisonment it may effect service and therefore a lenient view may kindly be taken against the convict. Heard. Since the offences u/s 138 NI Act are on the rise and to maintain the sanctity of the negotiable instruments, the legislature has even provided for imprisonment in case of offence u/s 138 NI Act. Case No. 267/1 Perusal of the file shows that the present complaint was filed in the month of May, 2005 and since then the convict has been regularly appearing in this court, therefore, delay in trial can not be solely attributed to the convict. Therefore, this court is of the view that imprisonment shall not be apt punishment in the present case. However, the convict is sentenced to pay a fine of Rs.13,000/­ (Rs. Complainant filed its pre-summoning evidence. Considering the same, prima facie offence u/s 138 NI Act was made out. Consequently, the accused were summoned u/s 138 NI Act. Statement of accused u/s 313 Cr.PC r/w 281 Cr.PC: 5. In his statement accused admitted his signatures on the cheques in question. Accused further stated that the cheques were issued in blank as advance to the complainant against the goods to be supplied however material was not received by the accused so there is no liability qua the cheques in question towards the complainant. Accused further denied receiving of legal demand notice issued by the complainant. Defence Evidence: 6. In order to prove his defence accused stepped into the witness box as DW1 by taking the permission of this court u/s 315 Cr.PC. In his examination CC No.2219/1 5/ 15 in chief accused denied placing of order to the complainant for the supply of goods to Oswal Sugar Limited, Hoshiar Pur and Venus Sugar Limited Moradabad, U.P. and denied receiving of goods on behalf of the same. Accused further deposed that the cheques in question were lying with the complainant in blank except his signatures thereon on account of old dealings with the complainant. Accused further deposed that he has not received any payment from Oswal Sugar Limited, Hoshiar Pur and Venus Sugar Limited Moradabad, U.P. in respect of transaction in question nor he stood as guarantor to the same. Accused denied having any liability towards the complainant and also denied receiving of legal demand notice issued by the complainant. Reasons for Decision: 7

title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: nor he stood as guarantor to the same. Accused denied having any liability towards the complainant and also denied receiving of legal demand notice issued by the complainant. Reasons for Decision: 7. Accused admitted his signatures on the cheques in question and issuance of the same to the complainant, therefore, execution of the cheques stands duly proved. Once, the execution is proved, the presumptions of law u/s 118 and 139 N.I Act comes in favour of the complainant and the initial burden of proof shifts upon the accused. The presumptions of law are rebuttable. Let us see whether the accused has been able to rebut the same by adducing sufficient evidence on record or not. 8. Ld. Counsel for the accused has raised a contention that accused has never been served with the legal demand notice issued by the complainant as the same was not sent on the complete address therefore no cause of action arises. Hence the complaint is liable to be dismissed on this account. On the other hand, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that CC No.2219/1 6/ 15 accused has admitted in his cross examination that generally the correspondence is received by him at the address given on record. Which means that non mentioning of word "Sirkiwalan" does not create any hurdle for the purposes of correspondence. Hence, plea taken by the accused stands rebutted. Moreover the accused has appeared before this court upon the service of the process issued against the accused at the same address therefore, the presumption u/s 27 of General Clauses Act can be drawn and the legal notice should be deemed to have been served

title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: service of the process issued against the accused at the same address therefore, the presumption u/s 27 of General Clauses Act can be drawn and the legal notice should be deemed to have been served. The admission made by accused in his cross examination that he received the letters at his address generally if the word Sirkiwalan is not mentioned there on the address and admittedly the complainant never filed any complaint in the postal department for non service of any letter which shows that each and every correspondence is being received by the accused at the same address on which legal demand notice have been sent by the complainant to the accused. Moreover, the process issued against the accused by this court has also been served upon the accused on the same address following which the accused has appeared before this court. So, in view of the judgment passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as C.C. Alavi Haji Vs. Palapetty Muhammed and another (2007) 6 SC 555 the presumption can easily be drawn against the accused as the service of the legal notice deemed to have been effected and in view of section 27 of General clauses Act also the presumption can be drawn as the notice have been sent upon the correct address of the accused. Hence, the contention raised by the accused stands rebutted. 9. Ld. Counsel for the accused has raised two main contentions in order to rebut the presumption of law lying in favour of the complainant. The same CC No.2219/1 7/ 15 are dealt below one by one:- Firstly it is the argument of Ld. Counsel for the accused that the AR of the complainant Sh

title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: of law lying in favour of the complainant. The same CC No.2219/1 7/ 15 are dealt below one by one:- Firstly it is the argument of Ld. Counsel for the accused that the AR of the complainant Sh. Ravinder Rana is not the competent person to prosecute the present complaint as he has failed to produce the minute book nor any witness have been examined for proving his authorization. Hence, complaint should be dismissed. On the other hand ld. Counsel for the complainant argued that the board of resolution Ex.CW1/1 and Special Power of Attorney Ex.CW1/2 are already filed on record and have been duly proved by the complainant so there is no question of incompetency of the AR Ravinder Rana for filing and prosecuting the present complaint. Hence, contention raised by the accused is without any substance. It is well established law that only board of resolution / extracts of minutes of meeting is required for showing the authorisation in favour of the authorised representative and for proving the same neither the minutes of board of meeting are required nor the Directors of the company are required for deposing qua the board of resolution unless the authenticity of the same is challenged. Here is this case the accused has neither disputed the board of resolution Ex. CW-1/1 nor the Special Power of Attorney Ex.CW1/2 executed in favour of Mr. Ravinder Rana. Not even a single suggestion disputing the authenticity of document Ex.CW1/1 has been put by the accused to complainant witness Ravinder Rana. Both the documents have been duly proved by the complainant in his evidence. Merely, the non production of minutes book will not cast any doubt upon the document Ex.CW1/1. Moreover the accused did not ask the witness to produce the same

title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: by the complainant in his evidence. Merely, the non production of minutes book will not cast any doubt upon the document Ex.CW1/1. Moreover the accused did not ask the witness to produce the same. Hence, I do not find any force in the argument put forth by the ld. Counsel for the accused therefore the contention stands rebutted. I would rely upon the CC No.2219/1 8/ 15 judgment passed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in CRL.M.C. 3019/2006 & CRL.M.A.No.4950/2006, Ravi Gupta Vs. R.C Tiwari in support of my finding. 10. The other fold of argument made by ld. Counsel for the accused is that there is no document placed on record by the complainant which can show that the transaction between the complainant and the accused have taken place. Hence, the basis of the complaint is missing and the cheques are left without any consideration, therefore the accused cannot be held liable u/s 138 of NI Act. On the other hand Ld. Counsel for the complainant argued that as a matter of practice followed no written purchase order was ever placed and on the verbal orders the goods were supplied by the complainant to the accused. Admittedly, there had been transaction prior to the present transaction in question when the complainant being the sole distributor of M/s. Jindal pipes supplied goods to the accused on verbal orders without any written purchase order

content: prior to the present transaction in question when the complainant being the sole distributor of M/s. Jindal pipes supplied goods to the accused on verbal orders without any written purchase order. Counsel for the accused submitted that neither the original invoices nor there carbon copies have been produced by any complainant witness so there photocopies placed on record cannot be ready into evidence. title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: placed on record cannot be ready into evidence. Hence, there is no proof to show that the goods have been supplied by the complainant to the accused. While considering the above contention raised by the accused and the argument put forth by the complainant to the said contention few things have been cleared. Firstly, there is no dispute to the fact that complainant and accused had transactions in the past as well apart from the questioned transaction. Secondly, admittedly no written purchase order were placed by the accused to the complainant in respect of previous business transactions and the fact claimed by the complainant that there is no such practice followed by the parties in the said trade is also not disputed by the accused at any point of time. On the contrary the testimony of the accused as DW1 has many infirmities and contradictions that wipe out its veracity. Secondly, no plausible explanation came from the accused that why the cheques in question were issued by him to the complainant

title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: of account whereas he failed to produce a single document qua the same. Secondly, no plausible explanation came from the accused that why the cheques in question were issued by him to the complainant. It is highly improbable to believe that blank signed cheques of accused being a valuable document remained in the possession of the complainant without any purpose and the accused did not take any steps either to prevent the misuse of the same by stopping the payment through his banker or for recovering back his cheques by taking some legal recourse. Accused has been so callous that he does not even remember the time or date when he issued the cheques to the complainant company. title: Titled As C.C. Alavi Haji vs . Palapetty Muhammed And Another ... on 24 January, 2014
content: alleged in the present complaint. Again, no books of accounts or any other record has been produced by the accused to that effect. CC No.2219/1 11/ 15 12. I agree to the argument put forth by the ld. Counsel for the accused that the invoices / bills placed on record by the complainant are not the original or carbon copies and are only the photocopies of the same, which cannot be read into evidence as not proved in accordance to law but the mere fact that the original invoice not filed on record does not dis-entitle the complainant to establish his case. In the complaint u/s 138 of NI Act the complainant has to establish that the cheques in question have been issued in discharge of legal liability by the accused and if the issuance of cheque is proved the presumption of law u/s 139 comes in favour of the complainant. The initial burden of proof is upon the accused to prove that the same was not issued for any consideration. If in the instant case the invoices / bills are set apart, the testimony of the complainant witnesses are sufficient to prove the case of the complainant beyond reasonable doubt. As per the judgment passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in a case titled as Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan Criminal Appeal No. 1020 of 2010, the accused is only expected to rebut the presumptions of law on the scale of preponderance of probabilities by adducing sufficient evidence on record. In the present case, no cogent evidence has been adduced by the accused to probabalise his plea of defence. Therefore, no reasonable probable defence has been raised which can compel the court to believe in its existence. The accused has drastically failed to explain his stand of issuance of cheques to the complainant and his failure to get back the same

Act and could not raise a reasonable probable defence. 14. All the essential ingredients of offence u/s 138 are made out. title: Addl. Commissioner Of Income-Tax vs S.R.Y. Ankineedu Prasad on 26 August, 1977
content: JUDGMENT S. Obul Reddy, C.J. 1. The assessee, S. R. Y. Ankineedu Prasad, is an individual. He purchased during the year of account ending with March 31, 1966, 48,123 equity shares of a public limited company called "Challapalli Sugars Ltd." from his brother for Rs. 6,58,804, i.e., at Rs. 13'69 per share. This purchase of equity shares in Challapalli Sugars Ltd. was made by him in order to obtain controlling interest in the said company in which he (the assessee) and his another brother had substantial shareholdings. The consideration paid by him for purchasing the shares in Challapalli Sugars Ltd. consisted partly of cash of Rs. 1,00,000 and partly by transfer of 12,724 equity shares in K. C. P. Ltd., Vuyyur, another public limited company. He transferred the equity shares in K. C. P. Ltd. at the face value of Rs. 10 per share and for the balance of consideration of Rs. 4,34,346, he executed a promissory note in favour of his brother.
