(III) ISSUANCE OF THE CHEQUE IN QUESTION IN DISCHARGE OF LEGAL DEBT OR LIABILITY. 14. The crux of penal liability under Section 138 of the NI Act is that the cheque must be issued by the drawer for the discharge of any legal debt or liability. Existing of legal debt or liability is sine qua non for constituting the offence. 15. Before I advert to the above said ingredients, it is imperative for me to notice the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments.--Un­ til the contrary is proved, the following presumptions CC No. 4750/14 Indiabulls Vs. Sube Singh Page7 /11 shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, nego­ tiated or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be pre­ sumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 16. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Ja­ nardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of "preponder­ ance of probabilities". 17

title: Indiabulls Financial Services ... vs . on 27 May, 2014
content: 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of "preponder­ ance of probabilities". 17. In Rangappa Versus Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities' and if the ac­ cused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the ex­ istence of a legally enforceable debt or liability the prosecution can fail and for this the accused can even rely on the materials submitted by the com­ plainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. 18. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judg­ ments the position of law which emerges is that once the execution of the promissory note is admitted as has happened in the instant case, the pre­ sumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is rebuttable. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused discharges the initial onus of proof show­ ing that the existence of consideration was improbable or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would CC No. 4750/14 Indiabulls Vs. Sube Singh Page8 /11 disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instru­ ment

title: Indiabulls Financial Services ... vs . on 27 May, 2014
content: prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would CC No. 4750/14 Indiabulls Vs. Sube Singh Page8 /11 disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instru­ ment. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponder­ ance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he re­ lies. In case, where the accused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the complainant would in­ variably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 19. Now coming to the case in hand, in the instant case the accused has examined himself as DW­1 and has admitted that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/D bears his signatures. Further the accused has admitted that he has taken loan of Rs. 35,000/­ from the Complainant in the year 2005. However with respect to the cheque in Question Ex. CW1/D the accused has stated that he has not issued the same in discharge of his liability and the same was given by him to the complainant as a security at the time of taking of the loan in the year 2005. 20. As per the statement of account Ex. CW1/X which is placed on record by CW­1 it is also clear that the loan of Rs. 35412/­ was granted by the complainant to the accused on 07.09.2005 and the same was to be repaid by the accused in 36 monthly installments of 1865/­ each. Therefore it is evident that the entire loan amount was to be repaid by the accused till September 2008. Interestingly, perusal of statement of account Ex. CW1/X reveals that a payment of Rs

title: Indiabulls Financial Services ... vs . on 27 May, 2014
content: each. Therefore it is evident that the entire loan amount was to be repaid by the accused till September 2008. Interestingly, perusal of statement of account Ex. CW1/X reveals that a payment of Rs. 1900/­ has been received by the complainant from the accused on 11.09.2007 and thereafter no payment has been received by the complainant from the accused till 31.01.2011 when last payment of Rs. 4000/­ is alleged to have been given by the accused on 31.01.2011. It is surprisingly to see that when loan was to be repaid by the accused till September 2008 the complainant chooses to remain silent for more than 2 years. It is highly improbable that a finance company would remain silent when no payment is being received by it from the borrower for more than 2 year after expiry of the loan tenure. Further the complainant has not even disclosed as to when the accused has approached them for the CC No. 4750/14 Indiabulls Vs. Sube Singh Page9 /11 purposes of handing over of the cheque in question Ex. CW1/D. 21. Further it is the case of the complainant that in discharge of his outstanding liability arising out of the agreement dated 07.09.2005 the accused agreed to pay a sum of Rs. 37,604/ vide cheque in question Ex. CW1/D bearing No.85472 dated 16.05.2012 i.e. six years after the agreement. This acknowledgment even as per the complaint was much after the statutory period of three years which is the prescribed period of limitation for the recovery of an outstanding amount. Furthermore an acknowledgment to be encompassed within the ambit of Section 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act has to be an acknowledgment in writing as well as within the prescribed period of limitation. It was thus not a valid acknowledgment as the Cheque in question Ex

title: Indiabulls Financial Services ... vs . on 27 May, 2014
content: 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act has to be an acknowledgment in writing as well as within the prescribed period of limitation. It was thus not a valid acknowledgment as the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/D was clearly outside the period of limitation. The complainant has also not placed on record any document which states that there was an acknowledgment on the part of the accused well before the prescribed period. Therefore, the cheque cannot be even said to be issued in respect of legally recoverable debt 22. In Vijay Polymers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr 162 (2009) DLT 23 relying upon the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sasseriyil Joseph vs. Devassia 2001 Crl.LJ 24 the Hon'ble Delhi High court had held that cheques issued on a time barred debt would not fall within the definition of 'legally enforceable debt' which is the essential requirement for a complaint under Section 138 of NI Act. 23. In the instant case, the cheque which is the subject matter of this complaint was for the discharge of a liability of a debt arising out of the agreement dated 07.09.2005 which debt had become time barred. Therefore this debt was not a legally enforceable debt within the meaning of Section 138 of the NI Act. 24. All the aforesaid circumstances/factors rebut the presumptions provided under Section 139 of the NI Act. This court do not find any force in the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the Complainant that CC No. 4750/14 Indiabulls Vs. Sube Singh Page10 /11 the accused has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. Presumption is not in itself evidence but it only enables a party in whose favour it exists to show that he has a prima facie case

title: Indiabulls Financial Services ... vs . on 27 May, 2014
content: has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. Presumption is not in itself evidence but it only enables a party in whose favour it exists to show that he has a prima facie case. In the case in hand the presumptions under Section 139 of NI Act alone cannot be the sole basis to prove the case of the complainant. The materials and evidence available on the record brought by the complainant do not bridge the gap. Therefore, I hereby hold that the Complainant has not been able to prove and substantiate the allegations that the cheque in question CW1/D was issued by the accused in discharge of legally recoverable debt or other liability. 25. Furthermore, mere non payment of cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of legal notice is not itself sufficient to fasten any liability U/s 138 of the NI Act as it is established that the cheque in question was not issued by the accused in discharge of a legal recoverable debt. 26. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I hereby hold that the complainant has not been able to prove and substantiate its allegation against the accused. Accordingly, accused Sube Singh S/o Sh. Fateh Singh is hereby acquitted for the offence u/s 138 NI Act. This judgment contains 11 pages. WHETHER THE CHEQUE IN QUESTION HAS BEEN ISSUED IN DISCHARGE OF ANY LEGAL DEBT OR OTHER LIABILITY: 9. Some overwriting have also been observed at figures of dated i.e. '19'; figures of amount '1,9......' as well as in writings 'One.....', it is also observed that these overwritten strokes were made in the figures of amount i.e. 1,90,000/­. 3. No sign of alteration / addition / erasers could be observed in the writing '....... ninty ..........' in the amount 'One Lakh ninty thousand only....' and the ink used for writings show similar behaviour under different lighting conditions. Thus as per the FSL report there is no alteration, addition or erasion in amount in words, however, there is apparent alteration in amount in figures as in the original amount was Rs1,10,000/­ which was subsequently changed to Rs. 1,90,000/­. More interestingly there is a photocopy of the cheque as Mark X­1 in which the amount in words has been written as One Lakh Ten Thousand only

title: Cc No.110/13 Satpal Singh vs . C.P. Chauhan Page No. 1 Of Pages 15 on 21 December, 2013
content: which was subsequently changed to Rs. 1,90,000/­. More interestingly there is a photocopy of the cheque as Mark X­1 in which the amount in words has been written as One Lakh Ten Thousand only. On visual comparison of the CC No.110/13 SATPAL SINGH Vs. C.P. CHAUHAN page no. 11 of Pages 15 photocopy and original cheque everything appears to be similar except the word "Ten" & "Ninty" in amount in words and figure "9" and "1" in amount in figures. Thus apparently there is a doubt if the cheque was originally of Rs.1,10,000/­ and was subsequently changed to Rs.1,90,000/­. It can not be established who made these changes, whether the same were made by the accused prior to handingover the cheque to the complainant or if the same were done by the complainant after receiving the cheque of Rs.1,10,000/­ from the accused. It is established principle of law that whenever two views are possible the one in favour of the accused has to be accepted. Hence, in the present matter there is material alteration in amount in figures which makes the cheque in question void against the accused as per Section 87 of NI Act. iii) The cheque in question was dishonored due to the reason 'drawers signature differ' but the accused never disputed his signatures on the cheque. His main defence since beginning was that there is alteration in figure on the cheque in question this shows bonafide of the defence, as if the accused was not bonafide he could have said that the cheque does not bear his signatures as the cheque was itself dishonored due to difference in signature of the drawer. iv) It is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that there is promissory note Ex

title: Cc No.110/13 Satpal Singh vs . C.P. Chauhan Page No. 1 Of Pages 15 on 21 December, 2013
content: not bear his signatures as the cheque was itself dishonored due to difference in signature of the drawer. iv) It is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that there is promissory note Ex. DW1/DX1 on record admittedly signed by the accused wherein accused has admitted the receipt of Rs.1,90,000/­ from the complainant and CC No.110/13 SATPAL SINGH Vs. C.P. CHAUHAN page no. 12 of Pages 15 had also promised to pay the same, hence, the defence taken by the accused is frivolous and he is liable to make the payment of Rs.1,90,000/­ to the complainant. On the other hand it is submitted on behalf of the accused that this promissory note was signed by the accused at point 'A' and thumb impression was put at point 'B' at the time when this promissory note was blank. This promissory note is dated 18.11.2008 and the same was always in the possession of the complainant, however, the complainant did not mention anything regarding the same in his legal notice, complaint, affidavit or cross examination. It's only at the time of cross examination of the accused when this document was put to the accused for the first time. Admissibility of this document on record disputed by Ld. Defence Counsel, he also made an application to reject this document, the application is hereby dismissed as the document was duly filed on record. At the same time this Court has to say that this document does not inspire confidence of this Court as if this document was a genuine document and was always in the possession of the complainant, then the complainant should have filed this document along with complaint or should have mentioned this document in his legal notice, complaint or evidence

title: Cc No.110/13 Satpal Singh vs . C.P. Chauhan Page No. 1 Of Pages 15 on 21 December, 2013
content: in the possession of the complainant, then the complainant should have filed this document along with complaint or should have mentioned this document in his legal notice, complaint or evidence. The silence kept by the complainant in respect of this document creates a doubt if this document has been subsequently prepared after hearing and understanding the defence of the accused. Thus this document is not a reliable piece of evidence. The telephonic conversation CD of which is filed on record by the accused can CC No.110/13 SATPAL SINGH Vs. C.P. CHAUHAN page no. 13 of Pages 15 not be considered by this Court as the same has not been proved as per law. v) In the decision reported as 2006 (6) SCC 39 M.S. Narayana Menon @ Mani vs. State of Kerala & Anr., it was observed as under:­ "52. ............. If the defence is acceptable as probable the cheque therefore cannot be held to have been issued in discharge of the debt as, for example, if a cheque is issued for security or for any other purpose the same would not come within the purview of Section 138 of the Act. It has also been held by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Kumar D v. State of Delhi and anr. (Manu / DE /1538/2011) that: 9. Plain reading of the above provision of law shows that criminal liability under Section 138 NI Act is attracted only if the dishonored cheque was issued for the discharge in whole or in part of any existing debt or liability. The Section does not apply to a cheque issued to meet future liability which may arise on happening of some contingency

title: Cc No.110/13 Satpal Singh vs . C.P. Chauhan Page No. 1 Of Pages 15 on 21 December, 2013
content: issued for the discharge in whole or in part of any existing debt or liability. The Section does not apply to a cheque issued to meet future liability which may arise on happening of some contingency. Thus, it is clear that a post­dated cheque, if issued for discharge of a debt due, in the event of dishonor, would attract section 138 if the NI Act but a cheque issued not for an existing debt / liability but issued by way of security for meeting some future CC No.110/13 SATPAL SINGH Vs. C.P. CHAUHAN page no. 14 of Pages 15 contingency would not attract Section 138 of the NI Act. 16. From the above stated discussion it is established that complainant fails to prove his case. On the other hand the accused has been able to raise a probable defence that the cheque in question was given as security for arranging loan in his favour and the same was of Rs.1,10,000/­ only. It is established principle of law that the accused has only to create a doubt in the version of the complainant, while the complainant has to prove the guilt of the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt. In Kulvinder Singh v. Kafil Ahmed 2013(1) DCR 417 it was held by Hon'ble High Court: "The basic principle in criminal law is that the guilt of the accused must be proved beyond reasonable doubt and if there is a slightest doubt about the commission of an offence then the benefit has to occurred to him". 17. Thus from the above stated discussion it is clear that the accused has been able to prove his defence. He has rebutted the presumptions U/s 118 (b) and 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act. Considering the entire circumstances and evidence on record, it stands duly proved that the cheque in question was not issued and drawn in discharge of liability or a legally recoverable debt of the accused. 18

title: Cc No.110/13 Satpal Singh vs . C.P. Chauhan Page No. 1 Of Pages 15 on 21 December, 2013
content: the entire circumstances and evidence on record, it stands duly proved that the cheque in question was not issued and drawn in discharge of liability or a legally recoverable debt of the accused. 18. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I am of the considered opinion that the complainant has failed to prove its case against the accused, while accused has proved his defence. Accordingly, CC No.110/13 SATPAL SINGH Vs. C.P. CHAUHAN page no. 15 of Pages 15 accused Sh. C.P. Chauhan, S/o Sh. Surender Singh, R/o D­51, New Defence Colony, Bhopura, Ghaziabad (U.P.) stands acquitted of the offence U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act. Announced in the open court today i.e. 21.12.2013 (GAJENDER SINGH NAGAR) MM:KKD:DELHI:21.12.2013 Containing 15 pages all signed by the presiding officer. (GAJENDER SINGH NAGAR) MM:KKD:DELHI:21.12.2013

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE MUNICIPAL MAGISTRATE­01, KKD, EAST, NEW DELHI Presided by : Ms. Deepti Devesh Complaint No. 430/13 Unique ID No. 02402R0173802013 PS: Krishna Nagar Sukhmal Chand Jain, S/o Late Sh. Bhikkimal Jain, R/o A­35, Gali No.3, Delhi­51 ........Complainant VERSUS Praveen Kumar Jain, S/o Sh. Sukhbir Singh Jain, R/o H.No. 18, Gali No.13, New East Azad Nagar, Near Water Tank, Delhi­51 ........Accused Complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Ac t Offence complained of : U/s 138 NI Act Date of commission of offence : 12.05.2013 Plea of Accused : Not guilty Final Arguments heard & Concluded on : 14.11.2014 Date of decision of the case : 27.11.2014 Final Order : Acquittal BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE: 1 Vide this Judgment I shall finally dispose off this complaint U/s 138 CC No. 430/13 page no. 1 /12 NI Act by complainant Sukhmal Chand Jain against the accused Praveen Kumar Jain. The complainant's story in brief is that that in the first week of December 2012 the accused had approached the complainant for a friendly loan of Rs.90,000/­. On that the complainant gave loan of Rs.90,000/­ to the accused on the basis of friendly relationship with him. In order to repay the loan, the accused issued two cheques i.e. bearing no. 273697 dated 03.01.2013 for Rs.50,000/­ & bearing no. 273695 dated 03.01.2013 for Rs.40,000/­, both are drawn on ICICI Bank, Connaught Place branch in favor of the complainant and had assured the complainant that the same shall be honored on their presentation. The said cheques were presented by the complainant which was returned vide return memo dated 25.03.2013 with endorsement of "Account closed ". Thereafter the complainant issued legal notice dated 22.04.2013

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: cheques were presented by the complainant which was returned vide return memo dated 25.03.2013 with endorsement of "Account closed ". Thereafter the complainant issued legal notice dated 22.04.2013. The complainant has also stated that despite service of the legal notice the accused did not make any payment in discharge of his liability. 2 After the filing of the complaint and closing of pre­summoning evidence, vide order dated 04.06.2013, summons were issued to the accused for the offence U/s 138 NI Act. The accused was admitted to bail on 09.09.2013 which was confirmed on 09.10.2013. Thereafter notice U/s 251 Cr. PC was framed upon the accused on 09.09.2013 to which he did not plead guilty and claimed trial. 3 Application U/s 145(2) NI Act was filed by the accused on 09.10.2013, which was allowed vide order dated 29.10.2013. Thereafter the matter was fixed for CE. 4 In order to prove its case, the complainant examined himself as CW­1 who reiterated the contents of the complaint on Oath and filed evidence by way of affidavit. CW­1 exhibited original cheque bearing no. 273697 dated 03.01.2013 as Ex. CW1/A, cheque bearing no. 273695 dated 03.01.2013 as Ex. CW1/B, return memo dated 25.03.2013 as Ex. CW1/C & Ex. CW1/D, legal notice dated CC No. 430/13 page no. 2 /12 22.04.2013 as Ex. CW1/E, Registered post receipt as Ex. CW1/F, net tracking reports as Ex. CW1/G & Ex. CW1/H. During the cross examination of CW­1, he has also filed on record photocopy of his ITR as Ex. CW1/I (Colly). Thereafter CW­ 1 was cross examined and discharged. Complainant evidence closed vide separate statement of the complainant. 5 After that on 13.05.2014 the accused was examined U/s 313 Cr. PC and his statement was duly recorded

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: examined and discharged. Complainant evidence closed vide separate statement of the complainant. 5 After that on 13.05.2014 the accused was examined U/s 313 Cr. PC and his statement was duly recorded. All the incriminating evidence were put to the accused, to which accused submitted that he had not taken any loan of Rs.90,000/­ from the complainant and he had given cheques in question to the complainant as security as he had taken loans from the complainant in year 2010 and the cheques in question were given to the complainant in the year 2010 itself. It is further stated by the accused that he had taken loans from the complainant on a number of occasions, which used to be of Rs.20,000/­ that were to be paid by daily installments of Rs.500/­ running into 48 days. He admitted receiving legal notice from the complainant. He further stated that his security cheques have been misused by the complainant. The accused also stated that he wanted to lead defence evidence. 6 Accused examined himself as DW­1. He deposed in his examination in chief that he knows the complainant for last 13­14 years and that he had taken several loans from the complainant beginning from 12.12.2010 till 10.05.2011 and as on 01.11.2010 he was still to pay Rs.32,300/­ as interest to the complainant. He further deposed that he had given four cheques to the complainant, out of which two were blank and two cheques were filled but undated. He further sated that the complainant did not return any of his cheques and that when he took a loan of Rs.20,000/­ from the complainant @ interest of 20% per month, then the complainant asked him to give cheque of double the amount i.e. Rs.40,000/­

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: any of his cheques and that when he took a loan of Rs.20,000/­ from the complainant @ interest of 20% per month, then the complainant asked him to give cheque of double the amount i.e. Rs.40,000/­. He further stated that he has to pay Rs.40,000/­ against the loan of Rs.20,000/­ and he has already paid Rs.19,000/­ to the complainant, when he asked for a further loan of Rs.20,000/­. At that time the complainant asked him to give CC No. 430/13 page no. 3 /12 another cheque of Rs.50,000/­. He also produced the ledger account of complainant maintained by him which is exhibited as Ex. DW1/A and the cash book maintained by the accused which is exhibited as Ex. DW1/B. Thereafter DW­1 was cross examined and discharged, defence evidence was closed and matter was fixed for final arguments. 7 Final arguments were addressed and heard on behalf of both the parties. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has reiterated the averments made in the complaint. He has argued that the accused has failed to disclose any defence. Therefore all ingredients of U/s 138 NI Act stands fulfilled and the accused is liable to be convicted. 8 On the other hand, the Counsel for the accused has argued that the present complaint should be dismissed as there is no legal liability upon the accused to pay the complainant as no loan of Rs.90,000/­ was ever taken by the accused from the complainant. Infact the accused handed over the cheques in question to the complainant as security for loans previously taken from the complainant. He further argued that the accused has already returned a substantial amount of the loan taken from the complainant which is also shown from the entries made in Ex. DW1/B by the accused. 9 Arguments advanced by both the parties have been heard at length

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: a substantial amount of the loan taken from the complainant which is also shown from the entries made in Ex. DW1/B by the accused. 9 Arguments advanced by both the parties have been heard at length. I have also perused the judicial record. 10 For offence U/s 138 NI Act the necessary ingredients to be proved are: a) That the accused had a legal liability / debt towards the complainant. b) That the accused issued a cheque in discharge of the said legal liability / debt. c) That the accused was maintaining a bank account for the cheque issued by him. CC No. 430/13 page no. 4 /12 d) That the cheque was presented by the complainant within its validity period. e) That the cheque was dishonored on his presentation. f) That the complainant issued legal demand notice within 30 days from the date of dishonor of the cheque. g) That the accused failed to pay within 15 days of receipt of legal demand notice. If the above ingredients are proved then an offence punishable U/s 138 NI Act is committed. 11 In the present case, the accused has stated in the notice framed U/s 251 Cr. PC that the cheques in question were issued to the complainant as security / advance payment for business transaction along with two other cheques. He also admitted that the details on the cheques in question were filled by him except the date. He has reiterated the same in his statement U/s 313 Cr. PC. He has admitted receiving legal notice from the complainant. Hence, the disputed question to be decided is whether the cheques in question were issued in discharge of legal liability / debt to the complainant. 12 Now, the question of liability of the accused to pay the complainant shall be dealt with

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: is whether the cheques in question were issued in discharge of legal liability / debt to the complainant. 12 Now, the question of liability of the accused to pay the complainant shall be dealt with. In the present case the complainant has averred that the cheques in question were issued against discharge of liability arising out of loan transaction between the parties. Since the cheques in question are bearing the name of complainant and the present complaint has been filed by the complainant in his own name therefore, presumption arises U/s 118­A & 139 NI Act in favour of the complainant that the cheques were issued in discharge of a legal liability. Thus, the onus to rebut this presumption is on the accused. The accused has disputed his legal liability to make payment on the ground that there was no loan transaction of Rs.90,000/­ between the parties and that the cheques in question were security cheques which have been misused by the complainant. CC No. 430/13 page no. 5 /12 13 It is true that for offence U/s 138 NI Act, the accused is not expected to prove his defense beyond reasonable doubt in order to rebut the statutory presumption. Same has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513. It is also well settled law that in order to rebut the statutory presumption in favour of the complainant, the accused need not examine himself in evidence or adduce any other defence evidence also. The accused can rebut the statutory presumption on the material already available on record or such cogent evidence can be the cross­examination of the complainant also. The same has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde 2008 Cri.L.J 1172 (SC)

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: such cogent evidence can be the cross­examination of the complainant also. The same has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde 2008 Cri.L.J 1172 (SC). Now, it is to be examined if the accused has been able to rebut the statutory presumption U/s 118 & 139 of NI Act on basis of defence evidence or material available on record. 14 The complainant in the instant case has failed to mention the date of the loan amount either in his complaint or evidence by way of affidavit or in his cross examination. He has vaguely stated that the loan was advanced in December, 2012. He has further stated in his cross­examination that the cheques in question were given in the same day as the loan bearing date of January 2013. In the case of G. Veerashyam v. S. Shivashankar & Anr by Hon'ble Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal no. 358/2003 decided on 26.06.2007, it has been held that where the complainant failed to mention even the date of the loan then the fact of advancement of loan is itself doubtful. 15 The complainant has also failed to show his source of income for advancing the loan to the accused. He has stated in his cross­examination that his gross income must be around Rs.2,50,000/­ to Rs.4,00,000/­. He has also placed on record his ITR for the assessment year 2013­14 wherein his gross income is stated to be Rs.2,55,100/­. Furthermore he has furnished his computation for ITR 2013­14 wherein he has shown several loans advanced to different persons including to the accused as on 31.03.2013. The total amounts of CC No. 430/13 page no. 6 /12 loan advanced to all these persons including the accused is stated to be Rs.7,60,000/­. Firstly, the veracity of computation filed along with ITR 2013­14 i.e. Ex

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: of CC No. 430/13 page no. 6 /12 loan advanced to all these persons including the accused is stated to be Rs.7,60,000/­. Firstly, the veracity of computation filed along with ITR 2013­14 i.e. Ex. CW1/I (colly) is itself doubtful as the same has not even been stamped and signed by concerned C.A. or even the complainant himself. Secondly, even if the computation is assumed to be true then the complainant has failed to show any source of income for advancing such huge amount of loan totaling Rs.7,60,000/­. Further, it is not the case of the complainant that the alleged loan amount of Rs.90,000/­ has been advanced by way of any written acknowledgement or by way of cheque for which some documentary proof has been brought on record. Infact the complainant has admitted that the loan amount was given in cash. He has also stated that the said cash was available with him and that there is no limit of cash kept by him in his house in his cross­ examination. Such testimony of the complainant whereby his gross income is shown to be limited to approximately Rs.2,50,000/­, and admission that there is no limit of cash kept at his home, makes the complainant's story highly doubtful that the alleged loan transaction ever took place. No loan agreement has also been placed on record by the complainant. 16 The complainant has also admitted in his cross­examination that he has given friendly loans to other persons also. He has also admitted that he has not received any amount back from other persons also. He has further admitted that he has taken cheques from other persons also at the time of giving loan to them. These admissions of the complainant clearly establish that the complainant frequently gives friendly loans and along with it takes cheques from the persons to whom loans are given

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: loan to them. These admissions of the complainant clearly establish that the complainant frequently gives friendly loans and along with it takes cheques from the persons to whom loans are given. The same method has been adopted by the complainant in the instant case also. Since, this is routine practice with the complainant to take cheques at the time of giving loans itself, it appears to be probable that the cheques so taken including from the accused, were taken as security. Further, these admissions also established that the complainant has not received back any amount from any persons and therefore, it again became doubtful as to how the complainant had arranged money to give loan to the CC No. 430/13 page no. 7 /12 present accused also when his previous loans have not been returned to him. 17 Further, if the complainant story is assumed to the true that the cheques in question were given on the day of loan with date of January, 2013 mentioned on them, then also the complainant has offered no reasonable explanation for not depositing the cheque in question on the date mentioned on the cheques in question when they became due and payable to the complainant. He has admitted that he has deposited the cheques in question on 22.03.2013. The complainant has stated in his cross­examination that he had requested the accused to return his money and only after that he deposited the cheque in question. No written demand notice has also been produced by the complainant to show that he had asked the accused to return his money before presenting the cheques in question

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: the cheque in question. No written demand notice has also been produced by the complainant to show that he had asked the accused to return his money before presenting the cheques in question. Hence, without any reasonable explanation coming from the complainant about whey he waited for almost three months before depositing cheques in question, it appears to be probable that the complainant waited for so long because the cheques in question were meant to be security cheques only. 18 Further, the complainant has stated that the cheques in question were given on the same day as the loan transaction of Rs.90,000/­. Any reasonable person would give only one cheque for repayment of one loan, however, the complainant has claimed that the accused has given two cheques of Rs.50,000/­ & Rs.40,000/­ respectively for repaying the loan of Rs.90,000/­ on the same day. The complainant story also appears to be unbelievable because if the cheques in question were issued on the same day then the accused would have issued the cheques in question in continuous series, but the cheques in question are bearing numbers 273695 & 273697, which are not in continuous series. Further, the accused has stated in his examination in chief that he had earlier issued the cheque for Rs.40,000/­ against a loan of Rs.20,000/­ to the complainant and then later on issued the cheque of Rs.50,000/­ against another loan of Rs.20,000/­ from the complainant. The accused's story appears to be more credible in the face of the fact that the cheques in question are not of CC No. 430/13 page no. 8 /12 continuous series and therefore they must have issued one after the other on different dates as claimed by the accused

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: of the fact that the cheques in question are not of CC No. 430/13 page no. 8 /12 continuous series and therefore they must have issued one after the other on different dates as claimed by the accused. 19 The complainant has also admitted taking loans from his sons Neeraj Kumar Jain & Pravesh Kumar Jain which has also been shown by him in his ITR. In the judgment of J. Prakashan v. P.K. Surenderan 2007(4) CCC 713 (SC), the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that where the complainant shown to be himself borrowing money, his capacity to advance loan is doubtful. 20 From the discussion above it is clear that the material coming on record through cross­examination of the complainant shows that the accused has been able to discharge the burden of rebutting the statutory presumptions in favour of the complainant on the basis of preponderance of probability. Now it is to be examined if the accused has been able to strengthen the rebuttal by adducing evidence in his favour. 21 The accused has stated in his notice framed U/s 251 Cr. PC that the cheques in question were given as security along with two other cheques to the complainant. He has also stated that he did not write the date on the cheques in question while all other details have been filled by him. He has reiterated this in his statement U/s 313 Cr. PC where in he has stated that the cheques in question were given in 2010 for loans taken from the complainant in 2010. He has stated the same under oath in his examination in chief wherein he has stated that he had given cheque in question along with two other cheques to the complainant after filling in all the details on the cheque in question except for the date. Therefore the accused has been consistent throughout the trial in his statements

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: two other cheques to the complainant after filling in all the details on the cheque in question except for the date. Therefore the accused has been consistent throughout the trial in his statements. Further, not only has he been consistent, but he has been diligent in maintaining record of loans taken from the complainant and has provided the exact date of loan with the loan amount in his examination in chief. Infact he has confronted the complainant with the same dates for different loan amounts during his cross­ examination by way of suggestions. On the other hand the complainant, who is CC No. 430/13 page no. 9 /12 the lender in the instant case has not been able to tell any exact date for the loan given to the accused and has also not been able to furnish any written record pertaining to the loan taken in December 2012. This is so, when the complainant being the lender, as a reasonable prudent person should be more interested in keeping record of loans advanced to the accused. Therefore, viewing the statement of the complainant where date of the loan has not been specifically mentioned alongside the statement of the accused where he has given complete details of different loans taken with loan amount on different dates, the statement of the accused appears to be more believable than the complainant's. 22 The accused has also produced his cash book maintained by him showing payment made to the complainant on different dates for loans taken from him as Ex. DW1/B, wherein the relevant entry encircled in red from pages1­ 122. Counsel for the complainant has argued that Ex. DW1/B is not reliable as this is the document prepared by and under the control of the accused and therefore, the accused can easily manipulate the same

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: for the complainant has argued that Ex. DW1/B is not reliable as this is the document prepared by and under the control of the accused and therefore, the accused can easily manipulate the same. He has also stated that during the cross­examination of the accused it has been brought on record that the accused has made wrong entries also which he has corrected by overwriting on the wrong entry and therefore, the same is not reliable. There is no doubt that the document is prepared by the accused himself in his own handwriting but it is no ground for outright dismissal of the evidence adduced by the accused being unreliable because it was under the control of the accused. It is natural that the accused would be the best person aware of the entire facts and circumstances of any given case and therefore is also the best person to adduce evidence in his defence. Counsel for the complainant has not been able to place anything on record to establish that Ex. DW1/B is a manipulated document. Further, perusal of Ex. DW1/B shows that the accused maintained diligent record not only in respect of complainant but in respect of other persons and his other transactions and has been maintaining the same for a long time i.e. since 01.11.2010. It does not appear to be credible that the accused would manipulate a document which contains entries since 2010 while he has been examined and cross­examined in CC No. 430/13 page no. 10 /12 September 2014. Infact Ex. DW1/B predates even filing of the present case which has been filed on 01.06.2013 and therefore, it appears to be incredible that the accused would manipulate or create false records for three years prior to the date of filing of the complaint

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: which has been filed on 01.06.2013 and therefore, it appears to be incredible that the accused would manipulate or create false records for three years prior to the date of filing of the complaint. The accused has also produced in his defence his ledger account of the complainant maintained by him as Ex. DW1/A wherein he has written about all the loans taken from the complainant since 01.11.2010 on page no.19 at point 'A'. Both the documents ex. DW1/A & Ex. DW1/B corroborates the consistent stands taken by the accused throughout the trial that he has taken loans from the complainant since 2010 and has also made payment to the complainant in small amounts since 2010. 23 Counsel for the complainant has argued that the accused has contradicted himself while putting suggestions to the complainant in his cross­ examination. He has pointed out that in one suggestion he has stated that he had taken loan from the complainant starting from 12.12.2010, while in another suggestion he has stated that he has started repaying the loan taken from the complainant from 02.11.2010. Therefore, it is clear from the contradiction that the accused started returning the loan even before taking the loan and thus the defence of the accused is not tenable. The contradiction pointed out by the counsel for the complainant is a minor contradiction wherein the accused due to long gap between the date of loan and the date of cross­examination of the complainant resulting in natural memory loss could have mistakenly forgotten to suggest loan taken from the complainant in the month of November 2010. Infact he has stated in his cross­examination that he had taken the first loan from the complainant on 01.11.2010 and then starting repaying the loan amount from 02.11.2010. Ex

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: of November 2010. Infact he has stated in his cross­examination that he had taken the first loan from the complainant on 01.11.2010 and then starting repaying the loan amount from 02.11.2010. Ex. DW1/A also corroborates the statement of the accused wherein the beginning the loan from the complainant is shown to be on 01.11.2010. Hence, such minor contradiction which is possibly the result of memory loss due to the long gap in time period is not sufficient to discredit entire defence of the accused. CC No. 430/13 page no. 11 /12 24 In view of the above discussion, the complainant has been unable to prove the loan transaction and therefore there is no question of any legal liability / debt of the accused towards the complainant and the present complaint is liable to be dismissed on this ground alone. Since the complainant has failed to file any document on record to show the liability of the accused, hence, the defence of the accused that the cheques were given undated to the complainant and that the same have been misused appears to be probable and credible defence. It is well settled that even though the statutory presumption for offence U/s 138 NI Act is in favour of the complainant, still, the prosecution is burdened with standing on its own legs and has to necessarily prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. In the instant case, there is no written loan agreement, no written receipt, doubt about the capacity of the complainant to advance such loan, no date mentioned for the loan, the cheques not being in continuous series and high probability that the cheques in question were given as security are enough to puncture holes in the complainant's story

title: Sukhmal Chand Jain vs Unknown on 27 November, 2014
content: mentioned for the loan, the cheques not being in continuous series and high probability that the cheques in question were given as security are enough to puncture holes in the complainant's story. Cumulatively, the above circumstances are sufficient to rebut the presumption arising in favour of the complainant U/s 139 NI Act. Accordingly, accused Praveen Kumar Jain, S/o Sh. Sukhbir Singh Jain, R/o H.No. 18, Gali No.13, New East Azad Nagar, Near Water Tank, Delhi­51 stands acquitted of the offence under section 138 NI Act. Bare perusal of Section 138 of the NI Act clarifies that five essential ingredients for completing the offence under Section 138 of the Act are as below: i. Drawing of the cheque, ii. Presentation of the cheque with the bank, iii. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank, iv. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque demanding payment of the cheque amount, and v. failure of the drawer to make payment within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. 16. It is pertinent to mention here that there are two presumptions of law as mandated by the Negotiable Instruments Act. According to Section 118 (a) of the Act, it shall be presumed that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. By virtue of this Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 17 of 30 clause, the Court is obliged to presume that the promissory note was made for consideration or until the contrary is proved. In Mallavarapu Kasivisweswara Rao Vs

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: & 1303/1 Page 17 of 30 clause, the Court is obliged to presume that the promissory note was made for consideration or until the contrary is proved. In Mallavarapu Kasivisweswara Rao Vs. Thadikonda Ramulu Firm and Others AIR 2008 SC 2898 it was held as under: ­ "... ... ... The bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff. To disprove the presumption, defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exist or its non­existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, shall act upon the plea that it did not exist...." 17. According to Section 139 of NI Act "it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for discharge in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." Under Section 139 NI Act there is a legal presumption that the cheque was issued for discharging a liability and that presumption can be rebutted only by the person who drew the cheque. This presumption can be rebutted by the accused by adducing evidence. So the burden of proof is on the accused. 18. In Hiten P. Dalal Vs. Bratindranath Banerjee AIR 2010 SC Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 18 of 30 1898 it was held as under: ­ "The words 'unless the contrary is proved' which occur in this provision (Section 139) make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: 'unless the contrary is proved' which occur in this provision (Section 139) make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted......". 19. From the entire defence raised by Ld. Counsel for the accused it can be deduced that defence of the accused is mainly four fold. One that he had not issued the cheques to the complainant. In fact the said cheques were lost by the accused and the same have been misused by the complainant. Second that the complainant has failed to show that he had financial resources to pay such a heavy amount of Rs. 17.5 lakhs. Third defence of the accused is that the complainant has not shown the said transaction in his ITRs therefore the same amounts to an illegal transaction and thus Section 138 of N.I.Act does not apply in such a case. Last defence of the accused is that the complainant has never appeared in person in the present Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 19 of 30 complaints. In fact the complainant bearing CC No.1149/1 was filed by the complainant through his attorney Sanjeev Bajaj. In CC No. 1303/1 the complainant disappeared after filing of the complaint and never appeared and the same has been pursued by his attorney Sanjeev Bajaj and he deposed on behalf of the complainant despite the fact that he was not having any personal knowledge of the facts of the case. 20

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: and the same has been pursued by his attorney Sanjeev Bajaj and he deposed on behalf of the complainant despite the fact that he was not having any personal knowledge of the facts of the case. 20. So far as first contention of the accused is concerned that the cheques in question were lost and the same have been misused by the complainant is concerned, the same does not inspire confidence at all. It has been alleged by the accused that the cheques in question were lost on 01.04.2005. However, it is admitted case of the accused that he had received the legal demand notice sent by the complainant but despite the fact that he had received the legal demand notice, the accused did not bother to reply the said notice. Legal demand notices were sent by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant on 29.10.2005 (In CC No.1149/1) and on 02.06.2005 (in CC no.1303/1) to the accused i.e. almost after 6 months of lost of the cheques and the accused has failed to show as to what was he doing during the period of 6 months. Keeping in view that he had lost so many Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 20 of 30 cheques, duly signed by him, no reasonable man will be sitting idle waiting for the misuse of the cheques if he had lost so many blank signed cheques unless and until he knew as to with whom those cheques are lying. From the defence of the accused it appears that it is just an afterthought and a concocted story of loss of cheques. The defence of the accused is further weakened by the fact if we carefully peruse the cheques in the present complaints, it appears that the name and signatures were filled by the same pen. It shows that the name of the complainant and the signatures were put at the same time

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: the cheques in the present complaints, it appears that the name and signatures were filled by the same pen. It shows that the name of the complainant and the signatures were put at the same time. Moreover, the accused had not denied that the cheques in question do not bear his signatures. Therefore, first contention of the accused is overruled. 21. Moreover the accused has also taken a defence that the cheques in questions were stolen cheques and on 01.04.2005 he had got a complaint registered with PS Karol Bagh to the effect and when lateron he came to know that the cheques were in possession of the complainant he had also lodged a case against the complainant in the year 2007 in Tis Hazari Courts. However the story of lost cheques does not inspire confidence at all. Because it is the accused who has Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 21 of 30 to prove as to how the complainant succeeded to get possession of those cheques. The accused could have led defence evidence to prove that the cheques in question were stolen by the complainant. 22. So far as second contention of the accused is concerned that the complainant had no financial resource to pay such a heavy amount of Rs.17.5 lakhs is concerned, it can be said that the onus was upon the accused to prove the same. In fact, the complainant has produced copies of statement of account for the year 2003 to 2005 to show the withdrawals made by the complainant from the account of the firm Radhe Krishnan Impex and also from his brother's firm Paras Bajaj Fab

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: of statement of account for the year 2003 to 2005 to show the withdrawals made by the complainant from the account of the firm Radhe Krishnan Impex and also from his brother's firm Paras Bajaj Fab. The statement of account furnished by the complainant clearly shows that several withdrawals were made by the complainant from his account which may not total upto Rs.17.5 lakhs but it certainly strengthens the case of the complainant and in view of the presumptions u/s 118 & 139 of N.I. Act the onus was upon the accused to show that these withdrawals were not meant for the purpose of partnership business. The complainant has failed to produce his ITRs of the relevant period but production of statement of account of the two firms mentioned above strengthens Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 22 of 30 the case of the complainant to the effect that he had withdrawn amounts on various occasions from the account of the said two firms. Therefore second contention of the accused is also overruled. 23. So far as third contention of the accused that the complainant has not shown the alleged transactions in his ITRs is concerned, it can be said that merely because the complainant has not shown this amount in his ITRs, does not make the transactions illegal per se, as envisaged u/s 138 N.I. Act. As per Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act no person shall take or accept from any other person any loan or deposit otherwise than by an account payee cheque or account payee bank draft if.­ a) the amount of such loan or deposit or the aggregate amount of such loan and deposit is more than Rs.20,000/­ 24. Penalty for failure to comply with the provisions of Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act has been provided in Section 271 D of Income Tax Act

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: amount of such loan and deposit is more than Rs.20,000/­ 24. Penalty for failure to comply with the provisions of Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act has been provided in Section 271 D of Income Tax Act. It provides that if a person take or accepts any loan or deposit in contravention of the provision of section 269 SS, he Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 23 of 30 shall be liable to pay, by way of penalty, a sum equal to the amount of the loan or deposit so taken or accepted. 25. A bare reading of these sections shows that although loan taken or deposit of an amount more Rs.20,000/­ in cash is prohibited however in the considered opinion of this court if the penalty is imposed upon the defaulter and he pays the penalty imposed, the transaction is deemed to be legalized. Therefore if the person fails to comply with provisions of Section 269 SS of I.T. Act it can not be said that the transaction is altogether illegal in terms of Section 138 of N.I. Act and that the same can not be recovered from the person to whom it has been made. Therefore this contention of the accused that the transaction was not in compliance of Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act and the same does not fall within the purview of Section 138 of N.I. Act, also stands overruled. 26. Last contention of the accused was that the present complaints are liable to be dismissed on the ground that the same had not been pursued properly by the complainant and in fact the complainant has never appeared in the present complaints and POA holder has no personal knowledge to proceed with the present complaint and further that in the absence of personal knowledge, the POA holder Case No

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: and POA holder has no personal knowledge to proceed with the present complaint and further that in the absence of personal knowledge, the POA holder Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 24 of 30 can not depose on behalf of complainant and therefore the entire defence led by the complainant is liable to be ignored. To establish his arguments Ld. Counsel for the accused has relied upon the following judgments M/s Shankar Finance & Investments Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh & Ors. Cri Appeal No. 1449 of 2003 and A.C. Narayanan Vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr 2013 (11) Scale. 27. I have gone through both the judgments filed by Ld. Counsel for the accused and the observations made by Hon'ble Supreme Court are not in dispute. In fact it is not understandable as to how these judgments helped the case of the accused. In both the judgments referred by Ld. Counsel for the accused, it has been very specifically observed by Hon'ble Suprme Court as under: "Where the proprietor of the proprietary concern has personal knowledge of the transaction and the proprietor has signed the complaint, he has to be examined under S.200 of the Code. But where the Attorney holder of the complainant is in charge of teh business of the payee­complainant and the Attorney holder alone is personally aware of the transactions, and the complaint is signed by the Attorney holder on behalf of the payee­complainant, there is no reason why the Attorney holder cannot be examined as the complainant." 28. In view of above discussed case law, this court is of the Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 25 of 30 opinion that if POA holder has personal knowledge of the case he can very well depose on behalf of the complainant

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: class="hidden_text" id="span_24">Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 25 of 30 opinion that if POA holder has personal knowledge of the case he can very well depose on behalf of the complainant. Both the complaints have been filed in the name of the complainant. In fact CC No. 1303/1 was filed by the complainant and subsequently he authorized his brother to pursue the present complaint. The GPA which is on record Ex. CW 1/1 has been duly proved vide which the Attorney has been authorized by the complainant to proceed with the present complaint and also to depose on his behalf. It has been very categorically stated in the affidavit filed by the Attorney holder that he has personal knowledge of the facts of the case and the onus was on the accused to show that the Attorney holder lacked personal knowledge so as to negate the evidence led by the attorney holder. In fact this issue has already been decided by this court vide order dated 31.03.2011. In that order Ld. Predecessor had allowed the Attorney holder to depose as complainant witness relying on the very judgment referred to by Ld. Counsel for the accused. Therefore, after perusing both the judgments this court is of the opinion that both the complaints fall within the ambit of the observations made by Hon'ble Supreme Court and as the Attorney holder had the personal knowledge of the facts of the case, this contention of the accused is Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 26 of 30 also overruled. Even though some inconsistencies have come in the deposition of the complainant but it can not be said to be fatal to the case of the complainant. The Attorney holder more or less has supported the case of the complainant. 29. I have gone through the case law referred to by Ld

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: but it can not be said to be fatal to the case of the complainant. The Attorney holder more or less has supported the case of the complainant. 29. I have gone through the case law referred to by Ld. Counsel for the accused. However, no case law referred to by Ld. Counsel for the accused comes to the aid of the accused as facts of those case law are apparently distinguishable from the facts under consideration. 30. The decision in the case G. Panakhakshi Amma Vs. Mathai Mathew (supra) referred to by the accused is not applicable in the present case as the same is related to chit fund transactions between the parties and the complainant was a money lender who failed to produce his books of accounts. 31. In Sanjay Mishra Vs. Ms. Kanishka Kapoor @ Nikki & Anr (supra) the case was of advancing a friendly loan of Rs.15 lakhs to the accused persons and it was agreed between the parties that the accused shall repay the amount within 3 months. In this case also the Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 27 of 30 complainant had not mentioned the transaction of loan in his ITR and therefore the complaint of the complainant was dismissed. 32. However, both the above case law are distinguishable from the facts in hand as the present complaint is regarding partnership deed executed between the parties and the same has been admitted by the accused. There is no dispute as to existence of partnership between the parties. Moreover the accused has himself admitted that some amount was paid by the complainant for the purpose of partnership business. The present case is neither a case of friendly loan nor of chit fund transaction

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: the accused has himself admitted that some amount was paid by the complainant for the purpose of partnership business. The present case is neither a case of friendly loan nor of chit fund transaction. Moreover the complainant has produced copy of statement of accounts of the relevant period which corroborated the case of the complainant to some extent. In fact the accused has himself admitted the case of the complainant to some extent and defence placed by him seems to be just an afterthought. Further the accused has failed to satisfactorily explain as to how these cheques came into the possession of the complainant. 33. The other case law P. Venugopal Vs. Madan P Sarthi (supra), M.S. Narayana Menon Vs. State of Kerala (supra) and Bharat Barrel & Drum Manufacturing Company Vs. Amin Chand Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 28 of 30 Pyare Lal (supra) are also of no assistance to the accused. In fact observations made in those case law go against the accused. In Bharat Barrel's case it was observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court as under: "The burden upon the defendant of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by brining on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. In such an event, the plaintiff is entitled under law to rely upon all the evidence led in the case including that of the plaintiff as well. In case, where the defendant fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) in his favour

title: Vide This Common Judgment vs . on 5 May, 2014
content: the initial onus of proof by showing the non­existence of the consideration, the plaintiff would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) in his favour. The court may not insist upon the defendant to disprove the existence of consideration by leading direct evidence as the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated and even if led, is to be seen with a doubt. The bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the onus of proving to the plaintiff. To disprove the presumption, the defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exist or its non­ existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, shall act upon the plea that it did not exist.". FINAL ORDER. 34. In view of above it can be said that the story put forth Case No. 1149/1 & 1303/1 Page 29 of 30 by the complainant is more believable. Whereas the story put forth by the accused does not inspire confidence and the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions raised against him under Section 118 & 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act. Accordingly, the accused is convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. I have also perused the judicial record. 10 For offence U/s 138 NI Act the necessary ingredients to be proved are: a) That the accused had a legal liability / debt towards the complainant. b) That the accused issued a cheque in discharge of the said legal liability / debt. c) That the accused was maintaining a bank account for the cheque issued by him. D) That the cheque was presented by the complainant within its validity period. e) That the cheque was dishonored on his presentation. f) That the complainant issued legal demand notice within 30 days from the date of dishonor of the cheque. g) That the accused failed to pay within 15 days of receipt of legal demand notice. In the present case the complainant has averred that the cheque were issued against discharge of liability under agreement dated 05.03.2013. Since the cheque in question is bearing the name of the complainant company, therefore, presumption arises U/s 118­A & 139 NI Act that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legal liability. Therefore, the onus to rebut this presumption is on the accused persons. The accused persons have disputed their legal liability to make payment on the ground that the complainant company did not handover possession of the shop as per agreement dated 05.03.2013. 13 On perusal of the agreement dated 05.03.2013 it is seen that the entire consideration for the shop was to be paid before taking over possession of the shop.
