content: instruction to his banker. DW­2 further stated that again the complainant Shukul Gupta approached him and stated that he should help him getting a loan of lesser amount from the accused Anuj Chandra. DW­2 further stated that he along with the complainant Shukul Gupta again approached the accused Anuj Chandra and the complainant Shukul Gupta returned the cheque to the accused and the accused Anuj Chandra gave the post dated cheque in question Ex. CW­1/C for a sum Rs. 2.20 lakhs to the complainant Shukul Gupta imposing the same condition of collateral security. DW­2 further stated that for the second time also the complainant Shukul Gupta failed to furnish collateral security and thereafter the accused Anuj Chandra again issued stop payment instruction to his banker. DW­2 also stated that the accused Anuj Chandra even asked him to get back his cheque from the complainant but the complainant avoided him on one Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets Vs. Anuj Chandra Page No. 10/14 pretext or other and thereafter he came to know about the institution of the legal proceedings between the complainant Shukul Gupta and the accused Anuj Chandra. 16. During course of arguments Ld. Counsel for the complainant argued that defence witness DW­2 is deposing at the instance of the accused and he also owes amount to the complainant in respect of his dealings with the complainant Shukul Gupta and suggestions to this effect is also put the witness during his cross examination by the counsel for the complainant. The suggestions were denied by DW­2

title: Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets vs . Anuj Chandra Page No. 1/14 on 27 September, 2014
content: dealings with the complainant Shukul Gupta and suggestions to this effect is also put the witness during his cross examination by the counsel for the complainant. The suggestions were denied by DW­2. Interestingly DW­2 was also confronted with e­mails Mark A and Mark B allegedly written by him to the complainant which shows amount due to be paid by him and one Mrs Chandra to the complainant which the witness has stated that they do not belongs to him. Surprisingly, no certificate to prove the genuineness of the said e­mails has been placed on record by the complainant. More so even if the witness owes any amount to the complainant that does not mean that he is deposing falsely at the behest of the accused Anuj Chandra. Further even believing that e­mail Mark B is referring to outstanding liability of Neelu Chandra still it is surprising to see that the same is dated 13th of July 2010 whereas as per the own claim of the complainant the transaction of delivery of carpet involved in the present complainant case took place on 16.10.2010. 17. Now, even believing the stand of the complainant it is interesting to see that the complainant CW­1 in his cross examination has stated that he has met the accused Anuj Chandra only two times firstly when the accused had handed over a cash of Rs. 3,00,000/­ to him and has taken back his cheque which was given by the accused Anuj Chandra for the purchase of carpets and for the second time in respect of the transaction in question. Therefore from the own admission of the complainant CW­1 two things are apparently clear firstly that he had dealt with the accused Anuj Chandra only two times and secondly prior to the transaction in question earlier also some transaction of Rs

title: Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets vs . Anuj Chandra Page No. 1/14 on 27 September, 2014
content: CW­1 two things are apparently clear firstly that he had dealt with the accused Anuj Chandra only two times and secondly prior to the transaction in question earlier also some transaction of Rs. 3,00,000/­ had taken place between the complainant and the accused. It is also surprising to see further that as per the own version of Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets Vs. Anuj Chandra Page No. 11/14 the complainant in the complaint, the complainant has stated that the amount for the carpet was to be paid within 3 days however no probable explanation has been given by the complainant as to what made him accept the cheque in question Ex.CW1/C dated 18.10.2010 and further wait for a month's time for realising his payment as the cheque in question Ex.CW1/C dated 18.10.2010 is dishonoured vide returning memo dated 22.11.2010 as it is also admitted fact by the complainant CW­1 in his cross examination that the accused Anuj Chandra is neither his friend nor his customer and as per the own version of the complainant the complainant has met the accused only two times, still the cheque as a mode of payment was accepted by the complainant and over and above it was presented for clearance allegedly at the instance of the accused after a month's time. It is highly inconceivable that if the bill was to be paid within three days the complainant after accepting the cheque would wait for a month's time for realising his payment only at the instance of the accused who admittedly is niether his friend nor a regular customer. Further, it is also surprising to see that no delivery challan for the goods delivered was prepared and neither any receiving was taken by the complainant for the carpet which was allegedly supplied by him to the accused Anuj Chandra and that too for a sum of Rs

title: Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets vs . Anuj Chandra Page No. 1/14 on 27 September, 2014
content: for the goods delivered was prepared and neither any receiving was taken by the complainant for the carpet which was allegedly supplied by him to the accused Anuj Chandra and that too for a sum of Rs. 2,20,000/­. Furthermore, the carriage bill/ transporters bill Ex.CW1/B placed on record by the complainant is generated on the own letter head of the complainant and it do not discloses as to what was delivered and to whom or whether any cheque in question Ex.CW1/C was given as payment against the delivery of the goods. Further, it is the own case of the complainant that the accused Anuj Chandra and Neelu Chandra has approached him for the purchase of the carpet, but interestingly, the Bill/ Invoice Ex.CW1/A is only in the name of accused Anuj Chandra which casts doubt about the bill/ invoice Ex.CW1/A as it appears that the complainant knew before hand that the amount would be paid by accused Anuj Chandra only. Further in the bill/invoice Ex.CW1/A in the column of delivery note, mode/term of payment, buyer's order number & date, dispatch document number & date, dispatch through and destination and in the terms of delivery there is complete blank. Furthermore the cheque in question Ex.CW1/C has been Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets Vs. Anuj Chandra Page No. 12/14 dishonoured on account of payment stopped by the drawer which also supports the case of the accused. Furthermore, consistent stand has been taken by the accused right from the threshold i.e. from his reply Ex. CW1/L given to the legal demand notice of the complainant till the conclusion of the trial. Also the testimony of DW­1 and DW­2 has gone unrebutted and there is no reason to disbelieve their testimony

title: Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets vs . Anuj Chandra Page No. 1/14 on 27 September, 2014
content: given to the legal demand notice of the complainant till the conclusion of the trial. Also the testimony of DW­1 and DW­2 has gone unrebutted and there is no reason to disbelieve their testimony. All the aforesaid circumstances surround the claim of the complainant with clouds of suspicion and satisfy the test of rebuttal on the strength of 'preponderance of probabilities'. 18. In a case of this nature, where the chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration. All the aforesaid circumstances/factors rebut the presumptions provided under Section 139 of the NI Act because they raise credible doubt over the veracity of the complainant's claims and satisfy the test of rebuttal on the strength of preponderance of probabilities thereby weakening the claim of the Complainant. 19. Therefore this court do not find any force in the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the complainant that the accused has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. Needless to say that presumptions are not in itself evidence but they only enables a party in whose favour they exists to show that he has a prima facie case. The question as to whether the presumptions stood rebutted or not must, is to be determined keeping in view the other evidences on record. In the case in hand the presumptions under Section 139 of the NI Act alone cannot be the sole basis to prove the case of the complainant as the materials and evidence available on the record do not bridge the gap. It is highly improbable that the accused Anuj Chandra has given the cheque in question Ex CW1/C in order to discharge his liability towards the purchase of carpet

title: Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets vs . Anuj Chandra Page No. 1/14 on 27 September, 2014
content: on the record do not bridge the gap. It is highly improbable that the accused Anuj Chandra has given the cheque in question Ex CW1/C in order to discharge his liability towards the purchase of carpet. Therefore, I hereby hold that the complainant has not been able to prove and substantiate all the allegations against the accused Anuj Chandra. Furthermore mere non Case No. : 2966/12 Vandana Carpets Vs. Anuj Chandra Page No. 13/14 payment of cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of legal demand notice is not sufficient to fasten any liability U/s 138 of the NI Act as it is established that the cheque in question Ex.CW1/C has not been issued by the accused Anuj Chandra in discharge of his liability towards the purchase of the carpet. 20. Accordingly, In view of the facts, evidence lead by both the parties coupled with my discussion above, I hereby hold that the complainant has not been able to prove and substantiate its allegation against the accused Anuj Chandra and all the ingredients for the offence under section 138 of the NI Act have not been proved against the accused Anuj Chandra. Accordingly, accused Anuj Chandra S/o Sh. Krishan Chandra is hereby acquitted for the offence u/s 138 of the NI Act. File be consigned to record room after due compliance. In our judgment, the above observations cannot be read to mean that in a criminal case where trial is yet to take place and the matter is at the stage of issuance of summons or taking cognizance, materials relied upon by the accused which are in the nature of public documents or the materials which are beyond suspicion or doubt, in no circumstance, can be looked into by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 or for that matter in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Code. It is fairly settled now that while exercising inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 or revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Code in a case where complaint is sought to be quashed, it is not proper for the High Court to consider the defence of the accused or embark upon an enquiry in respect of merits of the accusations. However, in an appropriate case, if on the face Page No. 13. Contd... ... ... CR No. 3/14. M/s Caparo Financial Solution Vs. Jasjit Singh Sawhney & Another. of the documents ­ which are beyond suspicion or doubt - placed by the accused, the accusations against him cannot stand, it would be travesty of justice if the accused is relegated to trial and he is asked to prove his defence before the trial court. In such a matter, for promotion of justice or to prevent injustice or abuse of process, the High Court may look into the materials which have significant bearing on the matter at prima facie stage." 10

The landmark judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court regarding vicarious liability of a Director of a company for the dishonouring of a cheque issued on behalf of company with the aid of Section 141 NI Act for the offence u/s 138 NI Act is the case of "SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. Vs. Neeta Bhalla and Another", (2007) 4 SCC 70, wherein it was held as under: ­ "The requirement of Section 141 is that the person sought to be made liable should be in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the relevant time. This has to be averred as a fact as there is no deemed liability of a Director in such cases." 11. Also, Hon'ble Supreme Court in a recent judgment titled as "A.K. Singhania Vs. Gujarat State Fertilizer Page No. 14. Contd... ... ... CR No. 3/14. M/s Caparo Financial Solution Vs. Jasjit Singh Sawhney & Another. Company Ltd. & Another", 2013 XI AD (SC) 1, held that "for making Director of a company liable for being summoned with the aid of Section 141 of NI Act for the offence u/s 138 NI Act, it is sufficient to allege that he was incharge and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company and it is not necessary to allege and prove that said Director had any specific role in respect of the transaction dealing to cheque in question". 12

title: Cr No. 3/14. M/S Caparo Financial ... vs . on 18 March, 2014
content: for the conduct of the business of the company and it is not necessary to allege and prove that said Director had any specific role in respect of the transaction dealing to cheque in question". 12. Thus, in view of the ratio in aforesaid two cases, it is clear that it was necessary for the complainant to allege in the complaint and to say so in its pre summoning evidence that a particular Director was incharge and responsible for the conduct or day to day affairs of the said company and then the said Director can be summoned with the aid of Section 141 NI Act for the offence u/s 138 NI Act. Besides that it was nowhere obligatory for the revisionist to specifically mention the exact role of any Director at initial stage although the said specific role has been mentioned. Further, any such Director, who has been summoned, can take all defence during cross examination of the revisionist­complainant and also in his defence evidence to show that he was not the person incharge or Page No. 15. Contd... ... ... CR No. 3/14. M/s Caparo Financial Solution Vs. Jasjit Singh Sawhney & Another. responsible for the conduct of the accused no. 1 company at the relevant time or that he had nothing to do with the accused no. 1 company. 13. The Form 32 of the accused no. 1 company filed on behalf of the respondent no. 2 reveals that in column no. 5, the name of the said Director is mentioned as independent Non­Executive Director. Ld. counsel for revisionist had strongly contended that there is no tick mark mentioned in the square meant for Non­Executive Director and rather a cross has been mentioned and, hence, it cannot be inferred that he was a Non­Executive Director

title: Cr No. 3/14. M/S Caparo Financial ... vs . on 18 March, 2014
content: that there is no tick mark mentioned in the square meant for Non­Executive Director and rather a cross has been mentioned and, hence, it cannot be inferred that he was a Non­Executive Director. However, he has submitted that even if for arguments sake it is assumed that he was a Non­Executive Director, still he participated in the entire transaction as mentioned above and also in view of the fact that nowhere in Section 141 NI Act, it is mentioned that a Non­Executive Director, who participated in all the proceedings cannot be made liable for the offence u/s 138 NI Act with the aid of Section 141 NI Act, therefore, he is liable to be summoned. 14. Considering the totality of the facts and circumstances, specially in view of the fact that the role of the respondent Page No. 16. Contd... ... ... CR No. 3/14. M/s Caparo Financial Solution Vs. Jasjit Singh Sawhney & Another. no. 2 has been clearly described by the revisionist in execution of various documents relating to loan account in question by him also and pursuant to the same, as per the case of the revisionist, the loan in question was disbursed and the cheque in question was issued which had got dishonoured due to reason "payment stopped by drawer" and also in view of the fact that nowhere it is mentioned in Section 141 NI Act that a Non­Executive Director, who is incharge and responsible for the day to day conduct and affair of the business of the accused no. 1 company and participated in execution of various documents relating to sanction of loan for the accused no. 1 company, cannot be made liable with the aid of Section 141 NI Act for the offence u/s 138 NI Act

title: Cr No. 3/14. M/S Caparo Financial ... vs . on 18 March, 2014
content: and participated in execution of various documents relating to sanction of loan for the accused no. 1 company, cannot be made liable with the aid of Section 141 NI Act for the offence u/s 138 NI Act. Rather any person, even if he was not a Director, but was incharge and responsible to the company for the business of the company when the offence was committed, would be liable to be summoned for the offence u/s 138 NI Act with the aid of Section 141 NI Act. 15. The case law relied upon by the ld. Trial Court was not applicable to the facts of the present case as the same pertained to liability of a company relating to Page No. 17. Contd... ... ... CR No. 3/14. M/s Caparo Financial Solution Vs. Jasjit Singh Sawhney & Another. dishonouring of a cheque issued by a natural person in his individual capacity. 16. In view of the above, I am of the considered opinion that the impugned order of the ld. Trial Court has not been correctly passed and the ld. Trial Court has not considered the provision of Section 141 NI Act and the various judicial pronouncements of higher Courts on the said aspect. The judgments relied upon by the ld. counsel for respondent no. 2 does not help his case in any way, in view of the aforesaid discussions and case laws relied upon. 17. Since there is illegality and impropriety in the order of the ld. Trial Court, therefore, the same is, accordingly, set aside. The revision petition is allowed. 18. All the four cases are being disposed off vide a common judgment as the facts are the same and even the interconnected, therefore, all the cases are disposed off to avoid the repetition and also for the sake of brevity. Vide order dated 03.04.2007 all the four cases were clubbed together and CC no.207/05/03 was treated as the main case Therefore, by way of the present judgment, I shall dispose off four complaint cases filed under section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act, 1981 (as amended upto date). That on representation made by the accused persons, the complainant gave a loan of Rs.10.5lacs and the accused persons promised and agreed to return the same alongwith interest @ 15.6% pa. That towards the discharge of the liability, the accused persons issued eight cheques. 3. That all the cheques on presentation to the concerned bank got dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds. That the complainant immediately contacted the accused persons and informed them about the dishonour of the cheques and also asked for the payment of the cheque amount. That thereafter legal notice dated 05.09.2003 under registered AD cover as well as UPC was served upon the accused persons but the accused persons did not make any payment. That as a result of which the complainant has filed the instant complaint for prosecution of the accused persons under section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act. 4. After hearing the Ld. counsel for the complainant and considering the entire material and documents on record, summons were issued against the accused persons vide order dated 21.02.2004

content: Act. 4. After hearing the Ld. counsel for the complainant and considering the entire material and documents on record, summons were issued against the accused persons vide order dated 21.02.2004. On appearance of the accused persons, a separate notice under section 251 CrPC dated 27.09.2006 was served upon the accused persons to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 5. In order to prove his case, the complainant has got CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... examined three witnesses including himself as CW3, Sh. Jagdish Raj Sahrma as CW1 and Sh. Kaushik Sur as CW2 in support of the contents of his complaint. 6. In his explanation u/s 313 CrPC, it was stated by accused Mayur Pasricha that he had not issued the cheques in question to the complainant. It was further submitted that he had not received any legal notice. It was further submitted that the cheques in question were misused by the complainant or that he never took any loan from the complainant and also did not owe any liability towards him. The accused persons opted not to lead DE in support of their contentions. Facts in issues 7. In order to have the positive outcome in his favour, the complainant was required to show that the cheques Ex.CW1/1 to Ex.CW1/2 (in each case) were given by the accused in discharge of their liabilities which were dishonoured vide returning memos whereafter the accused had also failed to comply with the requirements of the legal notices Ex. CW1/5 (in each case). 8. On the other hand, the accused persons were required to show their defence on the scale of preponderance of the probabilities that they are not liable to the amount involved in the complaints. Legal Prepositions 9

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: the accused persons were required to show their defence on the scale of preponderance of the probabilities that they are not liable to the amount involved in the complaints. Legal Prepositions 9. The presumptions provided U/s 118 NI Act and 139 NI Act would come to the rescue of the complainant once the execution of the cheque in question is proved on record. CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... 10. As per section 118 NI Act, it is to be presumed in favour of the complainant during the trial that the cheque in question was given against consideration by the accused and that the complainant was the holder of the said cheque in due course. Further as per Sec. 139 NI Act, it is to be presumed in favour of the complainant during the trial that the cheque in question was received by the complainant against a legally enforceable debt or liability (Refer :- "Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan" SLP (Crl.) 407/06, Dated:- 07.05.2010). 11. It is well settled that both the aforesaid presumptions U/s 118 & 139 NI Act are rebuttable in nature and the onus to rebut the same squarely rests upon the accused. 12. The accused can rebut these presumptions not merely by examining his own witnesses but also through the cross examination of the complainant and his witnesses thereby bringing on record through the entire evidence available on record (inclusive of complainant's evidence and defence evidence, if any), that the complainant was a liar, that their was no existing liabilities between the parties and that the cheque in question was misused. It must be kept in mind that once evidence is brought on record from both sides, it becomes an evidence of the case and court can draw inferences from the said entire evidence either in favour or against any of the parties

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: that once evidence is brought on record from both sides, it becomes an evidence of the case and court can draw inferences from the said entire evidence either in favour or against any of the parties. Evidence is a complainant's evidence and accused's evidence only for the purposes of identifying it, but once it is adduced in the case, it becomes the evidence of the case and then the same has to be read as a whole. The court can not read the evidence of the complainant only to the extent it CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... favours the complainant and overlook the remaining evidence which supports the accused merely on the ground that it is the complainant's evidence. Similarly, from the evidence adduced by the accused, the court can draw inferences either in favour of the complainant or against the accused. The accused has a right to argue his case even on the basis of the cross examination of the complainant & his witnesses to show to the court that there existed no legally recoverable debt or liability between the parties. In order to rebut the legal presumption in question, it emerges that the accused need not require direct evidence to disprove the existence of consideration. 13. Preponderance of probabilities is the standard of proof upon the accused to rebut the above presumptions, which is not as high as that of the prosecution whereby the accused is only required to show the existence of a probable defence so as to rebut the above presumptions

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: to rebut the above presumptions, which is not as high as that of the prosecution whereby the accused is only required to show the existence of a probable defence so as to rebut the above presumptions. If the accused succeeds in raising a probable defence by referring to his own evidence (if any) and from the evidence of the complainant, then the onus would shift on to the complainant, who then would have to show beyond reasonable doubt the existence of consideration/existence of a legally recoverable debt or liability in respect of the cheque in question. Appreciation of Evidence 14. Complainant lays foundation of his case on the ground that accused no.1 is a partnership firm and accused no.2 to 7 are the partners of the same. That on representation made by the accused persons, he had given a sum of Rs.10.5lacs to the accused persons and CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... the same was agreed to be returned alongwith interest @ 15.6% p.a. and in discharge of their liability, the cheques in question were issued by the accused persons. The cheques issued by the accused persons got dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds. Thereafter, inspite of receiving legal notice accused failed to pay the amount involved in the present complaint. 15. Sh. Vinod Mahajan (CW3) in his examination-in-chief reiterated the contents of the complaint on oath before the court and filed an affidavit in evidence. While under cross-examination, it was admitted by the complainant (CW3) that as per tax returns his income during those period was not been mentioned as Rs.10/12lacs per year. It was deposed by the witness that he was leading a retired life. That he was not having any independent source of income except few tuitions

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: period was not been mentioned as Rs.10/12lacs per year. It was deposed by the witness that he was leading a retired life. That he was not having any independent source of income except few tuitions. That his income from the tuitions was hardly Rs.1,000/- to Rs.1200/- per month. It was further deposed by the witness that he do not remember whether as per ITR his income exceeded Rs.2lacs or not. That the entire transaction took place in the mid of January, 2003. That he do not remember how much money was lying in his bank account during the said period. It was further deposed by the witness that he has not shown the transaction pertaining to the present case in his ITR till date. That in the year 2003 his source of income was from tuitions and also the help from his parents. That he had not disclosed his source of income from the tuitions to any statutory authority including the IT Department. That he do not remember, if any amount was withdrawn from his bank. That he had no transaction with Gayatri Enterprises except the one in CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... question. 16. Sh. Jagdish Raj Sharma (CW1) is the official from the bank to prove the statement of account of the complainant. Sh. Kaushik Sur (CW2) is the bank official, who proved the bank memos. 17. The defence set up by the accused persons in the present case is that they have neither borrowed any loan from the complainant nor issued the cheque in question to the complainant. Further defence of the accused is that the statutory legal notice was not served upon them and that the cheques in question, lying in the custody of the complainant for the purpose of negotiation, were misused by him after filling up the same in his hand. 18. It is argued by the Ld

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: them and that the cheques in question, lying in the custody of the complainant for the purpose of negotiation, were misused by him after filling up the same in his hand. 18. It is argued by the Ld. counsel for complainant that from evidence on record, the complainant has proved that cheque in question were signed by the accused which were dishonoured vide memo and despite the legal notice accused did not make the payment. It is argued that during the cross examination of complainant nothing material has come out and the complainant has been able to prove his case. It is further argued that accused has failed to discharge the burden upon him to rebutt the presumption in favour of the complainant under the Act. 19. Now the question is whether the complainant proved his case, that whether the amount was legally enforceable debt. The offence under Section 138 of the Act is a technical offence and the complainant is only supposed to prove that the cheque issued by the accused was dishonoured, his statement that cheque was issued against liability or CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... debt is sufficient proof of the debt or liability and the onus shifts to the accused to show the circumstances under which the cheque was issued and this could be proved by the accused only by way of cogent evidence. 20. The accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence/evidence on preponderance of probabilities to prove that cheque in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: adduce direct evidence/evidence on preponderance of probabilities to prove that cheque in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, there is no need that the accused should disprove the non existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. 21. As per complainant, on representation he had given a loan of Rs.10.5lacs to the accused persons and they had promised to repay the same alongwith interest @ 15.6% p.a. in discharge of their liability. The accused did not admit the issuance of the cheques in question to the complainant. It is the defence taken by the accused that the cheques in question were lying in the custody of the complainant for the purpose of negotiation and the complainant mischievously misused the same after filling up the contents of the same and that he did not owe any liability towards the complainant. CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... Moreover, the loan amount allegedly given by the complainant to the accused was a large amount and was not payable within few months. The failure on the part of the complainant to disclose the same in his income tax returns or the books of accounts is sufficient to rebut the presumption u/s 139 of NI Act. However, he failed to furnish on record the income tax returns for the relevant year. 22

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: in his income tax returns or the books of accounts is sufficient to rebut the presumption u/s 139 of NI Act. However, he failed to furnish on record the income tax returns for the relevant year. 22. It is well settled law that in a criminal case, prosecution has to stand upon its own legs and it cannot take the advantage of the fact that accused has not led cogent defence evidence or accused is having a weak defence. The defence raised by the accused along with the evidence placed on record are cogent proof in support of the defence version makes it highly probable that the cheques in question were not issued towards the discharge of friendly loan liability as alleged by the complainant and at the same time it weakens the foundation fabrics of the present complaint case. The suspicious circumstances rising in the present case will certainly give advantage to the accused. Moreover, the complainant has not come to the court with clean hands and his conduct is not of a prudent man. Hence, in the present case, the accused raises a cogent suspicious circumstances in the version of the complainant which belies the foundation of the present complaint case and same is sufficient to rebut the presumption that the cheques in question were not for discharging the legal liability. Conclusion 23. I have gone through the entire material on record carefully and heard the arguments advance by the counsel for parties at length. After analyzing the evidence led by the parties, I am of the opinion that CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd....

title: Legally Enforceable Debt Or ... vs . Sri Mohan" on 27 August, 2014
content: carefully and heard the arguments advance by the counsel for parties at length. After analyzing the evidence led by the parties, I am of the opinion that CC No. 207/1, 206/1, 205/1 & 204/1 Contd..... accused has been successful in rebutting the presumptions under NI Act by raising cogent suspicion in the version of complainant and on the scale of preponderance of probabilities that the cheques in question may not be given to the complainant as alleged by him. 24. The rebuttal does not have to be conclusively established but such evidence must be adduced before the court in support of the defence that Court must either believe the defence to exist or consider its existence to be reasonably probable. In the present case accused has not only been able to raise a probable defence and adduced sufficient evidence to prove his defence but also been able to succeed in shaking the very foundation of the fabrics of the case of the complainant. 25. Once the accused has discharged his initial burden of proving its defence the onus rebutted back on the complainant. However in the present case, complainant has miserably failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. 26. Therefore, from the above discussions, this court is of considered view that in the circumstances appearing from the record of the case, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt. Accordingly, the accused is entitled to be acquitted and hereby stands acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act. A copy of the judgment be placed in each case file. Moreover, there is also force in the contention of counsel for plaintiff that benami transaction(Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not apply in the present case, since the suit property/land was purchased in 1972 and the said act become operative in the year 1988. Further, in the judgment titled as Binapani Paul vs Pratima Ghosh, (2007) 6 SCC 59, it was observed that benami transaction(Prohibition) Act, 1988 has no retrospective effect. Printer & ors vs Marcel Martins AIR 2002 Karnataka 191, wherein it was observed that if a person in whose name the property is purchased also has contributed consideration for purchase of the suit property in his name along with others whose name is not reflected in the sale deed, it would not amount to a benami transaction as defined under the Act. 23 In the present matter, both the parties contended that along with them their respective husbands have also contributed in purchasing the suit property. content: and possession of the defendant over half portion of the suit property was admitted by the plaintiff. Further, while deciding the issue no.1 and 2, it has Suit No. 81/10/09 Smt. Dayawati Vs. Smt. Bhagwati Devi been already held that the suit property was purchased jointly by the plaintiff and defendant and also both equally contributed for the purchase of the sale. Hence, the declaration in respect of entire suit property in favour of the plaintiff, as prayed by the plaintiff, can not be made. Moreover, the suit property has been admittedly owned in the joint name of the plaintiff and defendant vide sale deed Ex.PW1/1 dt. 20/6/1972 and as such, the plaintiff can not claim the ownership of the entire suit property. The plaintiff can not be held as the exclusive owner of the entire suit property. However, as the suit property has been registered in joint name of the plaintiff and defendant and as such plaintiff has every right of ownership in respect of half portion of the suit property as being the joint owner of the suit property. Therefore, as such, the plaintiff has ownership right in respect of only half portion of the suit property as the suit property being purchased in joint name of plaintiff and defendant and defendant has ownership right of the remaining half portion of the suit property. This issue is accordingly decided, thereby declaring that the plaintiff has ownership rights in respect of only half portion of the suit property being joint owner of the suit property. Plaintiff and her husband alleged that the defendant and her family members illegally entered into the portion of the premises of the plaintiff in the suit property after breaking the locks of the premises of the plaintiff. Though, the defendant has denied the allegation of the plaintiff, however, the defendant and her husband have not denied the factum of lodging of the complaint regarding the alleged breaking of locks. The copies of the police complaint dt. 25/3/2009 mark A and subsequent complaint dt. 28/5/2009 mark B' had been relied by the plaintiff so as to substantiate that the defendant and her family member illegally and unauthorizedly entered into the portion of the premises of the plaintiff after breaking the locks of the premises. The defendant has not produced any material on record that prior to March, 2009 (i.e. prior to the alleged illegally occupation of the portion of the premises of the plaintiff by the defendant after breaking the locks) Suit No. 81/10/09 Smt. Dayawati Vs. Smt. Bhagwati Devi the defendant was in possession of entire suit property. Therefore, in these circumstances, the plaintiff has established that the defendant had illegally dispossessed the plaintiff from half portion of the premises of the plaintiff in March, 2009. Though, the plaintiff is seeking possession of entire suit land, but, the plaintiff failed to brought on record any material that plaintiff has exclusively owned the suit property or the plaintiff was in possession of the entire suit land at any point of time

title: Smt. Dayawati vs Smt. Bhagwati Devi on 29 September, 2014
content: but, the plaintiff failed to brought on record any material that plaintiff has exclusively owned the suit property or the plaintiff was in possession of the entire suit land at any point of time. Hence, the plaintiff is only entitled for recovery of vacant and peaceful possession of half portion of the suit property i.e. the share of the plaintiff in the suit property. Accordingly, this issue is decided in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant in the aforesaid terms. 28 Relief. As held above, the plaintiff has failed to prove issue no.1 and defendant has also failed to prove issue no.2. While deciding the issue no.1 and 2, it has been held that the plaintiff and defendant had jointly purchased the suit property and further the plaintiff and defendant had equally contributed for the purchase of suit property. Further, while deciding issue no.3, it has been held that plaintiff has ownership rights in respect of only half portion of the suit property Suit No. 81/10/09 Smt. Dayawati Vs. Smt. Bhagwati Devi being joint owner of the suit property. In the issue no.4, it has been held that the plaintiff is only entitled for recovery of vacant and peaceful possession of half portion of the suit property i.e. the share of the plaintiff in the suit property. 29 Therefore, suit of the plaintiff is partly allowed and decreed as under: i) A decree is passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant, thereby declaring that the plaintiff has ownership rights in respect of only half portion as share of plaintiff in the suit property i.e. land bearing No. RZ-15, Gali No.7, Khasra No. 621, Palam Colony, Kailash Puri, New Delhi-45, as shown in the portion of plaintiff in the site plan Ex.PW1/2

title: Smt. Dayawati vs Smt. Bhagwati Devi on 29 September, 2014
content: of plaintiff in the suit property i.e. land bearing No. RZ-15, Gali No.7, Khasra No. 621, Palam Colony, Kailash Puri, New Delhi-45, as shown in the portion of plaintiff in the site plan Ex.PW1/2. ii) A decree of possession is passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant in respect of half portion as share of plaintiff in the suit property i.e. land bearing No. RZ-15, Gali No.7, Khasra No.621, Palam Colony, Kailash Puri, New Delhi-45, as shown in the site plan Ex.PW1/2 and defendant is hereby directed to hand over the vacant and peaceful possession of half portion of the suit property i.e. the share of the plaintiff in the suit property as shown in the portion of Suit No. 81/10/09 Smt. Dayawati Vs. Smt. Bhagwati Devi plaintiff in the site plan Ex.PW1/2 within two months from today. 30 Plaintiff is also entitled to cost. 31 Decree sheet be prepared accordingly. 32 File be consigned to the record room. The matter is coming up today for judgment. Vide my separate judgment of even date, suit of the plaintiff is partly allowed. Plaintiff is also entitled to cost. Decree sheet be prepared accordingly. title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF SHRI LOKESH KUMAR SHARMA ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE­04, NEW DELHI DISTRICT PATIALA HOUSE COURTS, NEW DELHI Unique I D No. : 02403R0181572013 Criminal Appeal Number : 1/1/14 dated 16.01.2014 CC No. : 1996/1 PS: : Connaught Place U/S: : 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act M/s Beardsell Limited 114/115, Jyotishikhar Building No.8, District Centre, New Delhi­110058 Through its representative .....Appellant versus M/s Videocon International Limited 27, Kasturba Gandhi Marg New Delhi­110001 Through its Authorized Signatory Sh. Yatinder Singh S/o Sh. Rajbir Singh .....Respondent Appeal received by Court : 16.01.14 Arguments concluded : 06.06.14 Date of order : 10.07.14 CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.1/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. JUDGMENT: 1 By way of present appeal, the appellant herein has challenged the impugned judgment of conviction dated 10.10.2013 passed by the court of Sh. Arul Varma, the then learned Metropolitan Magistrate, (NI Act­01), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi whereby the appellant herein was held guilty and convicted for an offence punishable under sections 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act (N.I. Act) and the consequent order on sentence dated 07.11.2013 in CC No. 1996/1 titled as M/s Videocon International Ltd. vs. M/s Beardsell Ltd. & Anr. whereby the learned MM had directed the appellant herein to pay twice of the total amount as mentioned in the cheque in question (i.e. Rs. 60,00,000/­) and had further directed to pay the aforesaid amount as compensation of Rs.60,00,000/­ to the respondent herein within one month from the date of order

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: the cheque in question (i.e. Rs. 60,00,000/­) and had further directed to pay the aforesaid amount as compensation of Rs.60,00,000/­ to the respondent herein within one month from the date of order. 2 Briefly stated the facts that had given rise to the filing of the present criminal appeal are succinctly given as under: That the respondent herein is a company incorporated and registered under the Companies Act, 1956, engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of electronic goods, had placed an Inter Corporate Deposit (ICD) with the appellant herein on the agreed terms and conditions for the period w.e.f. CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.2/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. 05.06.1993 to 04.06.1994 and the appellant herein had further agreed to repay the same to the respondent herein alongwith an interest @ 24% per annum on the aforesaid ICD for which the appellant herein had promised to issue a cheque at the time of maturity of the said ICD in favour of the respondent herein. As alleged, a cheque bearing no. 0345128 dated 18.01.1996 amounting to Rs. 30,00,000/­ drawn on Bank of India, Janpath, New Delhi was issued by the appellant herein in favour of the respondent herein towards the discharge of its liability in respect of the aforesaid ICD. On presentation, the aforesaid cheque was got dishonoured on 09.07.1996 for the reasons "payment stopped by the drawer". Despite service of legal notice dated 24.07.1996 the appellant herein had failed to make the payment to the respondent herein within the stipulated period in respect of the cheque in question, though the appellant herein had replied the said legal notice vide its reply dated 04.08.1996. Hence, the complaint was filed before the learned trial court

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: in respect of the cheque in question, though the appellant herein had replied the said legal notice vide its reply dated 04.08.1996. Hence, the complaint was filed before the learned trial court. 3 The appellant herein had caused his appearance through its representative before the learned trial court pursuant to the summons issued against it and was admitted to bail. Thereafter, notice of accusation under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was served upon the appellant herein to which he had pleaded not guilty and had claimed trial. Thereafter, the matter was postponed for CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.3/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. evidence. 4 In support of its case, the respondent herein had examined two witnesses namely Sh. Yatinder Singh (CW1) and Sh. Ashok Sawhney (CW2). Both these witnesses were duly cross examined by the appellant herein. Thereafter, the appellant herein was examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C. on 15.04.2010. 5 The appellant herein had also examined eight witnesses in all in his defence. 6 After conclusion of the trial, the learned trial court had held guilty and convicted the appellant herein under Section 138 of N.I. Act and had also passed the consequent order on sentence dated 07.11.2013. 7 The appellant herein had challenged the aforesaid impugned judgment on the following grounds: 8 That the impugned judgment passed by the learned MM is contrary to the law and against the established principles of law laid down by the superior courts and had not appreciated the evidence on record and thus, the impugned judgment was liable to be set aside

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: to the law and against the established principles of law laid down by the superior courts and had not appreciated the evidence on record and thus, the impugned judgment was liable to be set aside. 9 That the learned trial court had also failed to appreciate the fact that in the absence of a notice of 72 hours issued by the respondent herein to the appellant herein, the amount under the ICD could not be recalled and the judgment relied upon by the learned MM had no bearing to the facts of the present case and CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.4/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. thus the observations made in the impugned judgment regarding the contention of 72 hours notice, held no water and therefore, the judgment was liable to be set aside. 10 That the learned MM had also failed to observe that to constitute an offence of dishonour of cheque, there must be insufficient fund in the account of the drawer of the cheque, whereas in the present case the payment had been stopped by the drawer and the legal notice as issued by the respondent herein was duly replied by the appellant herein and the same was not taken into consideration by the learned MM while passing the impugned judgment. 11 It was further stated that the Ld. MM appeared to have taken into consideration the document Ex. CW1/DA containing the terms and conditions upon which ICD of Rs

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: passing the impugned judgment. 11 It was further stated that the Ld. MM appeared to have taken into consideration the document Ex. CW1/DA containing the terms and conditions upon which ICD of Rs. 30,00,000/­ was placed by the respondent with the appellant requiring 72 hours advance notice by the respondent company to the appellant before presentation of cheque and hence it was stated that since the presentation of cheque by the respondent was done without issuance of any such 72 hours prior notice which was clearly in breach of terms and conditions of ICD, hence dishonour thereof would not entail any action under section 138 of NI Act. 12 It had been stated further that judgment cited and relied upon by the Ld. MM in para 30 of the impugned judgment had no bearing upon the facts of the CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.5/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. present case. It merely provided that even if the payee was intimated before hand not to present the cheque for encashment and the bank was also informed not to make the payment against the cheque and if the cheque got dishonoured when payee ignored such an intimation and had presented the cheque, this section 138 NI Act would still be made out. 13 Another ground which had been taken by the appellant is that though the ICD placed on 5.6.1993 was for a maximum period of six months whereas the disputed cheque was dated 18.1.1996, hence it was axiomatic that there was no occasion for the appellant to issue such a cheque and that too after a lapse of two years to the respondent with referance to the said ICD

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: dated 18.1.1996, hence it was axiomatic that there was no occasion for the appellant to issue such a cheque and that too after a lapse of two years to the respondent with referance to the said ICD. 14 It had also been reiterated again that the reason for dishonourment of the cheque in the present case was not "insufficiency of funds", rather "stop payment" instructions were issued by the appellant, hence it did not attract the provisions of section 138 NI Act. It had also been contended that the cheque was not issued in discharge of any debt or any other legal liability. However, I am not impressed with this contention as now it is the settled preposition of law that dishonourment of a cheque for any reason whatsoever barring few exceptions shall essentially attract the provisions of section 138 NI Act. 15 Reliance had also been placed on cross­examination of Sh Yatinder Singh (CW1) recorded on 16.9.2009, as a ground of appeal, wherein he had stated CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.6/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. that he was not in a position either to admit or deny as to whether the cheque issued by the accused/appellant to the respondent was not issued towards any debt, rather only as device to fulfill the requirements of the accounts. 16 Another ground which had been taken by the appellant is that section 138 NI Act provided penal provisions and thus punishment in the said offence was provided as imprisonment of either description up to two years or with fine not exceeding double of the cheque amount or both, whereas section 357 Cr.P.C. dealt separately with the powers of the Court to award compensation to the complainant/victim to be paid by the convict out of the fine amount imposed upon him/her and section 357 (3) Cr.P.C

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: Cr.P.C. dealt separately with the powers of the Court to award compensation to the complainant/victim to be paid by the convict out of the fine amount imposed upon him/her and section 357 (3) Cr.P.C. further provided that if the penalty or fine was not a part of sentence, then the Court might have also ordered for compensation to be paid to the complainant/victim. However, the judgment dated 10.10.2013 followed by the order on sentence dated 7.11.2013, had made it manifestly clear that the Ld. MM, without imposing any fine upon the appellant herein had directed the payment of compensation to the respondent which was neither in accordance with the provisions of section 138 NI Act nor within the powers of the Ld. MM to have passed any such order and as such the impugned judgment and consequent order on sentence was liable to be set aside on this ground alone. 17 The other ground which had been raised before this court is that the CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.7/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. appellant/accused with all his bonafides had proved that the photocopies held by the appellant were adequate to draw a presumption that the cheque in question was not given to the respondent towards any debt or liability legally recoverable from the appellant but it was issued in connection with certain adjustments between Videocon Narmada Electronics Ltd and Nava Bharat Ferror Alloyes Ltd (NFAL) in relation to the transactions confined to them

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: appellant but it was issued in connection with certain adjustments between Videocon Narmada Electronics Ltd and Nava Bharat Ferror Alloyes Ltd (NFAL) in relation to the transactions confined to them. 18 It was also stated that the respondent had fraudulently presented the cheque in question for encashment because as per the contents of the complaint, the ICD had carried interest @ 24% per annum for a period of one year , that is from 5.6.1993 to 4.6.1994 and even if assumed for the sake of arguments that the interest @ 24% per annum was payable by the appellant to the respondent on the date of maturity, then also the amount mentioned in the cheque did not match with the principal amount and interest component computed thereon, hence the Ld. MM ought to have come to the conclusion that cheque in question was not at all issued in relation to discharge of any liability or debt, legally recoverable from the appellant. However, instead of arriving at such a conclusion, the Ld. MM had drawn an adverse inference against the appellant herein. 19 Lastly, it was stated that despite the Ld. MM observing regarding "sufficiency of funds" in the account of the appellant, he had miserably erred CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.8/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. in convicting the appellant for the aforesaid offence under section 138 NI Act without even examining the judgments cited and relied upon by the appellant in its written submissions submitted before the Ld. MM and hence his judgment was based on conjunctures and surmises as the appellant was guilty of misusing the settled principles of law and thus the appeal of the appellant deserved to be admitted on merits and the impugned judgment and consequent order on sentence were liable to be set aside

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: of misusing the settled principles of law and thus the appeal of the appellant deserved to be admitted on merits and the impugned judgment and consequent order on sentence were liable to be set aside. 20 I have heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and perused the material available on record. 21 During the course of oral submissions, Sh. Jagdeep Vats and Sh M. Sowaridev, Ld. Counsels appearing on behalf of appellant had also submitted before this court that there was an inordinate delay in the present case as the complaint was filed before the Ld. Trial Court in the year 1996 but the complainant/respondent herein had tendered his affidavit during pre­ summoning evidence in the year 2005 only and thus the said complaint was liable to be dismissed by the Ld. MM on this short ground of delay alone. However, I do not find any merits in the present contention because in case of filing of a criminal complaint before the court of Ld. MM, the point in consideration relates to the delay committed in filing of the complaint itself and not to the date when the pre­summoning evidence by way of an affidavit CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.9/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. was allegedly filed. 22 It was also submitted during the course of submissions that there were four Metropolitan Magistrates who had tried and dealt with the present case which was not in conformity of the latest law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court related to the case of such nature wherein it has been stated that the Ld. MM, who had recorded the evidence shall only dispose of the case and none other then him can pass a final judgment and any judgment if so rendered would be a nullity in the eyes of law

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: that the Ld. MM, who had recorded the evidence shall only dispose of the case and none other then him can pass a final judgment and any judgment if so rendered would be a nullity in the eyes of law. However, since the said judgment has been passed after recording of the evidence in the present case, hence same would be applicable in prospective manner and not in a retrospective manner and thus this contention raised on behalf of the appellant is also devoid of any merits and does not carry any weight in it. 23 Reliance has also been placed on para 30 of the impugned judgment wherein the Ld. MM had dealt with the issue related to the advance notice of 72 hours before presentation of the cheque in question and further reliance was placed on para 32 of the impugned judgment wherein the Ld. MM was pleased to observe as under: " To substantiate this defence, the accused examined eight witnesses. The gist of the testimonies of these witnesses in repect of the terms and conditions of the ICD for Rs. 30 lacs from the complainant (VIL) to the accused ( Beardsell) hinges upon the predication that the ICD was an CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.10/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. interest free deposit given by the complainant to the accused against outstanding of VNEL payable to NBFAL, as an accommodation loan till such amount was eventually settled by VNEL to NBFAL." 24 In the light of the aforesaid observations, it had been tried to be portrayed to this court that it was a finding of the Ld. MM that ICD was an interest free deposit given to the appellant by the respondent against the outstanding of VNEL payable to NBFAL, as an accommodation loan, till such amount was eventually settled by VNEL to NBFAL

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: an interest free deposit given to the appellant by the respondent against the outstanding of VNEL payable to NBFAL, as an accommodation loan, till such amount was eventually settled by VNEL to NBFAL. 25 However, I have no hesitation in holding that it is a mis­interpretation of the aforesaid para done by the appellant herein because it has been clearly observed by the Ld. MM in the impugned para itself that gist of the testimonies of the said eight witnesses examined by the appellant during its defence evidence was hinging upon the prediction that certain facts had happened and what had been tried to convey to the court by the witnesses cannot be substituted as an observation of the court, hence I do not find any merits in this submissions of the appellant as well. 26 So far as the contention related to the actual date of transaction of ICD and the date of cheque as had been taken as ground no. 8 in the present appeal is concerned, there is sufficient documentary evidence available on record to show that on none of the earlier occasions, the respondent herein had issued CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.11/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. any written instructions or intimation to the present appellant regarding renewal of the cheque and all documents and letters were sufficient enough to prove on record that it was always upon the telephonic instructions received from the respondent herein that the appellant used to replace the cheques drawn in favour of the respondent. Documents Ex. CW1/DB, Ex. CW1/DC and Ex. CW1/DD can be easily referred to in this regard. 27 So far as the contention of the appellant regarding adjustment of account as reflected in the document Ex

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: Documents Ex. CW1/DB, Ex. CW1/DC and Ex. CW1/DD can be easily referred to in this regard. 27 So far as the contention of the appellant regarding adjustment of account as reflected in the document Ex. CW1/DD is concerned, no document had been placed on record by the appellant to show that this proposal of the appellant herein was ever accepted or acted upon by the respondent herein. 28 Reliance has also been placed by the appellant on the document Ex. CW5/X­6. However, I have no hesitation in holding that the said document itself does not pertain to the present respondent. Rather it pertained to Videocon Narmada Electronics Ltd, which is a separate legal entity in itself and is distinct and different from Videocon International Ltd., who is respondent in the present case. 29 It is well settled preposition of law that each juristic person having been incorporated under any of the Indian laws, enjoys separate independent, individual personality in the eyes of law having its own rights and liabilities whatsoever which are independent of the rights and liability of such other CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.12/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. juristic person. 30 So far as the ground taken in para 10 of the appeal is concerned which is related to the deposition of CW­1 regarding his expression of lack of capability either to admit or deny the suggestion as put to him during his cross­ examination is concerned, mere inability of the witness either to admit or deny the existence of certain facts in itself is not sufficient to disprove the existence or otherwise of the said fact unless some more evidence either to prove its existence or non­existence is brought on record. Hence, even this testimony is also not going to help the appellant in any manner whatsoever

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: said fact unless some more evidence either to prove its existence or non­existence is brought on record. Hence, even this testimony is also not going to help the appellant in any manner whatsoever. 31 So far as the ground in relation to awarding of the compensation without imposing a fine is concerned, I have no hesitation in holding that the appellant had misread the provision of section 357(3) of Cr.P.C., which is independent of section 357(1) Cr.P.C. It is only when sentence of fine has been imposed upon the accused by the Court, then Court is bound to award compensation not exceeding the amount of such fine under section 357(1) Cr.P.C. However, section 357(3) Cr.P.C. is independent and does not restrict the powers of the Court to award any amount of compensation to the victim irrespective of its restrictive jurisdictional powers to impose fine. Although the Ld. MM had not categorically used the word "sentence of fine" in his order on sentence. However, plain reading of the same as appearing in paras 3 and 4 are CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.13/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. concerned, it becomes crystal clear that the aforesaid amount of Rs.60 lacs was to be realized from the appellant herein as a mode of fine and the entire fine as imposed was thus awarded by the Ld. MM to the respondent herein towards compensation. Hence, it cannot be held that the Ld. MM had committed any illegality or infirmity warranting of any interference of this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, by awarding such compensation in his order on sentence

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: the Ld. MM had committed any illegality or infirmity warranting of any interference of this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, by awarding such compensation in his order on sentence. 32 So far as the adjustment of the accounts of other two companies as agitated in paras 14 and 15 of the grounds of appeal are concerned, as observed earlier, each and every juristic person itself is an independent personality distinct from other and hence it can never be presumed that liability of one juristic person shall be adjusted by another juristic person against the third person . Therefore, this ground does not holds any substance in it. 33 Ld. Counsel appearing for the respondent Sh. B. S. Nagar, had drawn the attention of this Court to the deposition of DW6 examined by the appellant herein in its defence on 16.2.2012 as well as on 19.4.2012 and had stated that this witness himself had admitted existence of dispute between the parties to the present litigation in respect of non payment of ICD and this witness had further gone to the extent of stating that he had personal knowledge of the fact that the aforesaid ICD was placed with the appellant by the respondent at the CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.14/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. request of the appellant made on its behalf by one Sh. P

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: ICD was placed with the appellant by the respondent at the CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.14/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. request of the appellant made on its behalf by one Sh. P. Punniah and DW6 himself had taken the decision to place such ICD with the appellant, though relationship between the parties was only in respect of borrowing ICD and nothing beyond that, and thus it has been submitted that in the light of the aforesaid deposition of DW6 the very own witness of the appellant herein himself had deposed against the appellant and he was not even declared hostile by the appellant, hence his testimony can not be brushed aside or ignored at all and has to be essentially read as against the appellant herein as well. 34 After hearing rival contentions of the parties, I have no hesitation in holding that Negotiable Instruments Act is a Special Act constituting an offence punishable under section 138 NI Act, not only on mere dishonourment of the cheque but only upon consequent failure of the drawer to make payment to the drawee within 15 days from the date of receipt of notice. Further, by virtue of certain legal provisions incorporated in the said Act, certain presumptions have also been carved out therein which are in favour of the drawee and against the drawer as provided under sections 118 and 139 of the said Act itself and the onus to rebut these presumptions always rests upon the accused and not upon the complainant. Hence, an exception to the general principles of criminal law regarding presumption of innocence in favour of the accused has been dispensed with in this special legislation and onus rests upon CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.15/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: of innocence in favour of the accused has been dispensed with in this special legislation and onus rests upon CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.15/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. the accused who is presumed to be guilty to establish his probable defence on record by rebutting those presumptions existing against him. 35 If the legal preposition in this regard is examined in the light of the facts of the present case, then I have no hesitation in holding that even despite examining eight witnesses in its defence, the appellant herein had miserably failed to rebut those presumptions existing against it by adducing any cogent and relevant evidence on record. 36 On the other hand, the respondent had categorically established and proved on record the issuance of cheque by the appellant, its consequent dishonourment on presentation due to "stop payment instructions" issued by the appellant to its banker and failure of the appellant to make payment involved in the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period despite service of legal notice issued to it by the respondent in this regard. 37 Therefore, the respondent herein had discharged its onus successfully. Hence, I have no hesitation in holding that the judgment passed by the Ld. MM convicting the appellant for an offence punishable under section 138 NI Act, and the consequent order on sentence do not suffer from any illegality or infirmity warranting any interference of this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. 38 As a result, the appeal fails and the same is hereby dismissed. CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.16/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. 39 TCR be sent back with a copy of the judgment

title: M/S Beardsell Limited vs M/S Videocon International ... on 1 July, 2014
content: 38 As a result, the appeal fails and the same is hereby dismissed. CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.16/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd. 39 TCR be sent back with a copy of the judgment. 40 Appeal file be consigned to record room after completion of all other necessary formalities. Announced in the open Court on 10.07.2014 (LOKESH KUMAR SHARMA) ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE­04 NEW DELHI DISTRICT/ PATIALA HOUSE COURTS/NEW DELHI CA No. 1/1/14 Page No.17/17 M/s Beardsell Ltd. vs. M/s Videocon International Ltd.

title: Case No. : 5176/14 Raj Kumar Sharma vs . Pawan Kumar Page No. 1/12 on 17 May, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF SHRI RAVINDER SINGH­II METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE DWARKA COURTS, NEW DELHI Case No. : 5176/14 Unique Case ID No. : R0534662009 Raj Kumar Sharma S/o Sh. Before proceeding further it is imperative for me to go through the relevant provisions of law. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act reads as: "Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account:Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the Case No. : 5176/14 Raj Kumar Sharma Vs. Pawan Kumar Page No. 5/12 discharge, in while or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation:For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability
