content: in his cross examination that they had taken the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ to return it to the accused in first week of December 2011, but had not returned the same to accused and the cheque of Rs. 2.75 lacs was given by the accused to the complainant on that date. The complainant has categorically denied in his cross examination that there was any discussion between the parties on the issue of settlement of bill amount. It is further deposed by CW­1 that he has visited the office of the accused to settle the issue of dishonored cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ after the information that the accused were shifting their bank from ICICI Bank to Laxmi Vilas Bank. 29. Section 118 NI Act raises a number of presumptions of consideration, date, time of acceptance, time of transfer and status of holder in due course unless the contrary is proved. The section lays down special rule of evidence applicable to negotiable CC No. 673/01/2012 M/s Universal Offset Vs M/s Relio Quick India Pvt. Ltd. Page no. 12 of Pages instruments and presumptions are one of law and the court shall presume that the negotiable instrument which is the cheque in the present case, was made for consideration, was made on the date which it bears and that it was handed over to the complainant by the accused in due course. 30. Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act raises presumption that the holder of the cheque which is the complainant in the present case received the cheque for the discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. 31. These presumptions have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted to accused to prove otherwise

title: M/S Universal Offsets vs Unknown on 23 August, 2014
content: have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted to accused to prove otherwise. A presumption is not itself evidence, but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. 32. In the present case as the execution of the cheque has been admitted by the accused and is proved as well the burden has shifted upon the accused to prove that the complainant has not received the cheque for the discharge of any debt or liability. 33. The accused has failed to discharge their burden and rebut the onus as in the present case they have admitted their liability for the impugned cheque in question, however, have disputed to pay the amount of the same on the ground that pursuant to an oral CC No. 673/01/2012 M/s Universal Offset Vs M/s Relio Quick India Pvt. Ltd. Page no. 13 of Pages settlement agreed into between the parties, the complainant was to return the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ to them which was dishonored with the remarks payment stopped by drawer on 25.11.2011. 34. The defence of the accused that the payment of that cheque was stopped as the quality of the material was not proper was taken by them for the first time at the stage of defence evidence. There was no suggestion with respect to the same to the witness of the complainant at the stage of his cross examination. Even at the stage of notice and statement of accused there was no whisper regarding the defence of defective material. More so, in his cross examination it is admitted by DW­1 that they have not given any written letter or notice or e­mail to the complainant regarding defective material nor does he remember that they have sent back the defective material back to the complainant

title: M/S Universal Offsets vs Unknown on 23 August, 2014
content: they have not given any written letter or notice or e­mail to the complainant regarding defective material nor does he remember that they have sent back the defective material back to the complainant. In his voluntary statement it is further stated that he does not even remember whether they have received the defective material in the present case or not. Such kind of statement on the part of the accused cast a serious dent on the defence of the accused regarding whether any defective material was at all supplied and if there was no defective material supplied the deposition of the accused by itself regarding the stop payment of the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­, comes under CC No. 673/01/2012 M/s Universal Offset Vs M/s Relio Quick India Pvt. Ltd. Page no. 14 of Pages serious suspicion. 35. The accused had further relied upon an oral agreement. It is hard to contemplate that when all the transactions are taking between the parties in writing, how can an agreement regarding an amount to the tune of more than Rs. 10 lacs can be verbal. There is an admission of CW­1 that he has received a cheque of Rs. 2.75 lacs, however, it does not in any manner show that the complainant has waived their right with respect to the cheque of Rs, 10,92,399/­. 36. The defence of the accused that their bankers were to be shifted from ICICI Bank to Laxmi Vilas Bank also does not come to any aid of the accused with respect to the dishonor of the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ as in the present case, in his deposition itself it is admitted by the accused that the bankers were shifted on 5.1.2012 and the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ was dishonored in November 2011, regarding which legal notice was also sent on 24.12.2011. 37

title: M/S Universal Offsets vs Unknown on 23 August, 2014
content: it is admitted by the accused that the bankers were shifted on 5.1.2012 and the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ was dishonored in November 2011, regarding which legal notice was also sent on 24.12.2011. 37. Thus in view of the above said discussions and findings, it is held that the accused has failed to show before the Court that they have no liability with respect to cheque bearing no. 994430 of Rs. 10,92,399/­, which is the subject matter of CC No. 1027/01/2012. Further more the accused have failed to show that there was any CC No. 673/01/2012 M/s Universal Offset Vs M/s Relio Quick India Pvt. Ltd. Page no. 15 of Pages settlement pursuant to which the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ was to be returned back by the complainant to the accused. The accused have categorically deposed before the Court that he is admitting the liability of impugned cheque in question, however, subject to handing over of the cheque of Rs. 10,92,399/­ by the complainant to them. The accused has failed to show before the Court that they have no legally enforceable liability with repsect to that cheque and therefore, it is held that the accused persons have failed to discharge/rebut the onus U/s 118 and Section 139 of the NI Act. 38. In view of the above said discussions and findings accused persons are held guilty for the offence punishable U/s 138 NI Act. Accused persons are convicted for the offence punishable U/s 138 NI Act. 39. Let they be heard separately on the point of sentence. 40. Let convicts be provided with copy of judgment free of cost. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides that: "Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account:Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in while or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 4/13 Explanation:For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE IN THE LIGHT OF THE INGREDIENTS OF SECTION 138 OF THE NI ACT AND THE DEFENCE RAISED BY THE ACCUSED 7. It is not disputed by the accused that the cheque's in Question Ex. CW1/B is drawn on the account maintained by him in the name of his firm Sojat Traders. Further signature on the cheque in question has also not been disputed by the accused. Further the presentation, dishonor of the cheque in question and the cheque returning memo has also not been challenged by the accused. Therefore in view of the evidence on record it stands proved that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B is signed by the accused and the same is drawn on account maintained by him in the name of his firm Sojat Traders. Further it also stands duly proved that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B was dishonored vide cheque returning memo Ex. CW1/C dated 31.01.2009 with the reason "Funds Insufficient" 8. From the perusal of the entire evidence it has come to fore that two fold defence has been taken by the accused. Firstly, that he has not been served with the legal demand notice by the complainant. And secondly that the blank signed cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has been given by him to the complainant as security at the time of taking of the loan. 9

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: the legal demand notice by the complainant. And secondly that the blank signed cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has been given by him to the complainant as security at the time of taking of the loan. 9. Coming to the first line of defence taken by the accused that he has not been served with the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/D by the complainant. It is pertinent to note that CW­1 (AR) of the complainant has examined himself as CW­1 and has specifically stated in his evidence affidavit Ex. CW1/1 that the complainant has got issued the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/D to the accused. CW­1 has also placed on record the registered post receipt Ex.CW1/E on record. The accused has denied the receipt of the legal demand notice at the CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 5/13 time of framing of notice U/s 251 of the Code. Further a suggestion regarding non receipt of the legal demand notice was also put to CW­1(AR) by the counsel for the accused which was denied by the witness. Interestingly in his Statement U/s 313 of the Code the accused has admitted the receipt of the legal demand notice. Further, on perusal of the legal demand notice, it is revealed that the same has been sent to the accused at Village Dhakri, Teh. Sojat, Distt. Pali, Pali­306104. The same address of the accused have been furnished by the complainant on the complaint Ex. CW1/F. The accused throughout the trial has not disputed the address mentioned in the legal demand notice and the complaint and same address has been furnished by the accused on his bail bond. Therefore, it is evident that legal demand notice has been sent at the correct address of the accused. Further, the postal receipt Ex

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: same address has been furnished by the accused on his bail bond. Therefore, it is evident that legal demand notice has been sent at the correct address of the accused. Further, the postal receipt Ex. CW1/E vide which the legal demand notice has been sent to the accused is also on record. It is trite to say that when there is service of notice by post on the correct address which evidently has taken place in the present case, there is always a presumption that the legal demand notice has been duly served upon the accused unless some concrete evidence in rebuttal is adduced by the accused to establish that the legal demand notice has not been served upon him. It was for the accused to rebut the presumption about the service of notice and show that the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/D was never tendered or that the postal receipt Ex.CW1/E is incorrect or the address mentioned on the legal demand notice is incorrect. Except denials and suggestions the accused has not any lead any evidence to corroborate his stand. Therefore its stands proved that the legal demand notice Ex.CW1/D has been served upon the accused. As such non receipt of the legal demand notice as a defence on part of the accused has no force. 10. Coming to the second line of defence taken by the accused that he has not issued the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B to the complainant in partial discharge of his loan liability and the same was given by him as security in blank signed manner at the time taking of CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 6/13 the loan. 11. Taking up the first limb of the defence i.e except signatures no other particular in the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has been filled by the accused

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 6/13 the loan. 11. Taking up the first limb of the defence i.e except signatures no other particular in the Cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has been filled by the accused. It is not disputed by the accused that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/B is drawn on the account maintained by him. Further signature on the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has also not been disputed by the accused. However, it is also submitted by the accused that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B was given by him to the complainant as a security and except signatures no other particulars in the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/B has been filled by him. During the course of arguments Ld. Counsel for the accused also reiterated the same contentions. Surprisingly except denials and suggestions accused has not brought any evidence on record to support his stand that except signatures he has not filled the other particulars in the cheque in question. Furthermore even believing the stand of accused to be correct still there is also no evidence on record to show that he has not even authorized the complainant to fill the said particulars. More so it is trite to say that by putting the name and date there is no material alteration on the cheque U/s 87 of the NI Act as there is no rule of banking business that the name of the payee as well as the amount should be written by the drawer himself, as no law provides that in case of cheque the entire body has to be written by the drawer only

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: business that the name of the payee as well as the amount should be written by the drawer himself, as no law provides that in case of cheque the entire body has to be written by the drawer only. Therefore, once the signature on the cheque in question is admitted as has happened in the case in hand, the plea that particulars in the cheque in question has not been filled by the drawer is of no consequence unless some cogent evidence has been lead by the accused that he has not expressly or impliedly authorized the payee to fill the particulars therein. 12. Before I advert to the second limb of the defence taken by the accused i.e. the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B has been issued by him as a security to the complainant and not in discharge of his part liability towards the complainant, it is imperative for me to go through CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 7/13 the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instru­ ments.--Until the contrary is proved, the fol­ lowing presumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable in­ strument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or trans­ ferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the dis­ charge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 13. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: nature referred to in Section 138 for the dis­ charge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 13. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of preponderance of probabilities. The relevant portion of the said judg­ ment is reproduced here under (Paras 32 & 34): "32. An accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record. An accused has a constitutional right to maintain silence. Standard of proof on the part of the accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different. 34. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies." 14. In Rangappa Vs Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an ac­ cused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: a settled position that when an ac­ cused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 8/13 the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of proba­ bilities' and if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which cre­ ates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail and for this the accused can rely on the materi­ als submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to ad­ duce evidence of his/her own. 15. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judg­ ments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted as has happened in the instant case, the presumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is re­ buttable. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused discharges the initial onus of proof showing that the existence of consideration was improb­ able or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by refer­ ence to the circumstances upon which he relies

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by refer­ ence to the circumstances upon which he relies. In case, where the ac­ cused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­ existence of the consideration, the complainant would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 16. Coming back to the instant case. In the case in hand, it has been admitted by the accused that he has taken loan from the complainant for the purchase of the truck vide loan agreement no. TNJODRCVZ00303207 but throughout the trial the accused has denied the claim of the complainant and has stated that the vehicle has been repossessed by the complainant and the cheque in question Ex. CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 9/13 CW1/B has not been given by him to the complainant in part discharge of his liability and the same has been given by him as a security to the complainant at the time of taking of the loan. To corroborate his stand the accused has also examined himself as DW­1. It is interesting to see that CW­1 has placed the statement of account of the accused Ex. CW1/H on record bearing legacy Id number TNJODRCVZ00303207 and during his cross examination, the witness was confronted with another statement of account Ex.CW1/X. Interestingly, CW­1 has admitted in his cross examination that the statement of account Ex. CW1/X belongs to the complainant. Perusal of statement of statement of account Ex. CW1/X reveals that the same pertains to the loan account of the accused having same legacy Id number TNJODRCVZ00303207

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: belongs to the complainant. Perusal of statement of statement of account Ex. CW1/X reveals that the same pertains to the loan account of the accused having same legacy Id number TNJODRCVZ00303207. Therefore from the own record and admission of the witness (CW­1) it stands established that statement of account Ex. CW1/H & Ex. CW1/X both pertains to the loan account of the accused. The statement of account Ex.CW1/H filed by CW­1 only mentions the payments made by the accused and do not specify the mode in which the payment were made by the accused. Perusal of the statement of account Ex.CW1/X reveals that post dated cheques were presented by the complainant for clearance of the installments payable by the accused and on 01.06.2007 the first payment of installment was cleared in the loan account of the accused by a cheque bearing no. 998670 and subsequent payments were also cleared in the said account using the cheques of the same series till May, 2008 i.e. from cheque bearing No. 998670 to 998681. Further perusal of statement of account Ex. CW1/X also reveals that the payment for the month of July 2007 was bounced and the same was cleared by the accused through another cheque of the same series i.e 998687. Interestingly, the cheque in question Ex. CW1/B bears the no. 998667 i.e. prior in series to the cheques given for payment of the installments thereby making the stand of the accused highly probable that the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B was given by him to the complainant as a security at the time of taking of the loan. Further this payment made by the accused through subsequent cheques of the CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 10/13 same series i.e. from cheque bearing No

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: made by the accused through subsequent cheques of the CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 10/13 same series i.e. from cheque bearing No. 998670 to 998681 also make it highly inconceivable that a person would keep a previous single cheque leaf of the same series of which he has already given post dated cheques for the payment of his monthly EMI's and further would hand over the same to the complainant after one and a half years of the commencement of the loan. 17. During course of arguments, the ld. Counsel for the accused also argued that the vehicle for which the loan was taken by the accused was repossessed by the complainant and subsequently the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B has been presented for clearance. It is pertinent to note that during cross examination of CW­1 inventory of the vehicle Ex.CW1/X1 dated 06.01.2009 was put to the witness which has been denied by the witness stating that the same do not possess the seal of the complainant. Interestingly, the witness CW­1 has not disputed the repossession of the vehicle but has stated that the same was repossessed by the complainant in February, 2009 and not in January, 2009 as indicated from the inventory sheet Ex. CW1/X1. It is surprising to see that the complainant throughout the trial has not placed on record any document to show as to when the repossession of the vehicle was carried out by the complainant. Except denial of the inventory sheet Ex.CW1/X1 the complainant has not lead any evidence to show as to when the vehicle was repossessed by the complainant. Therefore, there is no reason to disbelieve the inventory sheet Ex.CW1/X1 whereby the vehicle was repossessed by the complainant in January 2009

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: when the vehicle was repossessed by the complainant. Therefore, there is no reason to disbelieve the inventory sheet Ex.CW1/X1 whereby the vehicle was repossessed by the complainant in January 2009. Therefore, I have no hesitation in holding that the vehicle was repossessed by the complainant vide inventory sheet Ex.CW1/X1 dated 06.01.2009. Now, what needs to be seen is, whether the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B is dated prior to the repossession of the vehicle or is dated subsequent to the repossession of the vehicle. Perusal of the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B reveals that the same is dated 13.01.2009 and was dishonoured vide cheque returning memo dated 29.01.2009, thereby making it clear that the cheque in question Ex.CW1/3 is dated subsequent to the repossession CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 11/13 of the vehicle on 06.01.2009. It is trite to say that in hirer purchase agreement between the financial institution and the hirer the agreement executed stands determined by the act of repossessing of the vehicle by the financial institution and the cheque given would be instrument without consideration. The very fact that the complainant has repossessed the vehicle from the complainant on 06.01.2009 and has also admittedly sold it off subsequently shows that there was no occasion for the complainant to present the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B as by repossessing the vehicle the complainant has exhausted one of its remedy which might have been available to the complainant under the agreement. 18

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: to present the cheque in question Ex.CW1/B as by repossessing the vehicle the complainant has exhausted one of its remedy which might have been available to the complainant under the agreement. 18. In a case of this nature, where the chances of false implication cannot be ruled out, the background fact and the conduct of the parties together with their legal requirements are required to be taken into consideration. All the aforesaid circumstances/factors rebut the presumptions arising in favour of the complainant provided under Section 139 of the NI Act because they raise credible doubt over the veracity of the complainant's claims and satisfy the test of rebuttal on the strength of preponderance of probabilities thereby weakening the claim of the Complainant. 19. In light of my discussion above I hereby hold that the accused has been able to raise probabilities and has been able to rebut the presumptions which were raised against him. The defence raised by the accused is sufficient to discharge the initial burden of proof raised on him. This court do not find any force in the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the Complainant that the accused has failed to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. It is trite to say that presumptions are not in itself evidence but it only enables a party in whose favour it exists to show that he has a prima facie case. In the case in hand the presumptions under Section 139 of NI Act alone cannot be the sole basis to prove the case of the complainant. The materials and evidence available on the record do CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 12/13 not bridge the gap

title: Cc No. 4522/14 M/S G E Capital ... vs . Ismlile Khan Page No. 1/13 on 12 November, 2014
content: case of the complainant. The materials and evidence available on the record do CC No. 4522/14 M/s G E Capital Transportation Financial Services Ltd. Vs. Ismlile Khan Page no. 12/13 not bridge the gap. It is highly improbable that the accused has given the cheque in question Ex CW1/B in order to discharge his part liability. Therefore, I hereby hold that the Complainant has not been able to prove and substantiate the allegations that the cheque in question Ex CW1/B was issued by the accused in part discharge of his legal liability. Furthermore, mere non payment of cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of legal notice is not itself sufficient to fasten any liability U/s 138 of the NI Act as it is established that the Cheque in Question Ex. CW1/B was not issued by the accused in discharge of his part legal liability. 20. Accordingly, I hold that complainant has not been able prove all the ingredients of the offence U/s 138 of NI Act against the accused. Accordingly, accused Ismile Khan Proprietor of Sojat Traders is hereby acquitted of the offence U/s 138 of NI Act. title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: I have heard Ld. Counsels for both the parties and have also perused the entire record of the case file. Before proceeding further it is imperative for me to go through the relevant provisions of law. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides that: "Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account:Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in while or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 5/14 fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation:For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE IN THE LIGHT OF THE INGREDIENTS OF SECTION 138 OF THE NI ACT AND THE DEFENCE RAISED BY THE ACCUSED 8. The issuance of the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 to the complainant by the accused has not been disputed. It is also not disputed by the accused that the cheque in Question Ex. CW1/2 is drawn on the account maintained by him. Further signature on the cheque in question CW1/2 has also not been disputed by the accused. The presentation, dishonor of the cheque in question and the cheque returning memo has also not been challenged by the accused

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: the cheque in question CW1/2 has also not been disputed by the accused. The presentation, dishonor of the cheque in question and the cheque returning memo has also not been challenged by the accused. Therefore, In light of the evidence on record it stands duly proved that the cheque in question Ex CW1/2 is issued by the accused from his own account and the same is also signed by the accused. Further it also stands duly proved that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 was dishonored vide cheque returning memo Ex. CW1/2A with the reason "Insufficient Funds". Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 6/14 9. From the perusal of the entire evidence it has come to the fore that two fold defence has been taken by the accused. Firstly, that he has not been served with the legal demand notice by the complainant and Secondly that he has never entered into any property transaction with the complainant and the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 has also not been issued by him to the complainant for return of any consideration amount in respect of the property transaction as alleged by the complainant. 10. Coming to the first line of defence taken by the accused that he has not been served with the legal demand notice from the complainant, it is pertinent to note that the complainant as CW­1 has specifically stated in his affidavit Ex. CW1/A that the complainant has got issued the legal notice of demand dated 10.11.2010 to the accused which is Ex. CW1/3 and it was sent to the accused on 11.11.2010 vide registered Post and UPC. CW­1 has also tendered in evidence the UPC receipt as Ex. CW1/4 and the registered post receipt as Ex.CW1/5. 11. The accused has denied the receipt of the legal demand Ex

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: registered Post and UPC. CW­1 has also tendered in evidence the UPC receipt as Ex. CW1/4 and the registered post receipt as Ex.CW1/5. 11. The accused has denied the receipt of the legal demand Ex. CW1/3 in his statement U/s 313 of the Code and also during his cross examination as DW­1. I have perused the legal notice of demand Ex. CW1/3. It bears the same address of the accused as mentioned by the complainant in the complaint. Interestingly, the accused during his cross examination as DW­1 has admitted that the complaint and the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/3 bears his correct address. Further the same address has been furnished by the accused on his bail bond. Further the complainant has also placed on record the registered post and UPC receipts issued by the postal authorities in ordinary course vide which the legal demand notice has been sent to the accused. Therefore it is evident that the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/3 has been sent at the correct address of the accused. It is trite to say that when there is service of notice by post on the correct address which evidently has taken place in the present case there is always a Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 7/14 presumption that the legal demand notice has been duly served upon the accused unless some concrete evidence in rebuttal is adduced by the accused to establish that the Legal Demand Notice has not been served upon him. It was for the accused to rebut the presumption about the service of notice and show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address or that the address mentioned on the notice was incorrect or that the notice was never tendered or that the postal receipts placed on record by the complainant are incorrect

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: brought to his address or that the address mentioned on the notice was incorrect or that the notice was never tendered or that the postal receipts placed on record by the complainant are incorrect. Except denials the accused has not any lead any evidence to corroborate his stand. Moreover, In "C.C. Alavi Hazi Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr." Reported in (2007) 6 Supreme Court case 555, it has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that the course open to the drawer where he claims not to have received the notice sent by post but has received copy of the complaint with the summons is that he can within 15 days of the receipt of summons make payment of the cheque amount and he then cannot contend that there was no proper service of notice, which evidently the accused in the instant case has not done despite receiving of the summons. As such non receipt of legal demand notice as a defence on part of the accused has no force. 12. Coming to the second line of defence taken by the accused that he has never entered into any property transaction with the complainant and the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 has also not been issued by him to the complainant for return of any consideration amount in respect of the property transaction as alleged by the complainant. 13. Before I advert to the above said defence taken by the accused, it is imperative for me to go through the provisions of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act which read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instru­ ments.--Until the contrary is proved, the fol­ lowing presumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: instru­ ments.--Until the contrary is proved, the fol­ lowing presumptions shall be made­ (a) of consideration.--that every negotiable Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 8/14 instrument was made or drawn for considera­ tion, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiat­ ed or transferred for consideration;" "139. Presumption in favour of holder.--It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 14. The Division bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Krishna Janardhan Bhat Vs. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54, has held that the accused can discharge the burden of presumption U/s 118 and U/s 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence on the strength of preponderance of probabilities. The relevant portion of the said judgment is reproduced here under (Paras 32 & 34): "32. An accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the materials already brought on record. An accused has a constitutional right to maintain silence. Standard of proof on the part of the accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different. 34. Furthermore, whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies." 15. In Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that it is a settled position that when an ac­ cused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prose­ cution can fail. The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 9/14 complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. 16. From the reading of the above said provisions and the judg­ ments the position of law which emerges is that once execution of the promissory note is admitted as has happened in the case in hand, the presumption under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is re­ buttable. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: 139 of the NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. Such a presumption is re­ buttable. The accused can prove the non­existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. If the accused discharges the initial onus of proof showing that the existence of consideration was improb­ able or doubtful or the same was illegal, the onus would shift to the Complainant who will be obliged to prove it as a matter of fact and upon its failure to prove would disentitle him to the grant of relief on the basis of the negotiable instrument. The burden upon the accused of proving the non­existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by refer­ ence to the circumstances upon which he relies. In case, where the ac­ cused fails to discharge the initial onus of proof by showing the non­ existence of the consideration, the complainant would invariably be held entitled to the benefit of presumption arising under Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act in his favour. 17. Now coming back to the case in hand, in the instant case it is the case of the complainant that on 01.09.2009 the accused and the complainant has entered into an agreement for sale of the property RZ 50 G. It is further the case of the complainant that he has given Rs. 7 lacs to the accused as an earnest money and out of the said seven lacs the payment of Rs. 3 lacs has been made by him through cheques on 01.09.2009 and on 03.09.2009 for a sum of Rs. 1 lakh and 2 lakh respectively and remaining Rs. 4 lakh was paid by cash. It is further the case of the complainant that thereafter the accused transferred the property RZ 50 G to a third person and to refund the payment made by Case No

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: Rs. 4 lakh was paid by cash. It is further the case of the complainant that thereafter the accused transferred the property RZ 50 G to a third person and to refund the payment made by Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 10/14 him the accused has issued two cheque out of which one cheque was encashed and the second cheque i.e. the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 was dishonored. The accused has denied the claim of the com­ plainant and examined himself as DW­1 and has stated that he has never entered into any agreement with the complainant in respect of the property RZ 50 G. It is also stated by the accused that he has taken loan of Rs. 3 lacs from the complainant through a person named Vijen­ der and he has repaid the same. It is further stated by the accused that one payment of Rs. 1,44,000/­ was made by him to the complainant by way of cash on 28.03.2010 and he has also given two cheques of Rs. 1 lakh each to the complainant dated 29.03.2010 and 18.04.2010 respec­ tively and out of the said two cheques one cheque bearing No. 740140 dated 29.03.2010 was encashed and in respect of the second cheque bearing No 7040140 dated 18.04.2010 the complainant has filed the in­ stant case by misusing the said cheque despite the payment being made by him against the same by way of cash on 18.05.2010. The ac­ cused has also stated that the complainant has also got him to sign on various blank papers and a stamp paper at the time of granting loan. 18. Interestingly perusal of para 2 of the agreement Ex. CW1/1 reveals that the said deal in respect of the property RZ 50 G was to be completed after 10 days of finalization of the case pending in District Courts, Delhi titled as 'Radhey Shyam Vs. Kavita Devi'

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: reveals that the said deal in respect of the property RZ 50 G was to be completed after 10 days of finalization of the case pending in District Courts, Delhi titled as 'Radhey Shyam Vs. Kavita Devi'. Further in cross examination of CW­1 it is stated by CW­1 (Complainant) that he knew that the property RZ 50 G belongs to one Kavita Devi and Vijender. It is further stated by the complainant (CW­1) that he also contacted Kavita Devi and Vijender and they informed him that the accused herein is competent to execute and deal in the property on their be­ half. It is further stated by the complainant that the agreement exe­ cuted by the said Kavita Devi in favour of the accused was also given by the accused to him at the time of the execution of the agreement Ex. CW1/1. Meaning thereby that the complainant was aware that the said property do not belongs to the accused and further from the testi­ Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 11/14 mony of CW­1 it is also apparently clear that the accused herein repre­ sented himself as an ostensible owner of the said property genuine­ ness of which has been ascertained by the complainant. Now coming to the question as to whether the accused was having any relation/deal­ ing with the property RZ 50 G which has been wholly denied by the ac­ cused. It is surprising to note that during cross examination of the ac­ cused as DW­1 the accused has admitted that he has filed an applica­ tion for impleadment in the case titled as 'Radhey Shyam Vs. Kavita' involving the property RZ 50 G . Thereby falsifying his own claim that he has no concern with the property RZ 50 G otherwise, the accused has no occasion to file any application for impleadment in the case pending in respect of the property RZ 50 G

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: his own claim that he has no concern with the property RZ 50 G otherwise, the accused has no occasion to file any application for impleadment in the case pending in respect of the property RZ 50 G. Further during cross ex­ amination of the accused as DW­1 a new story was propounded by the accused that at the instance of Vijender he has filed the said applica­ tion for impleadment in the case in respect of the property RZ 50 G ti­ tled as 'Radhey Shyam Vs. Kavita' and thereafter the said Vijender has helped him in obtaining the loan from the complainant. Surprisingly this fact was never disclosed by the accused in his statement under section 313 of the code or in his examination in chief as DW­1. Now even believing the claim of the accused that he have no dealing in re­ spect of the property RZ 50 G of Kavita and he taken loan from the com­ plainant through Vijender, it is surprising to see that the accused has neither examined the said Kavita or the said Vijender in his defence to corroborate his stand especially when the said Kavita Devi was the owner of the property RZ 50 G and the said Vijender has allegedly helped him procure loan from the complainant. Furthermore, in his evidence as DW­1 the accused has also stated that he made a payment of Rs. 1,44,000/­ to the complainant by cash on 28.03.2010 and further it is also stated by the accused that the last payment of Rs. 1,02,000/­ was made by him by way of cash to the complainant against the cheque in question for the return of the remaining loan on 18.05.2010 in the presence of Sh. Anil Kumar and he has also demanded back his cheque and blank signed papers from the complainant. Surprisingly, Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: in the presence of Sh. Anil Kumar and he has also demanded back his cheque and blank signed papers from the complainant. Surprisingly, Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 12/14 the said Anil Kumar has also not been examined by the accused in his defence in whose presence alleged last payment against the cheque in question was made and the cheque and blank signed papers were de­ manded back by the accused from the complainant. Furthermore, the accused has not placed on record any cash receipt either in respect of the alleged payment made by him to the complainant on 28.03.2010 and on 18.05.2010. Now even believing this theory of the accused that after making the last payment against the loan to the complainant on 18.05.2010 the accused had demanded back his cheque and the blank papers which were not returned by the complainant, it is interesting to see that the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 was presented on 13.10.2010 and was dishonored vide returning memo 15.10.2010. It is highly improbable that a debtor who has repaid his entire loan on 18.05.2010 would sit quite for more than a period of four months just waiting for his documents to be misused. This supports the stand of the complainant that he has presented the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 dated 18.04.2014 after waiting for a considerable time at the re­ quest of the accused. Further the complainant to corroborate his stand has also examined Sh. Tejpal as CW­2 and the said witness also stated that the entire transaction between the complainant and the accused in respect of the property RZ 50 G took place in his presence and is also witnessed by him. CW­2 has also tendered in evidence the payment receipt Ex. CW2/1 and Ex. CW2/2 which are part of the agree­ ment Ex. CW1/1 dated 01.09.2009

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: G took place in his presence and is also witnessed by him. CW­2 has also tendered in evidence the payment receipt Ex. CW2/1 and Ex. CW2/2 which are part of the agree­ ment Ex. CW1/1 dated 01.09.2009. Furthermore it is admitted by the accused that the agreement Ex. CW1/1 and the receipts Ex. CW2/1 and Ex. CW2/2 also bears his signatures. All the aforesaid circumstances create serious doubts about the claim of the accused and dents his stand and supports the claim of the complainant that the accused dealt with him in respect of the property RZ 50 G and the cheque in question Ex. CW1/2 has been issued by him to the complainant for re­ turn of the consideration amount in respect of the property transac­ tion. 19. It is settled that mere denial and putting suggestions to Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel V/s Virender Singh Page No. 13/14 the witnesses without leading any corroborative evidence in support of the same would not absolve the accused from any liability. It was for the accused to prove by leading cogent evidence as to how and in what manner the cheque in question Ex CW1/2 has come in possession of the complainant. The accused has miserably failed to lead any evidence in this regard and inturn the presumptions U/s 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act raised against him by the statute stands unrebutted. Further from the evidence on record it also stands proved that the accused has failed to pay the cheque amount within 15 days from the receipt of legal demand notice. Accordingly, In view of the aforesaid discussion, I hereby hold that the complainant has proved and substantiated its allegation against the accused and all the ingredients of the offence under section 138 of the NI Act also stands proved against the accused. Accordingly, accused Virender Singh S/o Late Sh

title: Case No. : 2815/12 Uma Shankar Goel vs Virender Singh Page No. 1/14 on 15 October, 2014
content: its allegation against the accused and all the ingredients of the offence under section 138 of the NI Act also stands proved against the accused. Accordingly, accused Virender Singh S/o Late Sh. Tek Chand Solanki, is hereby convicted for the offence U/s 138 of the NI Act. This judgment contains 14 pages. title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE MUNICIPAL MAGISTRATE­01, KKD, EAST, NEW DELHI Presided by : Ms. Deepti Devesh Complaint No. 350/13 Unique ID No. 02402R0138602013 PS: Geeta Colony Radhey Shyam, S/o Sh. Khem Chand, R/o 10/31 Geeta Colony, Delhi­31 ........Complainant VERSUS Sh. Vicky Kapoor, S/o Sh. Roshan Lal Kapoor, R/o 131­B, Rani Garden, Delhi­31 ........Accused Complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Ac t Offence complained of : U/s 138 NI Act Date of commission of offence : 07.04.2013 Plea of Accused : Not guilty Final Arguments heard & Concluded on : 26.09.2014 Date of decision of the case : 29.10.2014 Final Order : Acquittal BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE: 1 Vide this Judgment I shall finally dispose off this complaint U/s 138 NI Act by complainant Sh. Radhey Shyam against the accused Vicky Kapoor. The complainant's story in brief is that the accused approached the complainant, CC No. 350/13 page no. 1 /11 having friendly relations with the complainant and on 10.10.2012 had approached the complainant for a friendly loan of Rs.50,000/­ for a period of three months, which was advanced to the accused. In order to repay the loan, the accused issued a cheque bearing no. 361083 dated 07.03.2013 for Rs.50,000/­ drawn on Punjab & Sind Bank, Old Geeta Colony branch in favor of the complainant and had assured the complainant that the same shall be honored on its presentation. The said cheque was presented by the complainant which was returned vide return memo dated 08.03.2013 with endorsement of "funds insufficient". Thereafter, the complainant issued legal notice dated 20.03.2013. The complainant has also stated that despite service of the legal notice the accused did not make any payment in discharge of his liability

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: the complainant issued legal notice dated 20.03.2013. The complainant has also stated that despite service of the legal notice the accused did not make any payment in discharge of his liability. 2 After the filing of the complaint and closing of pre­summoning evidence, vide order dated 14.05.2013, summons were issued to the accused for the offence U/s 138 NI Act. The accused was admitted to bail on 05.06.2013. Thereafter notice U/s 251 Cr. PC was framed upon the accused on 05.06.2013 to which he did not plead guilty and claimed trial. 3 Application U/s 145(2) NI Act was filed by the accused on 05.07.2013, which was allowed on the same day as not opposed by the Counsel for the complainant. Thereafter, the matter was fixed for CE. 4 In order to prove its case, the complainant examined himself as CW­1 who reiterated the contents of the complaint on Oath and filed evidence by way of affidavit. CW­1 exhibited original cheque bearing no. 361083 dated 07.03.2013 as Ex. CW1/A, return memo dated 08.03.2013 as Ex. CW1/B and duplicate copy of return memo dated 08.03.2013 as Ex. CW1/B1, legal notice dated 21.03.2013 as Ex. CW1/C, Registered postal receipts as Ex. CW1/D & Ex. CW1/E and delivery report for legal notice as Mark­B. Thereafter, CW­1 was cross examined and discharged. CC No. 350/13 page no. 2 /11 5 After that on 16.01.2014 the accused was examined U/s 313 Cr. PC and his statement was duly recorded. All the incriminating evidence were put to the accused, to which the accused denied taking any loan from the complainant. The accused has further stated that he had given the cheque in question as security for a loan of Rs.30,000/­ taken by him from the complainant in April 2012

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: taking any loan from the complainant. The accused has further stated that he had given the cheque in question as security for a loan of Rs.30,000/­ taken by him from the complainant in April 2012. It is further stated that till August 2012 he had returned an amount of Rs.15,000/­ to the complainant and he also paid an interest of Rs.1000/­ per month to the complainant from April 2012 till August 2012. It is further stated by him that since he had paid half of the loan amount to the complainant, hence, requested the complainant to lower the interest amount but he did not agree to the same, hence, the complainant did not accept further payment from him. It is further stated by the accused that he is only liable to pay Rs.15,000/­ to the complainant and is still ready to pay the same to the complainant. He denied receiving legal notice from the complainant. The accused also stated that he wanted to lead defence evidence. 6 Accused examined himself as DW­1. He stated that in April 2012 he had taken a loan of Rs.30,000/­ from the complainant and at that time he had handed over a blank cheque to the complainant as security. In August 2012 he had returned Rs.15,000/­ to the complainant out of total loan of Rs.30,000/­ and he had also paid monthly interest of Rs. 1,000/­ to the complainant upto August 2012. Thereafter, he stopped making payment of the interest as he requested the complainant to reduce the interest amount from Rs. 1,000/­ to Rs.500/­ but the complainant did not agree to the same

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: 2012. Thereafter, he stopped making payment of the interest as he requested the complainant to reduce the interest amount from Rs. 1,000/­ to Rs.500/­ but the complainant did not agree to the same. He further stated that after receiving summons from the court on 30.5.2013, he called the complainant and recorded the telephonic conversation in which the complainant admitted that he had given only loan of Rs.30,000/­ and that he had filled the amount of Rs.50,000/­ in the cheque in question on the advice of his counsel. The accused also placed on record CD containing record of the conversation along with certificate U/s 65­B Indian Evidence Act and transcript of the conversation which is exhibited as Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages). Counsel for the complainant has objected to Ex. CC No. 350/13 page no. 3 /11 DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages) on the ground that the CD containing the telephonic conversation is not proved as per law. The said objection is decided in succeeding part of the present judgment. Thereafter, DW­1 was cross examined and discharged, defence evidence was closed and matter was fixed for final arguments. 7 Final arguments were addressed and heard on behalf of both the parties. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has reiterated the averments made in the complaint. He has argued that the accused has failed to disclose any defence. Therefore all ingredients of U/s 138 NI Act stands fulfilled and the accused is liable to be convicted. 8 On the other hand, the Counsel for the accused has argued that the present complaint should be dismissed as there is no legal liability upon the accused to pay the complainant as no loan of Rs.50,000/­ was ever taken by the accused from the complainant

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: that the present complaint should be dismissed as there is no legal liability upon the accused to pay the complainant as no loan of Rs.50,000/­ was ever taken by the accused from the complainant. Infact the accused handed over the cheque in question to the complainant as security for a loan of Rs.30,000/­. He has further argued that the complainant has infact demanded Rs.50,00,000/­ from the accused in his legal notice and therefore has contradicted himself and hence, the present complaint is liable to be dismissed. Counsel for the accused has further stated that the cheque in question has been misused by the complainant. 9 Arguments advanced by both the parties have been heard at length. I have also perused the judicial record. 10 For offence U/s 138 NI Act the necessary ingredients to be proved are: a) That the accused had a legal liability / debt towards the complainant. b) That the accused issued a cheque in discharge of the said legal liability / debt. c) That the accused was maintaining a bank account for the cheque CC No. 350/13 page no. 4 /11 issued by him. d) That the cheque was presented by the complainant within its validity period. e) That the cheque was dishonored on his presentation. f) That the complainant issued legal demand notice within 30 days from the date of dishonor of the cheque. g) That the accused failed to pay within 15 days of receipt of legal demand notice. If the above ingredients are proved then an offence punishable U/s 138 NI Act is committed. 11 In the present case, the accused has stated in the notice framed U/s 251 Cr. PC that he has taken only a loan of Rs.30,000/­ from the complainant and has already repaid a sum of Rs.15,000/­ to the complainant

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: case, the accused has stated in the notice framed U/s 251 Cr. PC that he has taken only a loan of Rs.30,000/­ from the complainant and has already repaid a sum of Rs.15,000/­ to the complainant. He stated further that he only signed on the cheque in question and other details have not been filled by him. He has reiterated the same in his statement U/s 313 Cr PC. He has also stated that the cheque in question was given as security to the complainant. It has been denied by the accused that he received legal notice from the complainant, although the statutory presumption of delivery of notice is in the favour of the complainant and also the accused has stated in his cross examination that the address at which the legal notice was sent has been his residence since last 20 years. Further, as per the Judgment of Hon'ble supreme court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. P. Mohammad (2007) 6 SCC 555, it is not the case of the accused that he was willing to make payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of the summons and therefore, it is immaterial whether the legal notice was received or not by the accused. Counsel for the accused has also argued that the legal notice is for the demand of Rs.50,00,000/­ and therefore, is not in respect of the cheque in question. However, perusal of the legal notice shows that the loan amount is mentioned to be Rs.50,000/­ only and the demand has been made for total value of the cheque Ex. CW1/A which shows the amount of the cheque is Rs.50,000/­ in para no.3. The complainant has also CC No. 350/13 page no. 5 /11 stated in his cross­examination that the amount in figure i.e. Rs.50,00,000/­ in incorrect which is a typographical error and that the amount in words is correctly written as Rs.50,000/­

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: no. 5 /11 stated in his cross­examination that the amount in figure i.e. Rs.50,00,000/­ in incorrect which is a typographical error and that the amount in words is correctly written as Rs.50,000/­. This appears to be probable as the legal notice mentions Rs.50,000/­ everywhere else. Hence, the only disputed question to be decided is whether the cheque in question was issued in discharge of legal liability / debt to the complainant. 12 Now, the question of liability of the accused to pay the complainant shall be dealt with. In the present case the complainant has averred that the cheque in question was issued against discharge of liability arising out of loan transaction between the parties. Since the cheque in question is bearing the name of complainant and the present complaint has been filed by the complainant in his own name therefore, presumption arises U/s 118­A & 139 NI Act in favour of the complainant that the cheque was issued in discharge of a legal liability. Thus, the onus to rebut this presumption is on the accused. The accused has disputed his legal liability to make payment on the ground that there was no loan transaction of Rs.50,000/­ between the parties and that the cheque in question was given as security which has been misused by the complainant. 13 It is true that for offence U/s 138 NI Act, the accused is not expected to prove his defense beyond reasonable doubt in order to rebut the statutory presumption. Same has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513. 14 The complainant in the instant case has failed to disclose his source of income for the alleged loan of Rs.50,000/­ advanced to the accused

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: in Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets (2009) 2 SCC 513. 14 The complainant in the instant case has failed to disclose his source of income for the alleged loan of Rs.50,000/­ advanced to the accused. The complainant has further stated in his cross examination that he does not have any money lending license and he has not even shown the present loan in his ITR as he does not file the same. Further, the complainant has stated that no written document or loan agreement was executed for the loan transaction. He has also stated that he has not withdrawn the said loan amount from the bank as he had CC No. 350/13 page no. 6 /11 available with him Rs.50,000/­ in cash. The alleged loan of Rs.50,000/­ is evidently in contravention of Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act, 1961 as the loan amount has not been reflected in writing anywhere by the complainant. No written acknowledgement / receipt was also taken from the accused for the loan amount. Hence, it is doubtful whether the complainant had actually given loan of Rs.50,000/­ to the accused. 15 Although the complainant has stated that he knows the accused as the accused used to visit the shop of his son for last 10 years, but he has also admitted that he was not on visiting terms with the accused in his cross­ examination. He has further admitted in his cross examination that he had never visited the house of the accused prior to the date on which he had given the said loan to him. He also did not remember the address of the accused. Thus the complainant has also failed to establish friendly relations with the accused

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: to the date on which he had given the said loan to him. He also did not remember the address of the accused. Thus the complainant has also failed to establish friendly relations with the accused. Further, nothing has been brought on record to substantiate the claim of the complainant of having friendly relations with the accused and advancing friendly loan to the accused and it is indeed very strange that any loan would be advanced to a person who is not a family member, without charging any interest. Infact the complainant has contradicted himself as at one place in his cross­ examination he stated that the accused has not paid any interest till date, while at another place he admits that the accused has paid an interest of Rs.1000/­ per month for two to four months only to the complainant. He has further contradicted himself in his cross­examination wherein at one place he deposed that he handed­over the sum of Rs.50,000/­ to the accused at his home, while at another place he has stated that the accused had come outside his home in the street to take the loan amount. Due to the said contradictions in the testimony of the complainant, the complainant does not inspire confidence of this court as a witness and his testimony is considered to be unreliable. 16 Further, the accused has also stated in his notice U/s 251 Cr. PC, statement U/s 313 Cr. PC and also in his examination in chief that the cheque in CC No. 350/13 page no. 7 /11 question was given to the complainant as security for loan of Rs.30,000/­ taken from the complainant. He has also denied filling in the details on the cheque in question and has only admitted his signatures on the cheque in question

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: as security for loan of Rs.30,000/­ taken from the complainant. He has also denied filling in the details on the cheque in question and has only admitted his signatures on the cheque in question. The complainant has stated in his cross­examination that the cheque in question was filled by a friend of the accused who was accompanying him at the time when the cheque in question was handed­over to him. However, complainant has conveniently failed to even mention the name of that friend of the accused who has purportedly filled in the details in the cheque in question. Hence, the fact that the complainant is admitting that certain details in the cheque in question was filled by somebody else, without disclosing even that person's name, probabalizes the defence raised by the accused that the cheque in question was given without mentioning the certain details, because it was meant to be security cheque. 17 The accused has admitted liability of Rs.15,000/­ towards the complainant as he has consistently stated in notice U/s 251 Cr. PC, statement U/s 313 Cr. PC & examination in chief that he had taken loan of Rs.30,000/­ from the complainant, out of which he had returned Rs.15,000/­. Despite the said admission of the accused, yet it does not help the complainant's story much as the accused has admitted the loan amount to the tune of Rs.30,000/­ and not Rs.50,000/­, which is the cheque amount in the present case. Hence, the accused has not admitted his liability with respect to the cheque amount and thus, the accused can rebut the statutory presumption of liability in favour of the complainant on the basis of preponderance of probability. 18 The accused has produced a CD along with certificate u/s 65­B Indian Evidence Act and transcript of the conversation Ex

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: in favour of the complainant on the basis of preponderance of probability. 18 The accused has produced a CD along with certificate u/s 65­B Indian Evidence Act and transcript of the conversation Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages) to prove that he had taken loan amount of Rs.30,000/­ only from the complainant. However, Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages) has been objected to by the counsel for the complainant on the ground that it is not proved as per law. CC No. 350/13 page no. 8 /11 Section 65­B (4) states: In any proceedings where it is desired to give a statement in evidence by virtue of this section, a certificate doing any of the following things, that is to say,­ a) identifying the electronic record containing the statement and describing the manner in which it was produced; b) giving such particulars of any device involved in the production of that electronic record as may be appropriate for the purpose of showing that the electronic record was produced by a computer; c) dealing with any of the matters to which the conditions mentioned in sub­section (2) relate, and purporting to be signed by a person occupying a responsible official position in relation to the operation of the relevant device or the management of the relevant activities (whichever is appropriate) shall e evidence of any matter stated in the certificate; and for the purposes of this sub­section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: of any matter stated in the certificate; and for the purposes of this sub­section it shall be sufficient for a matter to be stated to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it. On bare reading of the above mentioned provision of law, it is clear that the certificate U/s 65­B has to contain averments in respect of any of the sub clauses of Section 65­B (4) and also has to be signed by a person who is in a responsible official position in relation of the operation of the relevant device from which the electronic evidence is produced. In the instant case, the certificate U/s 65­B Indian Evidence Act has been given by the accused himself and he has stated in the said certificate that the data of the memory card of the mobile phone was copied to the computer and then converted and copied on the CD which is part of Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages). However, the accused has stated in his cross­ examination that the said certificate and copy of the CD has been prepared by his friend Amit @ Sanjay and he has further stated that he has no knowledge of CC No. 350/13 page no. 9 /11 computers. In the instant case the accused has admitted to having no knowledge of computers and also that the said CD has been prepared by his friend, therefore, the certificate U/s 65­B Indian Evidence Act forming part of Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages) is not a valid certificate as per Section 65­B Indian Evidence Act and hence, Ex. DW1/1 (colly for 16 pages) is inadmissible in evidence. 19 However, even if Ex. DW1/1(colly for 16 pages) is inadmissible in evidence, yet it does not negate the defence of the accused as the accused only has to prove the same according to the standard of preponderance of probabilities

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: for 16 pages) is inadmissible in evidence, yet it does not negate the defence of the accused as the accused only has to prove the same according to the standard of preponderance of probabilities. The accused has consistently maintained the same stand in his defence disclosed in notice U/s 251 Cr. PC, in his application U/s 145(2) NI Act, statement U/s 313 Cr. PC and in his evidence. Nothing has come in his cross examination which demolishes his claim that the cheque in question was issued as security for a loan of Rs.30,000/­ only. Further, the testimony of DW­1 is consistent and nothing has been brought in cross examination to show that DW­ 1 is not a credible witness. In these circumstances since the accused is required to prove his defence on the basis of preponderance of probabilities, the defence taken by the accused that the said cheque was issued in blank signed condition stands proved. 20 In view of the above discussion, the complainant has been unable to prove the loan transaction and therefore, there is no question of any legal liability / debt of the accused towards the complainant and the present complaint is liable to be dismissed on this ground alone. Since the complainant has failed to file any document on record to show the liability of the accused, hence, the defence of the accused that the cheque was given in blank signed condition to the complainant and that the same has been misused appears to be probable and credible defence. It is well settled that even though the statutory presumption for offence U/s 138 NI Act is in favour of the complainant, still, the prosecution is burdened with standing on its own legs and has to necessarily prove its case CC No. 350/13 page no. 10 /11 beyond reasonable doubt

title: Radhey Shyam vs Unknown on 29 October, 2014
content: NI Act is in favour of the complainant, still, the prosecution is burdened with standing on its own legs and has to necessarily prove its case CC No. 350/13 page no. 10 /11 beyond reasonable doubt. In the instant case, there is no written loan agreement, no written receipt, no ITR filed by the complainant even for the period in which the alleged loan transaction took place and cheque in question not filled up by the accused are enough to puncture holes in the complainant's story. Cumulatively, the above circumstances are sufficient to rebut the presumption arising in favour of the complainant U/s 139 NI Act. Accordingly, accused Sh. Vicky Kapoor, S/o Sh. Roshan Lal Kapoor, R/o 131­B, Rani Garden, Delhi­31 stands acquitted of the offence under section 138 NI Act.
