content: him when he came to the office of the complainant. However, CW­1 has conveniently failed to even name the manager of the accused who has purportedly filled in the details in the cheques in question. Hence, the fact that the complainant is admitting that certain details in the cheques in question were filled by somebody else, without disclosing even that person's name, probabalizes the defence raised by the accused that the cheques in question were given without mentioning the name of payee and date, because they were meant to be security cheques. 20 The said defence also appears to be credible as Ex. DW1/2 (OSR) & Mark DW1/3 clearly shows that the cheques in question were issued in 2009 and one cheque bearing no.005587 was even encashed in 2009, which was stated by the accused in his statement u/s 313, Cr.PC Ex. DW1/2 (OSR) & Mark DW1/3 also probabalizes that the cheques in question, which belong to the same cheque book to which the cheque bearing no.005587 for Rs.5000/­ belonged, which were issued to the complainant in 2009 itself, and the same was used by the complainant only in 2012. Counsel for the complainant has argued that Ex. DW1/2 (OSR) can not be relied upon as it is a document which is in the possession of the accused and therefore can be easily manipulated by him. This submission can not be accepted as there is no law which states that evidence in possession of the accused is, on the face of it, unreliable. It is for the complainant to show unreliability of any defence evidence by way of cross­examination. Nothing is come in the cross­examination which suggests that the evidence adduced by the accused is untrustworthy or unreliable. Counsel for the complainant has also argued that Mark DW1/3 is a photocopy and therefore is inadmissible in evidence

title: In The Court Of Metropolitan ... vs Unknown on 29 August, 2014
content: suggests that the evidence adduced by the accused is untrustworthy or unreliable. Counsel for the complainant has also argued that Mark DW1/3 is a photocopy and therefore is inadmissible in evidence. However, it is seen from the record that no such objection as to the mode of the proof had been taken at the time of marking of the document and hence, the objection is deemed to have been waived CC No. 32/12 page no. 11 /13 and can not be raised at this stage. Hence, it is probable that the cheques in question were given for security purposes by the accused in 2009, when he had taken goods worth Rs.5000/­ from the complainant company. It has been held by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Kumar D v. State of Delhi & Another Manu / DE / 1538/ 2011 that a cheque issued for security to meet some future liability does not attract Section 138 NI Act. In view of this precedent, since the defence of the accused is proved to the extent that the cheques in question were given as security cheques, hence, there is no legal liability / debt against the accused U/s 138 NI Act. Hence, the presumption u/s 138 NI Act has been rebutted by the accused and the onus has again shifted back on the complainant to prove that the accused was liable towards the complainant company for the cheque amount. It has been argued that if the accused had no liability, then the accused would have issued stop payment instructions as any prudent person and that absence of any such instructions sufficiently disproves the claim of the accused that the cheques in question were issued as security cheques. It is true that the accused should have issued stop payment instructions

title: In The Court Of Metropolitan ... vs Unknown on 29 August, 2014
content: instructions sufficiently disproves the claim of the accused that the cheques in question were issued as security cheques. It is true that the accused should have issued stop payment instructions. However, the return of the cheques in question is not in doubt, and that it is also immaterial for what reason the same were returned, for making out offence u/s 138 NI Act. It is, however, not sufficient to discharge the onus on the complainant as the complainant has not brought sufficient evidence to prove even the transaction in question for which the cheques in question were allegedly issued. 21 Another contention / defense raised by the accused is that the present complaint is not maintainable as it has been filed by an authorized representative who does not have proper authorization to file the present complaint. The complainant has filed Ex. CW1/8 (OSR), which is extracts of the Minutes of Board meeting dated 29.06.2008, to prove authority of the AR to file the present complaint. Ex. CW1/8 (OSR) gives sufficient authority to the AR to file complaints and take other necessary actions with respect to all court cases of the complainant company. All court cases naturally include cases u/s 138 NI Act. There is nothing to CC No. 32/12 page no. 12 /13 bar the AR from filing the present case even if no specific authorization with respect to the cheques in question has been given to the AR. It is well settled that even general authority is sufficient to pursue cases on behalf of companies. 22 From the above discussion, it is established that the complainant has failed to prove the liability of the accused to pay the cheque amount. No written document has been placed on record by the complainant to show that the accused was liable for the cheque amount

title: In The Court Of Metropolitan ... vs Unknown on 29 August, 2014
content: has failed to prove the liability of the accused to pay the cheque amount. No written document has been placed on record by the complainant to show that the accused was liable for the cheque amount. It is well settled that the prosecution has to stand on its own legs and has to prove his case beyond reasonable doubts, while the accused only need to puncture holes to create reasonable doubts in the prosecution story. In the present matter, there is no written agreement, no receiving or acknowledgement on the bill dated 03.03.2012, no evidence to prove supply of goods to the accused, plea of alibi of the accused, another person filled the details on the cheques in question and that they were given as security, cumulatively probabalize the defence raised by the accused which is sufficient to rebut the presumption of law arisen in favour of the complainant. Accordingly, accused Sh. Anuruddh Kumar Jain, S/o Sh. Vijay Kumar, R/o 238 Bazar Barua Sagar, Jhansi (U.P.) stands acquitted of the offence under section 138 NI Act. Accused is directed to furnish bailbond and surety bond in the sum of Rs.10,000/­ U/s 437 Cr. PC for the next six months. Announced in the open court today i.e. 29.08.2014 (DEEPTI DEVESH) MM:KKD:DELHI:.29.08.2014 (DEEPTI DEVESH) MM:KKD:DELHI:.29.08.2014 CC No. 32/12 page no. 13 /13

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: IN THE COURT OF SH. ASHU GARG, Judge, Small Causes Court -cum- Addl. Senior Civil Judge -cum- Guardian Judge -cum- Metropolitan Magistrate (New Delhi), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi CC No. 102/13 Unique Case ID No. Date of Institution: 20.04.2004 [OLDEST] Date of reserving judgement: 20.09.2014 Date of pronouncement: 14.10.2014 In re: Commissioner of Customs ICD, TKD, New Delhi ... Complainant versus A-1) M/s. Lokesh Garments Pvt. Ltd. 315, FIE Patparganj Industrial Area, Delhi A-2) Sh. Lokesh Chand Chopra Director, M/s. Lokesh Garments Pvt. Ltd. 315, FIE Patparganj Industrial Area, Delhi ... Accused persons JUDGMENT: 1.The present complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (NI Act) has been filed by the complainant with respect to dishonour of a cheque no. 764474 dated 15.12.2003, for a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs, drawn on Punjab National Bank, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi, in favour of the complainant Commissioner of Custom (Export) by the the accused no. 2 Lokesh Chand Chopra, CC No. 102/13 Page 1 of 15 Director of the accused no. 1 company M/s. Lokesh Garments Pvt. Ltd. The cheque got dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds vide memo dated 07.02.2004. 2.The initial complaint was filed against seven accused persons but the court had summoned only the accused no. 1 company and its Director accused no. 2 (signatory). As per the complaint, the accused no. 2 was controlling the day to day business and activities of the accused no. 1 company as well as of proprietorship concerns accused no. 4 to 7 (sic: 3 to 7) namely M/s. Puja Hi Fashion, M/s. Kapil Impex and M/s. Chopco Fashion. Accused no. 3 and 4 were also stated to be the Directors of the accused no. 1 company

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: concerns accused no. 4 to 7 (sic: 3 to 7) namely M/s. Puja Hi Fashion, M/s. Kapil Impex and M/s. Chopco Fashion. Accused no. 3 and 4 were also stated to be the Directors of the accused no. 1 company. It had been alleged that the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) had been investigating into the exports of ready-made garments made by the accused persons and during the course of investigation, it observed that the said company and business concerns had availed undue duty drawback / export benefits in respect of the goods whose sale proceeds had not been realized within the stipulated period. As per the investigations, the said company and concerns had availed undue duty drawback / export benefits fraudulently to the tune of Rs. 2,51,06,277/- in aggregate. This fact was admitted by the accused no. 2 in his voluntary statement dated 15.10.2003 tendered under section 108 of the Customs Act, 1962. It is informed that the accused no. 2 had voluntarily tendered six cheques (including the cheque in question) worth Rs. 2.5 crores for repayment of wrongly availed drawback and export benefits. The accused no. 2 and 3 further undertook that they would produce drafts CC No. 102/13 Page 2 of 15 in lieu of the said cheques and if they failed to do so, then the cheques may be presented to the bank for encashment. When the accused persons failed to tender the drafts despite lapse of three months, the complainant presented the cheques for encashment. However, the cheque in question was returned dishonoured with the remarks "insufficient funds" vide memo dated 07.02.2004. Legal notice dated 05.03.2004 was sent to the accused persons but despite service, no payment was made, though a reply dated 16.03.2004 was given

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: "insufficient funds" vide memo dated 07.02.2004. Legal notice dated 05.03.2004 was sent to the accused persons but despite service, no payment was made, though a reply dated 16.03.2004 was given. Hence, the present complaint was filed in the court. 3.Pre-summoning evidence was lead and the accused no. 1 and 2 only were summoned by the court vide detailed order dated 29.04.2004. The accused no. 1 company never participated at the trial and notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC for the offence punishable under section 138 NI Act was framed against the accused no. 2 vide order dated 05.07.2005. The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 4.At the trial, the complainant examined three witnesses in its support. CW-1 Sh. Yashpal, CW-2 Sh. Balram, and CW-4 Sh. Ravinder Nath were examined (it is to be noted that no CW-3 was examined by the complainant and the witnesses have been numbered incorrectly). 5.CW-1 Sh. Yashpal, Superintendent, Customs, tendered his affidavit and reiterated the contents of his complaint filed in discharge of his official duties. He proved on record the original cheque, the cheque return memo, legal notice, postal receipts as well as the photocopy of CC No. 102/13 Page 3 of 15 the statement of accused no. 2 made under Section 108 of the Customs Act. He was duly cross-examined by the Ld. Defence Counsel wherein he admitted that no authorization in his favour has been filed on record. He accepted that the cheque was not handed over to him. He had no personal knowledge of the matter and did not know if there were any dues against the accused on the day when the cheque was issued

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: He accepted that the cheque was not handed over to him. He had no personal knowledge of the matter and did not know if there were any dues against the accused on the day when the cheque was issued. He stated that he was deposing only on the basis of available record and had no personal knowledge of the facts of the case. 6.CW-2 Sh. Balram and CW-4 Sh. Ravinder Nath were bank officials from Punjab National Bank, Barahkhamba Road, New Delhi and Punjab National Bank, IG Airport, New Delhi, respectively, who produced the summoned bank records and registers pertaining to the cheque in question. 7.Statement of the accused no. 2 was recorded under section 313 CrPC on 07.12.2012, wherein he denied the averments and pleaded innocence. He claimed that the statement of under section 108 of the Customs Act was taken under threat and force and that he never issued the cheques voluntarily. He took stands that the officials of the complainant had detained him and took his signatures forcibly and claimed that he had no liability against the cheque in question. No evidence in defence was however led by the accused. 8.It is in these circumstance, that the Ld. Counsel for complainant has argued that the complainant had been able to prove its case against the CC No. 102/13 Page 4 of 15 accused persons. Ld. Counsel has relied upon the testimony of CWs together with the statement of the accused made under section 108 of the Customs Act, coupled with the presumption of law in its favour. It is submitted that such statement of the accused under section 108 of the Customs Act is admissible in evidence and taking into account the presumptions in favour of the complainant, the burden would shift upon to the accused to establish otherwise

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: under section 108 of the Customs Act is admissible in evidence and taking into account the presumptions in favour of the complainant, the burden would shift upon to the accused to establish otherwise. It is argued that the accused has failed to establish any defence in his favour and has failed to lead any evidence in defence. 9.On the other hand, the Ld. Defence Counsel has filed written submissions and has contended that no case is made out against the accused. It is submitted that there is no authorization in favour of the witnesses to depose on behalf of the complainant and that no liability to the tune of the cheque amount has been proved on record. It is submitted that the accused is not required to step into the witness box to rebut the presumptions and he can point out the infirmities in the evidence of the complainant to rebut the same. It is submitted that the cheque taken from the accused under force and threat would not be covered under the offence punishable under section 138 NI Act. 10.I have heard the arguments advanced by both the sides and have carefully perused the material available on record. 11.The law with respect to offences punishable under section 138 of the Act is well settled. The law has been laid down by the Hon'ble CC No. 102/13 Page 5 of 15 Supreme Court of India, in the precedent titled as M/s. Kumar Exports v. M/s. Sharma Carpets [2009(2) SCC 513], wherein it has been held that: "The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: of India, in the precedent titled as M/s. Kumar Exports v. M/s. Sharma Carpets [2009(2) SCC 513], wherein it has been held that: "The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the non-existence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent CC No. 102/13 Page 6 of 15 man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: was so probable that a prudent CC No. 102/13 Page 6 of 15 man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on to the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act. The accused has also an option to prove the non-existence of consideration and debt or liability either by letting in evidence or in some clear and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial. Once such rebuttal evidence is adduced and accepted by the court, having regard to all the circumstances of the case and the preponderance of probabilities, the evidential burden shifts back to the complainant and, thereafter, the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act will not again come to the complainant's rescue". 12.Keeping these principles in mind, it is seen that the accused has not disputed the factum of the cheque in question to have been issued by him or bearing his signatures. He has never denied the fact that the CC No. 102/13 Page 7 of 15 cheque had been drawn on a bank account maintained by him with the Punjab National Bank, New Delhi

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: denied the fact that the CC No. 102/13 Page 7 of 15 cheque had been drawn on a bank account maintained by him with the Punjab National Bank, New Delhi. He has also not denied that the cheque was filled by him in favour of the complainant and for this particular amount, though he claims that the same was got filled by him under threat and force. It is not the defence of the accused that the cheque did not bears his signatures or that his signatures had been forged or that it was issued blank or was otherwise materially altered or modified. The genuineness of this cheque has not been disputed by him. 13.Similarly, the accused has not questioned the genuineness of the cheque returning memo or the factum of the dishonour of the cheque due to the reason as mentioned on this memo. It is not the case of the accused that the funds in his bank account were sufficient to honour this cheque. As such, it is clear that the cheque in question got dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds in his bank account. 14.The accused has never denied the receipt of the legal demand notice. He rather replied to that notice. He admitted receipt of the notice in his statement under section 313 CrPC. It is also not denied by the accused that he did not make the payment despite expiry of fifteen days from such service of legal demand notice. 15.Once these facts are proved, the court has to see if there existed a debt or other liability towards discharge of which the cheque in question might had been issued. 16.In this regard, the court has nothing material before it except the testimony of CW-1 Sh. Yashpal, as the CW-2 and CW-4 are only formal witnesses who had only produced the bank records

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: issued. 16.In this regard, the court has nothing material before it except the testimony of CW-1 Sh. Yashpal, as the CW-2 and CW-4 are only formal witnesses who had only produced the bank records. During his evidence, he admitted that the cheque was not given to him by the accused. It is apparent that the cheque had been received by the complainant through the DRI officials who had investigated into the alleged duty drawback / export benefits by the accused, his company and various other business concerns. Admittedly, he was not a witness to the circumstances under which the cheque had been issued by the accused. The DRI officials who had carried out the investigation and to whom the cheque had been given have not been examined by the complainant. And precisely on this ground that he was not a witness to such proceedings, CW-1 could not answer material questions as to the existence and extent of the liability of the accused when the cheque had been given. He categorically stated that he had no personal knowledge of the matter and was deposing only on the basis of records. Thus, he could not depose as to what was the liability assessed against the accused. There is nothing to show if any show cause notice had been issued by the complainant to the accused assessing his liability, though he claimed that a show cause notice had been issued and was adjudicated in the year 2007. Since he was not CC No. 102/13 Page 9 of 15 present at the time of handing over the cheque, he could not have admitted or denied if the cheque was obtained under threat or force

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: class="hidden_text" id="span_9">CC No. 102/13 Page 9 of 15 present at the time of handing over the cheque, he could not have admitted or denied if the cheque was obtained under threat or force. 17.In this position, it is clear that there is nothing on record to show that any such duty drawback / export benefits existed on the day when the cheque was issued by the accused. It is apparent that no such duty or benefit had been ever assessed by any department against the accused. There was no basis as to how the amount of Rs. 2,51,06,277/- was calculated or assessed as narrated in the complaint. It is well settled that for the purposes of offence under section 138 NI Act, the debt or liability has to be an existing liability and not future liability. The complainant has to show that a definite liability up to the cheque amount (or more than the amount) existed when the cheque had been issued. Mere oral submission of a witness, who was otherwise not concerned with the investigation, that the such amount was to be paid by the accused, would not be sufficient to establish that there existed a legally recoverable debt or liability. There are no records to show how this amount was arrived at. 18.Though there is no evidence lead by the accused to show that the cheque was obtained under any threat or force, yet it is clear that the material on record is not sufficient to ascertain the extent and existence of debt or liability against which the cheque might had been issued by him. Failure of the complainant to bring any evidence showing existence of legally recoverable debt or liability would make its case weak. There is nothing on record to show if any duty CC No

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: to bring any evidence showing existence of legally recoverable debt or liability would make its case weak. There is nothing on record to show if any duty CC No. 102/13 Page 10 of 15 drawback / export benefits had been ever assessed by any department against which the cheque had been issued. If the cheque amount happens to be more than the assessed duty, no liability under section 138 NI Act can be fastened against the accused. Similarly, if the cheque was given towards discharge of duty that was yet to be assessed in future, no offence under section 138 NI Act would be made out in case of dishonour of such cheque. In such a case, the department would be entitled to proceed under the relevant laws against the accused, but as far as such cheque is concerned, it cannot be said to have been issued towards discharge of an existing debt or liability. 19.The statement under section 108 of the Customs Act, as being relied upon by the complainant, has never been proved as record as per law. Only a photocopy of the said statement was placed on record, the contents of which are also not completely legible. The original statement was never brought on record and the investigating officer Sh. H.S. Sahni, before whom the said statement was made on 15.10.2003, was also not examined on record. Thus, the said photocopy of a statement cannot be considered as proved as per law. Such a photocopy is neither primary evidence nor secondary evidence, and is rather no evidence at all in the eyes of law. It cannot be relied upon to ascertain the liability of the accused in the manner sought by the complainant

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: evidence nor secondary evidence, and is rather no evidence at all in the eyes of law. It cannot be relied upon to ascertain the liability of the accused in the manner sought by the complainant. 20.Further, there is no show cause notice ever issued to the accused showing any assessment of such duty on account of drawback or export benefits on his part. Though CW-1 claimed that such a notice had been issued and also adjudicated in the year 2007, no such record was produced before the court. In the absence of any such assessment, it cannot be ascertained as to what was the liability against which the cheque had been issued. As already noticed, the accused is not required to lead evidence in defence to rebut the presumptions. In order to rebut the presumptions, he can point out the infirmities and deficiencies in the case of the complainant with or without leading evidence in defence. Thus, merely because no evidence in defence has been led by the accused, that would not give any benefit to the complainant. The evidence led by the complainant is not sufficient to prove the existence of debt or liability against the accused when the cheque had been issued. 21.The stand of the accused is squarely covered by the precedent relied upon by the Ld. Defence Counsel titled as Veena Ahuja v. Central Excise [Crl MC No. 1430/10, Delhi High Court, dated 23.03.2011) wherein the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi was pleased to quash the proceedings under section 138 NI Act on the ground that the liability assessed by the Central Excise Department had not attained finality on the date when the cheques had been obtained. In the present case also, no such liability had assessed by the complainant on the date of obtaining the cheques and even thereafter

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: attained finality on the date when the cheques had been obtained. In the present case also, no such liability had assessed by the complainant on the date of obtaining the cheques and even thereafter. Apparently, there is no order, decree or adjudication of any competent authority assessing the CC No. 102/13 Page 12 of 15 liability of the accused. The accused has not yet been held liable to pay any sum of money for evasion of customs duty and there is nothing to show that he is liable to pay any quantified customs duty on the date when the cheque had been issued. The proceedings of show cause notice, as claimed to have been adjudicated by CW-1 have not been placed on record. 22.At this stage, it is also to be noted that as per the complaint, the accused persons had undertook to produce drafts in lieu of the cheque in question and had agreed that in case they failed to do so, the cheque might be presented for encashment. The cheque was therefore presented when the accused to failed to tender the drafts even after lapse of three months. It would be thus seen that the cheque in question had not been actually issued towards discharge of any existing debt or liability but only as security to ensure payment by drafts. The accused persons were required to pay the amount by way of drafts and it was only upon their failure to do so that the cheque could have been presented. 23.It is now well settled that dishonour of a cheque, if issued as security for repayment of any money, would not make out an offence punishable under section 138 NI Act. In that case, the same would be civil liability and not a criminal liability under section 138 NI Act. In recent precedent titled as Indus Airways Pvt. Ltd. v. Magnum Aviation Pvt. Ltd. [Crl

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: NI Act. In that case, the same would be civil liability and not a criminal liability under section 138 NI Act. In recent precedent titled as Indus Airways Pvt. Ltd. v. Magnum Aviation Pvt. Ltd. [Crl. Appeal no. 380/2014, decided on 07.04.2014], the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held that to CC No. 102/13 Page 13 of 15 attract an offence under Section 138, there should be legally enforceable debt or other liability subsisting on the date of drawal of the cheque. Thus, drawal of the cheque in discharge of existing or past adjudicated liability is sine qua non for bringing an offence under Section 138. The Hon'ble Court held the law laid down in Shanku Concretes Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat [2000 CrLJ 1988] to be a correct law. In the said case, the liability was to repay the advance amount after six months, and to ensure said repayment, the cheques were issued. Thus, the liability was held to be a future liability, that was yet to arise upon happening of an event, that is, non-payment of amount after six months. Similar was the view in M/s. Collage Culture v. Apparel Export Promotion Council [2007 (4) JCC (NI) 388]. Thus, if a post dated cheque is issued for discharging a future liability that was yet to arise upon happening of a contingent event and as a collateral security, would not attract the provisions of section 138 NI Act. 24.In the case in hand, the cheque was given as security only as it could have been presented on a future date when the accused would have failed to pay the duty amount through drafts in future. Thus, in such a case, when the cheque in question was delivered, there was no existing debt or liability

title: In Re: vs Unknown on 14 October, 2014
content: date when the accused would have failed to pay the duty amount through drafts in future. Thus, in such a case, when the cheque in question was delivered, there was no existing debt or liability. The same would have come into existence only upon happening of a future contingent event, that is, failure of the accused to make the payment by way of drafts at a future date, as stated by the complainant itself. Therefore, even from this angle, CC No. 102/13 Page 14 of 15 accused persons cannot be held criminally liable under section 138 NI Act for dishonour of the cheque in question. 25.In view of the above discussion, the case of the complainant suffers a dent and is liable to fail. The complainant has not been able to establish that the cheque in question was issued towards discharge of existing debt or liability so as to make out the offence. The accused has been able to rebut the presumptions in favour of the complainant by raising a probable defence. 26.The accused persons are therefore acquitted of the charges. The bail bond of accused no. 2 shall however remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC. 27.File be consigned to the record room. Announced in the open court this 14th day of October 2014 (ASHU GARG) JSCC/ASCJ/GJ/MM Patiala House Courts, New Delhi CC No. 102/13 Page 15 of 15

title: P.V. Rajgopal And Ors. vs Union Of India And Ors. on 21 April, 1998
content: ORDER T.N.C. Rangarajan, J. 1. This batch of writ petitions relate to the question of deduction of tax at source with reference to the income chargeable under the head 'Salaries'. Pleadings : 2. Writ Petition No.27804/1995 has been filed by the Officers in the Research and Development Division of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited. (A Government of India Undertaking). They obtained House Building Advance from H.D.F.C., L.I.C., and other Financial Institutions in respect of which monthly instalments are deducted from their salary. The difference between the rate of interest charged by the Financial Institutions and the rate of interest at which the House Building loans are generally sanctioned by the Company was reimbursed to the petitioners. On 23-3-1995, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (for short 'C.B.D.T.') informed the Chief Commissioner of Income-tax, Hyderabad that where the employer directly bears a part of the interest burden of the employees by reimbursing a portion of the interest payable by the employee in respect of building loans, such reimbursement is taxable as income from 'Salaries' under Section 17(2)(iii) of the Income-tax Act. This was forwarded to the Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax of each zone and circulated to the Company. This writ petition challenges that letter by claiming that the interest on reimbursement is not a perquisite and prays for a declaration that the said letter is illegal and ultra vires the provisions of the Income-tax Act. 3. Writ Petition No.26797/1997 has been filed by the trade union of the workers of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited

title: P.V. Rajgopal And Ors. vs Union Of India And Ors. on 21 April, 1998
content: the said letter is illegal and ultra vires the provisions of the Income-tax Act. 3. Writ Petition No.26797/1997 has been filed by the trade union of the workers of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited. It is stated that an order under Section 201 was passed on 21-3-1995 against the Company for the assessment years 1989-90 to 1993-94 raising a demand of Rs.1,61,16,601/-with penalty of Rs.72,94,881/-. Consequently, the Company issued a Circular on 5-7-1995 intimating the employees that the interest subsidy will be treated as a perquisite for deducting the tax at source. It is stated that a similar order for earlier year was set aside in revision and yet the Income-tax Department was persisting and for that reason it is prayed that there should be a direction not to treat the interest subsidy as a perquisite while deducting the tax at source. 4. The Fact Situation : 14. The Facts in respect of which these provisions are to be applied arises from a welfare measure by the Central Government for providing funds for acquisition of houses by its employees. As far as the Central Government employees arc concerned house building loans are sanctioned by the Government at a concessional rate. As far as the Public Sector Undertakings owned by the Government arc concerned, similar schemes were in vogue. It was found that the Public Enterprises had to use the available funds in their own enterprises and their internal resources were not large enough to meet the weeds of the employees for housing loans. At the same time, Financial Institutions were also granting loans for building houses but at a rate which was higher than the rate at which the Government was granting house building advances

At the same time, Financial Institutions were also granting loans for building houses but at a rate which was higher than the rate at which the Government was granting house building advances. The Ministry of Industry considered this situation and by icltcr dated 2 (37)/85/ BPE (WC) dated 12-11-1986 decided that the Public Enterprises should adopt a scheme of interest subsidy to pay the difference between the rate of interest charged by specialised agencies and the rate of interest charged by the Central Government under House Building Advance Rules. Consequently, large Public Sector Undertakings framed their own rules providing for granting subsidy to the employees who had taken loans from other Financial Institutions instead of being granted loans by the Public Sector Undertaking itself. The question whether the grant of house building advances at a rate of interest below the market rate is a perquisite had been debated and the view of the Government itself was that the statutory provisions did not treat it as aperquisite. Consequently, Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1984, introduced an amendment with effect from 1-4-1985 inserting sub-clause (vi) to include as a perquisite, the amount of interest where the loan is given interest free and the amount of difference between the interest charged and the notified rate where the loan is given at a rate less than the notified rate prescribed for Central Government House Building Advance. This generated an adverse reaction from the salaried class as it amounted to taking back by way of tax what is given as a welfare measure. Consequently, even before the amendment could take effect, the Finance Act, 19,85 withdrew the said amendment

Is interest subsidy part of "salary" as such : 16. The Revenue argued that the word "salary" being denned in an inclusive manner, any amount paid by the employer falls within its scope, whatever its character. He referred to various dictionaries to support this contention. The word "salary" as such is not defined in the Act. Words in a statute dealing with the matters relating to general public are presumed to be used in their popular sense. The Supreme Court observed in State of Orissa v. Titaghur Mills Co. Ltd., ." "The dictionary meaning of a word cannot be looked at where the word is statutorily defined or judicially interpreted

content: The Supreme Court observed in State of Orissa v. Titaghur Mills Co. Ltd., ." "The dictionary meaning of a word cannot be looked at where the word is statutorily defined or judicially interpreted. But when there is no such definition or interpretation, the Court may take aid of dictionaries to ascertain the meanings of a word in common parlance, bearing in mind that a word is used in different senses according to its context and the dictionary gives all the meanings of a word and the Court lias, therefore, to select a particular meaning which is relevant to the context in which it has to interpret the word." We find that the word "salary" according to Chambers Dictionary is: "A periodical payment (usually at longer intervals than a week) for services other than mechanical According to Ramanatha Iyer it is "Salary is a periodical allowance made as compensation to a person, for his official or professional services or for his regular work, an agreed compensation for services, payable at regular intervals; the periodical compensation due to men in official and other situations; an annual or periodical payment for services, a stipulated periodical recompense; a stipend wages; hire; an allowance. A fixed sum paid to a person for his services, yearly, half yearly, or quarterly; stipend; wages; annual or periodical wages or pay; hire; fixed regular wages, as by the year, quarter, or month. Salary is strictly an agreed compensation for service payable at regular intervals." 17. Hence, the common understanding is that it is the periodical payments and does not include other special payments even though they may be from an employer to an employee and also because of that relationship

Thus, the context itself shows that the meaning of the word 'salary' is confined to what in the popular parlance is the monthly payment for service rendered and cannot include interest subsidy. Is interest subsidy a perquisite under Section 17 (2)(iv) ? 18. The learned senior Standing Counsel for the Revenue sought to make a distinction between the cases where loans are given by the employer free of interest or at a lower rate of interest, from cases where the difference between interest paid by the employee to a Financial Institution and the rate of interest chargeable in respect of Central Government House Building Loan arc reimbursed to the employee. He cited the decision of the House of Lords in Owen v. The second case cited is the decision of the Madras High Court in C.I.T. v. C. On the contrary, in respect of actual cash payments, such as reimbursement of medical expenses, this Court held in C.I. T. v. Thus, the scheme of the Act did not envisage the addition of cash payment as a perquisite in the nature of the benefit or amenity. Is interest subsidy a profit in lieu of 'salary ? 20. The Revenue then sought to bring the interest subsidy within the expression of "profit in lieu of salary" in Section 17(3). hi this context, he cited Hochstrasser v. Mayes, 1960 AC 376, where the employee was compensated for the loss incurred by selling his house due to his company transferring him to another factory. The house of Lords held that though the fact that the employment was causa sine qua non, it was not causa causans of the payment, and therefore, the compensation was taxable. The context, however, is the provisions of Section 156(2) of the Income-tax Act 1952 in England where the tax is charged on the profits and gains arising from any office or employment. But the present context is quite different as can be seen by a plain reading of Section 17(3) itself This provision was intended only to apply to all terminal benefits, the idea being that the employers should not camouflage salary or profits in lieu of salary, as terminal benefits. The items mentioned, are therefore, items which are paid on the termination of employment and they are exempted to the extent that they actually relate to the terminal benefits, and therefore, capital receipts. The Revenue submitted that this view of the Section was not shared by this Court in the case of M. Krishna Murthy v, C.I.T.

content: actually relate to the terminal benefits, and therefore, capital receipts. The Revenue submitted that this view of the Section was not shared by this Court in the case of M. Krishna Murthy v, C.I.T.. 152 1TR 163, where it was pointed out that the House Rent Allowance exempted under Section 10 (13-A) is mentioned in this Section and such House Rent Allowance is not a terminal benefit, and therefore, it would otherwise fall within the ambit of definition of profits in lieu of salary. That observation was, however, made for the purpose of treating leave encashment as "profits in lieu of salary", to understand the scope of that expression. We notice that Section 13-A was introduced in Section 17(3) simultaneously with its introduction in Section 10. Obviously, the draftsmen wanted to ensure that if it is not otherwise exempt under Section 10, it would be taxable under Section 16, for which, instead of inserting in Section 17(1), it has been inserted in Section 17(3). Such a mistaken insertion for the purpose of exclusion, cannot, in our considered opinion, change the meaning of the expression 'profit in lieu of salary'. Salary itself has been defined in Blacks Dictionary 'as a reward for recompense for services performed. In a more limited sense, a fixed compensation paid for services rendered. A stated compensation paid periodically as by the year, month, or other fixed period, in contrast to wages which are normally based on an hourly rate.' It is obvious that interest subsidy is not a reward or a periodically payment for services rendered. Nor is it paid in lieu of salary

content: in contrast to wages which are normally based on an hourly rate.' It is obvious that interest subsidy is not a reward or a periodically payment for services rendered. Nor is it paid in lieu of salary. We are, therefore, convinced that the interest subsidy which was given as a welfare measure to treat the employees of Public Sector Undertakings on par with the Central Government servants was never intended to be taxed. Is interest subsidy a perquisite as such ? 21. It was then argued that interest subsidy may be a perquisite as commonly understood without reference to the sub-clauses of Section 17(2) just as in the case of salary, the definition of 'perquisite' in Section 17(2) is an inclusive definition. It is, therefore, necessary to ascertain the popular meaning of that word. Chambers Dictionary gives the meaning as : "A casual profit anything left over that a servant or other has by custom a right to keep : a tip expected upon some occasions." Ramanatha Iyer gives the meaning as : "Perquisites. 'Perquisites means emolument, fee or profit attached to the office or position of an addition to salary or wages." 22. Therefore, one possible view is that interest subsidy is a perquisite because the employee gets it only because of his employment as incidental to his service conditions. But, the same benefit given indirectly has not been treated as a perquisite by the Revenue. If the employer takes a loan at a higher rate and advances it to the employee at a lower rate of interest, the difference is admittedly not treated as a perquisite. But where the loan is taken by the employee and the difference is reimbursed to the employee, it is sought to be treated as a perquisite. The Revenue submitted that the form makes a difference to the substance

So when it is not taken as a perquisite in the first situation, it has to be considered in the same way in the second situation as otherwise it will be discriminatory. B. Writ not a proper remedy : 26. It was then submitted that since it is the individual employees who are liable to tax, the proper remedy for them is to file a return and get a refund after adjudicating the issue whether the interest subsidy is taxable or not. He submitted that by filing the writ petition, the Revenue is denied the opportunity of properly adjudicating the issue after verifying the facts such as whether there is a scheme in the company for giving interest subsidy and the terms thereof. This is actually the crux of the case, namely, that the person, who is ultimately liable to pay the tax, is not given an opportunity to contest the liability before the tax is levied by deduction of tax at source. The alternative remedy can be an application for certificate under Section 197. But this will involve a great burden on the Income-tax Officer if thousands of employees were to make applications for such certificates as each employee has to make such individual applications. The burden is now placed on the employer to decide whether a particular amount paid is taxable or not and in view of the attitude of the Department with reference to Section 201, the employer is bound to decide the issues against the employees

In this case, itself we could see that having failed in the appeal against the order under Section 201, the employer indicated the intention to deduct the tax at source thus deciding the issue against the person liable to pay the tax. The remedy suggested by the Revenue that after deduction, the employee should file a return and seek refund would again involve thousands of appeals and long delay in granting refund by which a section of salaried class will be deprived of a portion of the salary due to them for a considerable time without any recompense. The scheme of deduction of tax at source is intended to be of benefit to the tax payer as well, apart from regularly collecting the tax painlessly.
